posts.title: From Cart to Confirmation: Checkout Orchestration
posts.question: What happens between "add to cart" and "order confirmed", and why do platforms restrict what merchants may change in checkout?

know: The difference between a cart (a draft that reserves and promises nothing), checkout (a clocked sequence that asks for final answers) and the order (the record the rest of the platform must keep).
What checkout calls, in what order, and how fresh each answer must be.
The four ways to run a checkout, and the mechanisms through which platforms let merchants change it.
believe: Checkout should own none of the facts it writes into the order.
The payment provider's signed message, not the thank-you page, decides that a payment succeeded.
can_do: Draw their own checkout's call sequence and say which answers come from copies.
Judge a proposal to customize checkout by its mechanism and by the vendor's support date for that mechanism.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a shopper who pays in her bank's app and never returns, and a payment notification delivered twice, the reader says when the order is created, what marks it paid and why the repeat changes nothing.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A shopper pays by iDEAL in her bank's app and never returns to the shop; the payment provider's notification then arrives twice. Using only this chapter: when should the order have been created, what marks it paid, and what does the second notification do?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The order is created at confirmation with the payment pending, keyed on the cart and the payment (an idempotency key), not on the thank-you page; the provider's signed webhook moves it to paid; the second webhook changes nothing because its event is recognized as already applied; a daily job asks the provider about orders still pending after the method's expiry window.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a checkout that kept selling a product the warehouse no longer had, the reader places the fault in the system that answered the availability call, not in checkout.
acceptance_criteria.probe: On a peak evening the checkout kept selling a jacket for up to two hours after the warehouse ran out. Using only this chapter: where was the fault, and is the fix in the checkout?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Checkout trusted the availability answer it was given, which came from the platform's copy of stock refreshed up to two hours earlier; checkout owns no stock figure. The fix is in who answers the availability call at order creation (a current answer from an availability service, W1), not in checkout.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given an agency's proposal to inject a script into the checkout, the reader names the sanctioned alternative and the two risks of the script.
acceptance_criteria.probe: An agency proposes to add a gift-wrap option by injecting a script into the checkout's payment page. Using only this chapter: what should the merchant do instead, and why?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Use a sanctioned extension point of the platform, which runs with a time limit and is versioned. A third-party script on the payment page falls under the card industry's script rules (PCI DSS) and can read every card number typed there, and a mechanism outside the sanctioned ones is withdrawn on a date the vendor announces (Shopify's checkout.liquid and Scripts); keep an inventory of each customization, its mechanism and the vendor's support date.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Why a price, the last unit or the payment answer can change while the shopper checks out; what checkout must call and how it creates one order despite retries; Eva's checkout as the worked example; four ways to run checkout; Shopify's 2023–2026 changes as the case for limits on customization. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's checkout, vendor documentation, Shopify's dated changelog.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: What happens between "add to cart" and "order confirmed", and why do platforms restrict what merchants may change in checkout?
thesis.claim: Between 'add to cart' and 'order confirmed', checkout asks each system that owns a fact for a final answer (price, tax, availability, delivery promise, payment), writes those answers into the order and creates the order exactly once, keyed on the cart and the payment rather than on a page load, leaving the payment provider's signed message, not the thank-you page, to mark it paid. Platforms restrict merchant changes to named extension points with time limits because every order passes through checkout: merchant code there can delay or fail order creation at peak, a script on the payment page can read the card numbers typed into it, and a template the merchant edits cannot follow the platform's upgrades.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that checkout is the storefront's last few pages, which a merchant or its agency may edit like any other page, and that the order exists, paid, once the shopper reaches the thank-you page.
thesis.so_what: Kestrel & Pine's checkout kept selling the Ridgewalker jacket for up to two hours after Duiven ran out on Black Friday 2026 because checkout wrote the answer of an out-of-date stock copy into each order and the warehouse could not keep those orders; the fix is to have a current availability service answer that call, not to change checkout. A merchant that accepts the claim lists what its checkout calls and which answers come from copies, creates orders keyed on the cart and the payment and settles them by webhook and a daily job, and customizes checkout only through sanctioned extension points listed with the vendor's support date; Shopify withdrew editable checkout templates and scripts on dated deadlines between August 2024 and August 2026.
thesis.how_why: The warehouse, finance and the customer all act on what checkout writes into the order, so a stale price or stock figure written there becomes their error. The shopper leaves for her bank's app or a 3-D Secure challenge and may not come back, and the provider's webhook arrives late, out of order or twice, so an order created on the thank-you page can be lost and one created per request without a key can be duplicated. Checkout carries every order at peak load and its payment page falls under the card industry's script rules, so code the platform cannot limit in time or isolate puts every order at risk; and the platform ships its own checkout changes (new payment methods, compliance fixes) into its template, so a merchant's edited copy misses them. Webhooks can also stop arriving, so a daily job asks the provider about every order still pending.

role.contribution: Shows the moment the catalog's answers become an order and introduces the two mechanisms the rest of the part relies on: the payment provider's message as the only source of the payment's outcome, and the key that makes a repeated request harmless.

transition_in.carries_over: The part's relay of one order through four owners, which starts at checkout.
transition_in.introduces: What checkout calls, in what order, and how it creates the order exactly once.

posts.title: Taking the Money: Payment Providers, Authorization, Capture and Refunds
posts.question: How does money move from the shopper to the merchant, and what can go wrong?

know: The parties to a payment (shopper, issuer, scheme, acquirer, payment provider) and its four stages: authorization, capture, settlement, payout; refunds and chargebacks as payments flowing back.
How payment methods differ by country (iDEAL, Bancontact, PayPal and purchase on account) and what each difference changes in the design.
What strong customer authentication, 3-D Secure, the liability shift and PCI DSS scope require of the payment design.
believe: Only the payment provider knows whether money moved; the order records the provider's confirmed outcome in its own small payment vocabulary.
A refund is a new payment, not an undo, and needs one writer and one key.
can_do: Name, for their own company, every system that holds a credential to refund, capture or create a payment, and the business key each request carries.
Say what a daily payment reconciliation compares and what it finds.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given returns refunded twice by two systems, the reader explains why the provider accepted the second refund and names the three controls that prevent it, before naming a new provider.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A returns portal refunds customers after inspection; support agents can also refund in the payment provider's console. Over three weeks some 200 returns are refunded twice. Using only this chapter: why did the provider accept the second refund, and what prevents it?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Two systems could refund and neither request carried a key naming the return, so the provider saw two valid requests. The controls: one writer per money action (the returns portal through the platform, the console read-only for everyone else); the return id as the refund's idempotency key; a daily comparison of the provider's refunds with the refunds the platform recorded. Not a new provider.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a card order shipped after its authorization window, the reader says what happens to the money and what should have prevented it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A shop takes card payments and captures them when the order ships. The warehouse ships one order on day eight after the purchase. Using only this chapter: what happens to the payment, and what should have been in place?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The authorization (valid about seven days for the major card schemes) has expired, so the funds were released and the capture fails; the parcel leaves unpaid. Capture at label print, an alert when an authorized order nears its window uncaptured, and a fulfillment hold when the window is close; a later charge needs a merchant-initiated transaction.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say why a card payment design cannot be reused unchanged for iDEAL.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: why can a Dutch shop not reuse its card payment design unchanged for iDEAL?
acceptance_criteria.expected: iDEAL is an instant, irrevocable transfer from the shopper's bank with no separate capture and no chargeback, and a 15-minute session; a refund is a new transfer back. A card is authorized, then captured inside a window, and can be disputed. A design that assumes one method's stages breaks on the other.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Why the shop's own page does not tell it whether money was reserved, collected or is still pending; payment providers, reserving and collecting money, customer authentication, payment notifications and refunds; Eva's iDEAL payment followed to payout, and a refund. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's payments, payment-provider documentation, EU payment law.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: How does money move from the shopper to the merchant, and what can go wrong?
thesis.claim: Money moves in four stages that the merchant only requests and the shopper's bank, the card or bank scheme and the payment provider carry out: authorization reserves the amount, capture takes it, settlement moves it between banks, and payout pays the merchant net batches on the provider's schedule, typically one per sales day; a refund or a chargeback is a new payment in the opposite direction, and each payment method changes the stages (an iDEAL payment is taken at once and cannot be charged back; a card authorization expires after about seven days). The failures that land on the merchant's own systems are acting on an outcome it did not see or moving money twice: an order marked paid or unpaid without the provider's confirmed message, a capture attempted after the authorization has expired, and one refund sent by two systems with no shared key.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that payments are the payment provider's concern: once a provider is integrated, 'paid' is a flag set at checkout, a refund is an undo anyone with console access may perform, and the main payment decision is which provider to use or whether to add a second one.
thesis.so_what: Kestrel & Pine refunded 212 returns twice in January 2027, €19,400, because the returns portal and support in the provider's console could both refund and neither request carried a key; bank-transfer refunds could not be recalled. Its fix was one writer, the return id as the key and a daily comparison, not a new provider. A merchant that accepts the claim lists who holds a credential to move money and with what key before it compares providers, and keeps one provider with that discipline until volume, countries or resilience require more.
thesis.how_why: The issuer and the provider decide whether money moved and report it by webhook, which arrives at least once, in no guaranteed order, and stops retrying after 26 hours (Mollie) or three days (Stripe), so only the provider's record, fetched when the decision matters, and a daily job for pending payments give the order the true state. A provider executes every valid request it receives; a refund that names only an order and an amount cannot be recognized as a repeat, whereas a request carrying the return id as its idempotency key returns the first result. An authorization lapses on the issuer's clock whatever the order's status, so a capture must be scheduled against that deadline; and each method fixes its own windows, so a design built on one method's stages misses another's deadlines.

role.contribution: Follows the money the order is waiting for through stages the merchant does not control and makes the single writer and the business key the rule for every action that moves money.

transition_in.carries_over: The order created with its payment pending, and the payment provider's webhook as the only source of the payment's outcome.
transition_in.introduces: The money's own life after checkout: the four stages, the methods that change them, and refunds and chargebacks as payments flowing back.

posts.title: The Order Record: Lifecycle, State and the Order Management System
posts.question: Where does the order live once it is placed, what states does it pass through, and when does a merchant need an order management system (OMS)?

know: What an order record holds (header, lines, money, promises, goods, references) and why the order number is the key for creating the order in every other system.
The order's three status lines (money, goods per shipment, returns) and how the status the customer sees is computed from them.
Routing, split shipments and backorders, and what an order management system holds and what it leaves to the shop platform and the ERP.
believe: A single status word on an order hides facts that systems need, and is a fault, not a simplification.
The order's home is chosen by which system must answer the customer's question about a parcel.
can_do: Decide whether a merchant needs an OMS by checking four conditions.
Say what a split order's status should read and what the customer should be told.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a two-parcel order whose systems show three different statuses, the reader says what the order should have shown and which design decision was missing.
acceptance_criteria.probe: An order for a fleece and socks ships the fleece first; the socks wait for replenishment. The shop shows 'Delivered', the warehouse 'In picking' and the ERP 'Not invoiced'. Using only this chapter: what should the order have shown, and what was missing in its design?
acceptance_criteria.expected: 'Partially delivered: 1 of 2 parcels' (and 'ships in two parcels' to the customer): the goods status is held per shipment and the summary is taken from the least-advanced shipment. The design had one status word, so the first parcel's delivery marked the whole order delivered, and no one system held the order across the platform, the warehouse and the ERP.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a merchant's channels and locations, the reader decides whether it needs an OMS by the four conditions and says why an OMS rather than the ERP holds the order.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A merchant sells through its own web shop and a marketplace and ships from two warehouses. A vendor offers it an OMS. Using only this chapter: does it need an order hub, and should that hub be the ERP or an OMS?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Yes: two of the four conditions hold (several channels create orders; several locations fulfil them), so one system must be the order's home. An OMS rather than the ERP, because the hub must route lines between the warehouses and answer a customer's question about a parcel, which a finance system running in batches cannot. Not decided by revenue.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say what happens when support cancels an order that has already shipped.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Support 'cancels' an order that has already shipped. Using only this chapter: what should happen instead?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A shipped order cannot be canceled; the cancellation becomes a return (return label, receipt, inspection, refund on receipt), a compensating step the order system coordinates. Edits lock once the warehouse has accepted the work.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Why a single 'shipped' status misleads when the parts of an order move separately; what an order record holds; its separate states; routing and split shipments; where the order should live and when an OMS is needed. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's Three-Status Order and its order-hub decision, platform and OMS vendor documentation.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: Where does the order live once it is placed, what states does it pass through, and when does a merchant need an order management system (OMS)?
thesis.claim: Once placed, an order should live in one system that holds it as one record, under one order number, with three separate status lines (money: authorized, paid, refunded, moved by the payment provider's events; goods: requested, accepted, shipped, delivered, held per shipment and moved by the warehouse and the carrier; returns: requested, received, inspected, refunded or exchanged) and computes the status the customer sees from all its shipments, so that the order reads delivered only when every parcel has been delivered. While one channel creates orders and one location fulfils them, that system is the shop platform; a merchant needs an OMS as the order's home once at least two of four conditions hold (several channels create orders, several locations fulfil them, promises depend on the location, service agents cannot see one order across systems), because an OMS, unlike the ERP, can route lines between locations and answer a customer's question about a parcel.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that an order has one status in whichever system took it, kept in step with the others by connectors, and that an OMS is a product for large retailers, needed by revenue or order volume rather than by how many systems create and fulfil orders.
thesis.so_what: Order #1052877 read 'Delivered' in the platform, 'In picking' in the warehouse and 'Not invoiced' in the ERP while the customer had a fleece and no socks, and produced 11 support tickets; with goods status per shipment it would have read 'Partially delivered: 1 of 2 parcels'. Kestrel & Pine meets all four conditions, so under W2 it makes a bought OMS the order hub, with the platform keeping the checkout and the ERP the books. A merchant that accepts the claim counts its order sources and fulfilling locations and names the order's home before it buys anything.
thesis.how_why: Money, goods and returns are changed by different systems at different times (the payment provider, the warehouse and the carrier per parcel, the returns portal), so one status word lets the latest message overwrite the others: one parcel's delivery scan marked a two-parcel order delivered. Every system that copies the order receives it at least once, so the copies stay one order only through one number family with the order number as the key. With one channel and one location the platform's record sees every change; with several sources, each with its own connector to the warehouse and the books, no system sees the whole order; one condition alone can be handled by the platform plus a connector, but two make the joins between systems the problem, and choosing which location ships which line needs rules over stock, capacity, cut-off times and cost that the platforms' priority and distance rules do not hold. The ERP holds the financial record and runs in batches, so it cannot answer a parcel question.

role.contribution: Gives the order one home and separate status lines, so that the payment outcome, each parcel and each return are kept without overwriting each other, and supplies the per-shipment record the ledger chapter invoices from.

transition_in.carries_over: The order marked paid by the payment provider's confirmed message, with the money's status kept in the order's own payment vocabulary.
transition_in.introduces: The rest of the order's life after 'paid': the goods and returns that move on their own status lines, the systems that hold copies of the order, and which of them is its home.

posts.title: Tax, Invoices and the Books: From Order to Ledger
posts.question: How does an order become tax, an invoice and entries in the books, and what does the commerce system owe finance?

know: The three outcomes the commerce system owes finance (the right tax, a valid invoice, books that match the bank) and the documents that carry them, each with its owning system.

The VAT rules that decide a rate: destination rates above the €10,000 One Stop Shop threshold, the reverse charge for EU business buyers with a valid VAT number, and tax-inclusive against tax-exclusive prices.
The ledger entries for a consumer order paid through a payment provider, and why Kestrel & Pine recognizes revenue for goods at delivery.
believe: The shop issues order confirmations; one system per legal entity issues invoices.
Nothing posts to the ledger from a webhook; the ledger is fed from documents.
can_do: Split a tax-inclusive consumer total into net and VAT.
Name the daily and monthly checks that prove the orders, the payouts and the bank agree.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given an order shipped in two parcels and invoiced only on 'order complete', the reader names what goes wrong and the invoicing rule that prevents it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: An order of two items ships in two parcels a week apart; the ERP issues the invoice only when the warehouse reports the whole order complete. Using only this chapter: what goes wrong, and what is the rule?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The invoice waits for the slowest line, so a shipped (and delivered) parcel stays uninvoiced for days. Invoice per shipment at dispatch, keyed on the shipment id, with a daily list of shipped orders that have no invoice.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a return of an invoiced and paid item, the reader names the documents that follow and says the invoice is not changed.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A customer's €199 jacket was invoiced and paid; she returns it for a refund. Using only this chapter: which documents follow, and may the invoice be changed?
acceptance_criteria.expected: No: an issued invoice is immutable. A credit note with its own sequential number, referencing the invoice, reverses the jacket line (net and VAT); the refund, sent by the one refund writer, references both, and the three reconcile to zero; the refund appears as a deduction in a later payout.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say why a payout differs from a day's sales and how finance shows that nothing is missing.
acceptance_criteria.probe: The payment provider's payout for one sales day is smaller than that day's sales. Using only this chapter: why, and how does finance show that nothing is missing?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The payout is net of fees and of refunds and chargebacks from earlier days, and arrives days later. Finance matches it line by line, using the order number passed to the provider and the batch or trace reference on the bank line, and posts fees from the report; matching totals only cannot find a missing line.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Why the amount reaching the bank differs from what the customer paid; following the VAT in Eva's order into the ERP; a Belgian wholesale invoice over Peppol; tax, invoices, credit notes, ledger entries and reconciliation. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's month-end close, EU and national tax rules, payment-provider and ERP documentation.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: How does an order become tax, an invoice and entries in the books, and what does the commerce system owe finance?
thesis.claim: An order becomes tax, an invoice and ledger entries through documents, not events: the tax is computed from three facts the shop owns (the ship-to address, the product's tax category, and whether the buyer is a consumer or a VAT-registered business) under rates kept in one place for every channel; the invoice is issued at dispatch for each shipment by one system per legal entity, numbered in one consecutive series, never edited and corrected only by a credit note that references it; and the ledger is posted from invoices, credit notes and the payment provider's payout reports. The commerce system owes finance the facts and identifiers those documents need (the tax basis frozen on the order, a shipment confirmation carrying the shipment id, the buyer references an e-invoice must carry, the order number passed to the payment provider, refunds from one writer), so that a monthly match of invoices, payouts and bank lines explains each difference.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that the shop platform's order confirmation is the invoice, that tax is a rate the platform adds at checkout, and that the books can be posted from the platform's payment events as they arrive, with differences found by comparing monthly totals.
thesis.so_what: Order #1052877 sat 'Not invoiced' for six days because the invoice waited for an 'order complete' message that a short pick prevented and no report listed shipped orders without an invoice; the Double Refund's second refund referenced no credit note; Ardennes Trail Co. rejected a Peppol invoice for a buyer reference the B2B portal never asked for. A merchant that accepts the claim makes the ERP the only invoice issuer, invoices per shipment and builds the shipped-not-invoiced list and the refunds-against-credit-notes job first, before an OMS or a PIM.
thesis.how_why: Rates depend on the destination country, the product category and the buyer's status, and change, so rates kept in several channels drift apart. A tax basis recomputed after the address or a rate changes no longer matches what the customer was shown, so the basis is frozen on the order and any difference listed. For goods the supply happens at dispatch, per shipment, so an invoice that waits for the whole order waits for the slowest line. The law requires a consecutive number unique to each invoice and an issued invoice kept unchanged for years, which only one issuing system per legal entity can guarantee. Where two systems can refund, both can refund the same return, so refunds come from one writer. A payout nets payments, refunds, fees and chargebacks from different days, so it never equals a day's sales and can be matched only line by line on identifiers carried from the order.

role.contribution: Follows the order into the documents that finance and the tax authorities rely on, extends the one-writer and key rules to invoices and credit notes, and performs the part's closing (the published chapter does not yet do so: it ends with the hand-off to Part IV only).

transition_in.carries_over: The order with one home, one number and its goods status per shipment, accepted by the warehouse.
transition_in.introduces: The tax it carries, the invoice each shipment produces and the entries those documents post in the books.

parts.title: Part IV — FULFILLMENT: From Warehouse to Doorstep and Back

know: The systems that witness Part IV's physical facts and what each writes: the warehouse system (on-hand stock, shipment confirmations, its cut-off, capacity and backlog), the carrier (scans of the parcel), the store's till (store stock and store sales) and the returns bench (the disposition of what came back).

How the order record instructs the place that does the work through a fulfillment order it accepts or rejects, and why the shipping status the customer sees is derived from carrier events mapped to one small vocabulary.
believe: A delivery date, a collection time or a refund is a promise computed from, or released by, an event of the system on the spot, not a sentence on a page or a status set by another system.
Notifications, the status page and the agent's screen must read one order record; a difference between them is a defect that reaches the customer as a contact.
can_do: For one order at their own company, name the system that witnesses each physical fact (stock on the shelf, the parcel's whereabouts, store stock, what came back), the event each customer-facing promise or message reads, the single writer of each refund and restock, and the measure that would show a broken promise.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every supporting claim of the part thesis is argued by at least one chapter, and every chapter supports at least one.
Each chapter's closing hand-off expresses the relationship its successor declares in transition_in.

Given four broken promises after checkout, a reader who has read only Part IV names for each the fact that was taken from a copy or a sentence instead of from the system that witnessed it, or the action two systems could take, before naming a faster warehouse, a new till or more support staff.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A shop's page says 'ordered before 22:00, delivered tomorrow' while on a busy evening orders reach the warehouse three hours late; a store-collection order is promised from last night's copy of store stock and the item is gone; a customer is refunded by support after the tracking shows the return 'delivered to warehouse' and again by the returns portal after inspection; a two-parcel order reads 'Delivered' after the first parcel. Using only Part IV: what was missing in each case?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The promise was a sentence, not computed from the warehouse's cut-off and backlog (a queue whose age moves the cut-off); store stock was promised from a nightly copy with no per-store buffer and no staff confirmation before 'ready' (store stock should reach availability as events from the till); two systems could refund, the refund was released by a carrier scan rather than the warehouse's disposition, and the requests carried no return id as key; the order had one status word instead of goods state per shipment, so nothing emitted 'ships in two parcels' and the page and the agent did not read one record. Not 'a faster warehouse', 'a new POS' or 'more agents' alone.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The page that carries the part's closing sets the part's incidents against the opening's order confirmed in seconds and still to be picked, and states what they have in common; it does not only hand off to Part V.

thesis.question: Once the order is placed, how are the promises made about it (a delivery date, a collection, a return and its refund, the status the customer sees) kept?
thesis.claim: Promises about a placed order are kept only where each physical fact has one system that witnesses and writes it (the warehouse system, the store's till, the carrier, the returns bench) and that applies each instruction once, as a keyed request it accepts or rejects; where each promise is computed from that system's events or released by its confirmation; and where the customer and the service agent read one status built from those events.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that fulfillment is operations' work rather than architecture: once checkout has taken the order and the money, promises are kept by enough pickers, reliable carriers and helpful agents, and the storefront's delivery sentence, the shop platform's order status and its default refund flow are enough.
thesis.so_what: Kestrel & Pine's four Part IV incidents were promises made without the witness's facts or acted on by more than one system: the Queue That Waited (roughly 8,000 Black Friday orders missed next-day delivery while the page promised it), the Store Stock Mirage (37 collection items already sold), the Double Refund (212 returns, €19,400) and the Three-Status Order (11 tickets). A merchant that accepts the claim names the witness and the writer of each physical fact, and the event each promise reads, before it buys a faster warehouse, a new till or more service capacity.
thesis.how_why: The storefront promises in seconds; the physical work happens hours or days later in buildings and vans the order record cannot see, and its facts (an empty pick location, a unit sold at the till, a parcel scan, a worn jacket on the bench) are known first by the system on the spot and reach the others by message, late or twice. A promise read from a copy or a static sentence is wrong whenever the copy lags or the queue grows; a status set by one integration overwrites what others know; and an action that two systems can take, such as a refund, is taken twice.

supporting_claims.claim: Each physical fact has one system that witnesses it and is its only writer: the warehouse system for on-hand stock at the warehouse, the till for store stock and store sales, the carrier's scans for the parcel's whereabouts and the returns bench's disposition for what came back; every other system holds a copy fed by that system's events.

The order record instructs the place that does the work through a fulfillment order that the place accepts or rejects and that carries a key, so a repeated instruction creates no second pick; after acceptance a cancellation or an edit is a request the place answers, and self-service and agents' actions check that state first.

A promise about time or place is computed from the warehouse's cut-off, capacity and backlog, the stock's location and the carrier's measured transit time per lane, with a buffer and a margin, and a promise against store stock becomes a commitment only when a person at the store confirms it.

On the way back, the warehouse's disposition is the event that releases the refund and the restock, and one system issues the refund with the return id as its key, whether the return started in the portal, at a store counter or on a marketplace.

The customer and the agent see one status, derived from these events and kept in one order record as separate goods (per shipment), money and return states; the notifications, the status page and the agent's view are read models over that record.

role.contribution: Shows the keeping side of the promise: warehouse, delivery, stores, returns and service.

additional_patterns.applies_to: warehouse-and-fulfillment, shipping-and-delivery and returns-and-exchanges: Eva's jacket out and back (picked at Duiven on 14 April 2027, delivered on 15 April, returned for size L from 19 to 22 April); stores-and-omnichannel sits between delivery and return as the alternative routes for the same order; customer-service-and-notifications spans 13 to 22 April

flow.rationale: Each chapter uses what the one before it fixed. The warehouse comes first because it defines the fulfillment order, the warehouse system as the writer of on-hand stock, and the cut-off, capacity and backlog; the shipping chapter computes the delivery promise from those three and adds the carrier's events and one vocabulary for them; the stores chapter reuses the fulfillment order, labels and carrier pickup for ship-from-store and the computed promise for collection, and adds the till as a second witness of stock and orders; the returns chapter needs the carrier's 'delivered' event, which starts the 14-day clock, the warehouse's receiving and stock events, and the store-return rule the stores chapter set, and adds the returns bench's disposition as the witness of what came back; the service chapter comes last because its messages, status page and agent view read the events every earlier chapter defined. Putting shipping before the warehouse would ask the reader to compute a promise from a cut-off and backlog not yet explained; putting stores before shipping would describe ship-from-store and the collection promise before labels, carrier pickup and the computed promise exist; putting returns before stores would leave its store-return section pointing forward; putting service earlier would describe messages for events whose emitters the reader has not met and would leave the part without the chapter that joins its events into one status.

hook.content: Checkout confirms an order in seconds, but someone still has to pick and pack the goods before the carrier's collection, and a late instruction or an empty shelf can push delivery back a day.

opening.bridge: From the confirmation the shopper sees in seconds to the physical work that follows over days, in a warehouse, a van, a store and on a returns bench; and to Eva's jacket: bought on 13 April 2027, picked and packed at Duiven on 14 April, delivered on 15 April, a day later than promised, size L requested on 19 April, the return inspected and the replacement shipped on 22 April, with store pickup and a counter exchange as the alternative routes.
opening.roadmap: Five chapters: the work instruction and response between order management and the warehouse (the Queue That Waited, a four-hour Black Friday backlog); carrier integration and credible delivery dates (Eva promised Wednesday and delivered Thursday); a step aside from Eva's parcel to the alternative routes through a store, with the till as another source of orders, stock and customer records (Utrecht's 37 items already sold); the return request, inspection, stock decision and money movement as separate states with owners (Eva's exchange, the 212 double refunds); messages, the status page and the support view built from shared facts (eleven tickets and the missing 'ships in two parcels').

closing.synthesis: The Queue That Waited, Eva's Wednesday promise, the Store Stock Mirage, the Double Refund and the eleven tickets look like five problems in five places: the warehouse feed, the storefront's text, store stock, refunds and support. Read together they are one: a promise or a status taken from a copy or a sentence instead of from the system that witnessed the physical fact, or an action two systems could take. Each chapter's remedy has the same parts: name the witness, compute the promise from its events and let a confirmation or a disposition commit it, give each money or stock action one writer and a key, and build one status from the same events.
closing.so_what: Kestrel & Pine's remedies are contracts and rules more than buildings or tills: a queue allowed to grow and a cut-off that moves with it, a transit table plus the warehouse's cut-off and backlog measured per lane, a two-unit store threshold and a staff confirmation, refund on disposition by one writer keyed on the return id, and the helpdesk pointed at the order hub. A reader can list, for their own operation, which system witnesses each physical fact and which promise reads it.
closing.callback: The part opening's order confirmed in seconds whose goods still have to be picked and packed before the carrier's collection.

takeaway.content: For each promise your shop makes after checkout (delivery date, collection, refund, order status), name the system that witnesses the fact it depends on, the event that carries that fact, and the measure that shows when the promise broke; start with promised-versus-delivered per lane and contacts per split shipment.

transition_in.carries_over: The order record and the payment taken.
transition_in.introduces: The physical work that has to match the record: picking, shipping, delivery and the way back.

posts.title: Part 4 introduction
posts.question: What does this part argue, and in what order should its chapters be read?

know: Part IV answers five questions in order: what the warehouse system must receive and report, how carriers are connected and a delivery date computed, what a store adds and how its cross-channel services work, how a return moves money and stock, and how the customer and the agent learn the order's status.
After checkout, the physical facts (stock on the shelf, the parcel's whereabouts, store stock, what came back) are known first by the system on the spot.
can_do: Pick the Part IV chapter that answers the decision in front of them.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of this page alone can name the five chapters' subjects in reading order.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only this page: what will each of the next five chapters tell you, in order?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The instruction and response between order management and the warehouse; carrier integration and credible delivery dates; the store's till as a source of orders, stock and customer records; the return request, inspection, stock decision and refund as separate steps with owners; notifications, the status page and the support view built from shared facts.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of this page alone can say why a shop can promise 'tomorrow' and deliver a day later although nobody was slow.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: why was Eva promised Wednesday and delivered Thursday, and what should the promise have been based on?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A static storefront rule ignored the warehouse's timing: her order came after the last dispatch work of the day. The promise should be computed from the warehouse's collection schedule and backlog, the stock's location and the carrier's performance, not written as a sentence.

role.contribution: Performs the part's opening: states the part thesis, places the part on Eva's jacket from Duiven on 14 April 2027 to the exchange shipped on 22 April, and gives the reading order.

posts.title: Pick, Pack, Ship: Warehouse Management and Fulfillment
posts.question: What happens to an order inside the warehouse, and what must the warehouse system receive from, and report to, the rest of the platform?

know: The warehouse steps (receiving, put-away, slotting, wave or continuous release, picking, packing, shipping confirmation, cycle counting) and what each changes; where automation and robots sit beneath the warehouse system.

The fulfillment order and its lifecycle (requested, accepted or rejected, in progress, shipped, closed incomplete, with cancellation as a request), the warehouse's four interfaces, and the four ways to get warehouse execution (ERP module, dedicated WMS, 3PL, marketplace fulfillment program).
Why the SSCC label and the despatch advice (DESADV) are generated from pack confirmation.
believe: The warehouse system is the only writer of on-hand stock; every other system derives from its events.
Whether an order ships on time depends on when it reaches the warehouse and on the cut-off and backlog, not only on how fast people pick.
can_do: Specify the platform-to-WMS integration: what the fulfillment order carries, its key, the accept-or-reject answer, cancellation after acceptance, shipment confirmations, stock events and the reconciliation behind them.
Say which warehouse facts (cut-off, capacity, backlog) the delivery promise must read.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a peak evening on which orders reached an adequately staffed warehouse hours late, the reader places the fault in the order feed and the promise, not in the warehouse, and names the four remedies.
acceptance_criteria.probe: On a peak evening the warehouse had staff to spare, but orders placed at 20:00 reached the warehouse system after midnight while the storefront kept promising next-day delivery for orders before 22:00. Using only this chapter: where was the fault, and what would have prevented it?
acceptance_criteria.expected: In the order feed into the warehouse system, which created orders one at a time with several calls each and was throttled by the vendor's rate limit, and in a promise that did not read the queue; the warehouse was never the limit. A queue allowed to grow without failing checkout, order creation in batches within the rate limit, a monitor on the age of the oldest unprocessed order, and a cut-off that moves when that age grows. Not a faster warehouse or more pickers.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a duplicated instruction and a late cancellation, the reader says what the fulfillment-order contract does in each case.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A timeout makes the integration send the same order to the warehouse twice; the next morning support cancels another order in the shop after the warehouse had already accepted it. Using only this chapter: what should happen in each case?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The fulfillment order carries an identity (an idempotency key), so the warehouse system recognizes the repeat and reuses the existing instruction: no second pick list, no second jacket. After acceptance a cancellation is a request that the warehouse answers; if picking has started it is rejected, the order stays in progress, support tells the customer, and the item comes back as a return.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say which system must generate the pallet label and the despatch advice for a retail customer, and from what.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A retail customer deducts money because the pallet labels do not match the despatch advice it received. Using only this chapter: which system should generate the SSCC label and the DESADV, and from what?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The warehouse system, at pack time, from what was actually packed (the pack confirmation), never from the order or the ERP's view of it; Kestrel & Pine's W6 moves both there after the €14,200 ASN Chargeback.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Why a missing unit or a late instruction becomes a delivery problem; what a warehouse system does from picking to shipping, and where automation and robots fit; the fulfillment order the warehouse receives and its acceptance step; the warehouse as owner of the physical stock count; cut-off, capacity and work release as inputs to the delivery promise; Eva's order at Duiven on 14 April. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's Duiven warehouse and vendor documentation.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: What happens to an order inside the warehouse, and what must the warehouse system receive from, and report to, the rest of the platform?
thesis.claim: Inside the warehouse an order becomes work that is released, picked, packed and confirmed as a shipment within the building's capacity and before the carrier's collection. The warehouse system must receive a fulfillment order it can accept or reject, carrying only what to ship and a key, so that a retried request creates no second pick list. As the only writer of on-hand stock, it must report shipment confirmations built from what was packed, every stock change as an event, and its cut-off, capacity and backlog.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that 'send the order to the WMS' is the whole specification: the warehouse receives the order as the shop holds it, any system may correct stock figures, and on-time dispatch is a matter of warehouse staffing and speed.
thesis.so_what: On Black Friday 2026 Duiven had the staff, but orders took four hours to reach its warehouse system and roughly 8,000 orders placed between 17:00 and midnight missed next-day delivery while the storefront promised it; the remedy was a queue, batches, a monitor on the oldest order and a moving cut-off, not a faster warehouse. Bergzicht deducted €14,200 because the despatch advice was built from the ERP's order rather than from what was packed. A merchant that accepts the claim writes the fulfillment-order contract, names the one writer of on-hand stock and feeds the cut-off to the promise before it buys a WMS, a 3PL or robots.
thesis.how_why: Physical work cannot be undone by changing a status: once the warehouse has accepted an instruction, picking may have started, so a cancellation needs the warehouse's answer. Prices, payments and customer history change for reasons the warehouse cannot act on and add data it must protect, so the instruction carries only what to ship. A request retried after a timeout arrives twice and, without a key, creates a second pick list. Only the warehouse counts shelves, so any second writer of on-hand stock produces phantom stock. An order that reaches the warehouse after the last wave ships the next day whatever the page said, so the promise must read the cut-off and the backlog. A pallet's SSCC and contents exist only at pack time, so the despatch advice must come from pack confirmation.

role.contribution: Gives the part its warehouse side: the fulfillment order as the contract between the order record and the warehouse, the warehouse system as the only writer of on-hand stock, and the cut-off, capacity and backlog that every later promise must read.

transition_in.carries_over: The part introduction's first question, the work instruction and response between order management and the warehouse, and Eva's paid order waiting for Duiven.
transition_in.introduces: What happens to the order inside the warehouse and what the warehouse system must receive and report.

posts.title: Getting It There: Carriers, Labels, Tracking and the Delivery Promise
posts.question: How does a merchant connect to its carriers for labels and tracking, and how does it make a delivery promise it can keep?

know: The shipping vocabulary (carrier, service, label, manifest, tracking event, pickup point, cut-off, lane, estimated delivery date, rate shopping, multi-carrier platform) and the three moments shipping touches an order: the promise at checkout, the label at packing and the tracking after collection.
The four ways to talk to carriers and the four ways to make the promise (static rule, transit table, promise service, predictive model), with what each needs and is blind to.
What consumer law sets around delivery: 30 days unless agreed, risk with the merchant until possession, refund of only the cheapest standard delivery.
believe: From the second carrier onward a normalizing layer between the merchant's systems and the carriers is necessary; the choice is whether to buy or build it.
A promise that is not computed cannot be measured, and the only on-time rate to trust is the one computed from the merchant's own scan history.
can_do: Specify a first delivery-promise component: its inputs, its safe default when it is unavailable, and the promised-versus-delivered measure per lane.
Say what stops one parcel from getting two barcodes and what alerts on a missed manifest.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given an order placed after the warehouse's last wave under a static next-day promise, the reader gives the date that should have been shown and the inputs that compute it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A Dutch storefront shows 'ordered before 22:00, delivered tomorrow'. A customer orders at 21:14 on a Tuesday; the warehouse released its last wave at 21:00, the carrier collects at 22:30, and transit on her lane is one day. Using only this chapter: what date should she have been shown, why, and what does showing it require?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Thursday, not Wednesday: the order ships on Wednesday because it missed the last wave, and transit adds one day. It requires a promise computed from the warehouse's cut-off and backlog, the stock's location, the lane's transit time and a margin, and measured as promised-versus-delivered per lane; not a reworded sentence.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a retried label call and parcels that never left 'label created', the reader names each fault and its prevention.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A label call times out and is retried; later that day a batch of labeled parcels is collected but still shows only 'label created' in tracking. Using only this chapter: what went wrong in each case, and what prevents it?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The retry booked a second shipment, giving one parcel two barcodes, because the call carried no merchant shipment reference; make the call idempotent by that reference and look up before creating. The second batch was never manifested: a label is not a booking until the day is closed with the carrier; make the close-out a scheduled job with an alert and watch for parcels stuck in pre-transit.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say what the order's shipping status should be derived from when several carriers use different codes.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Four carriers send their own scan codes, and the status page, the e-mails and the support agent each read them differently. Using only this chapter: where should the order's shipping status come from?
acceptance_criteria.expected: From every carrier's scans mapped onto one small normalized vocabulary (such as pre-transit, in transit, out for delivery, delivered, available for pickup, failure, return to sender, exception), keeping the original event; the status is derived from those events, never set by hand, and the page, the notifications and the agent read the same derived status; each event is stored with its lane.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: How a parcel gets a carrier, a label and a tracking history; one shared interface over several carriers and who builds it; one status vocabulary derived from tracking events; the delivery promise computed from the warehouse's timing and the carrier's transit; Eva's PostNL parcel and whether her date could have been promised correctly. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's carriers and storefront promise, carrier and vendor documentation, research on delivery promises.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: How does a merchant connect to its carriers for labels and tracking, and how does it make a delivery promise it can keep?
thesis.claim: From the second carrier onward a merchant connects through one normalizing layer, bought or built. The layer books each parcel once under the merchant's reference, closes each day's manifest and maps every carrier's scans onto one event vocabulary from which the shipping status is derived. A delivery promise the merchant can keep is computed from the warehouse's cut-off and backlog, the stock's location and each lane's measured transit time plus a margin set from the lane's late parcels, and checked against delivered dates.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that carriers are integrated one at a time by whoever packs the parcel, that the order's shipping status is whatever the latest carrier message or a person sets, and that a delivery promise is a line of storefront text ('ordered before 22:00, delivered tomorrow') that operations tries to meet.
thesis.so_what: Eva ordered at 21:14 on 13 April 2027, after Duiven's 21:00 last wave; the storefront's line, written when a 3PL in Tiel shipped the orders, promised Wednesday, and the parcel arrived on Thursday 15 April, the date a computed promise would have shown. On Black Friday 2026 the same line promised next-day delivery while orders queued for four hours. A merchant that accepts the claim buys the normalizing layer early, stores every scan with its lane, and measures promised against delivered per lane before it builds a promise service, as Noor's first version in May 2027 does with a transit table plus the warehouse's cut-off and backlog.
thesis.how_why: Each carrier has its own API versions and retirement dates, label format, manifest rule and status codes, so a merchant connected to each directly owns one migration per carrier; a normalizing layer absorbs them. A shipment call retried after a timeout books a second barcode unless it carries the merchant's reference, and a label is not a booking until the manifest is closed. Carrier codes differ, so systems reading raw scans disagree, while one vocabulary gives the status page, the notifications and the agent the same status. The promised date is the ship date, set by the cut-off and the backlog, plus the lane's transit time plus a margin for late parcels; a static sentence holds none of these inputs, so it is wrong after the last wave and whenever the queue grows, and nobody notices unless delivered dates are compared with promised ones.

role.contribution: Turns the warehouse's cut-off and backlog into a computed delivery promise, and adds the carrier's side of the part: one booking per parcel and one event vocabulary from which the shipping status every view reads is derived.

transition_in.carries_over: The parcel packed and confirmed at Duiven, and the cut-off, capacity and backlog that the storefront's promise ignored.
transition_in.introduces: The carrier's part: labels, manifests and tracking events, and a delivery promise computed from the warehouse's facts and the carrier's transit time.

posts.title: Stores Are Systems Too: Point of Sale and Omnichannel Fulfillment
posts.question: What does a physical store add to the architecture, and how do click-and-collect, ship-from-store, return-in-store and endless aisle work?

know: The four things a store adds (an order source, a stock location, a customer list, a payment path) and the two constraints a web shop lacks: offline operation and fiscal rules, with how those rules differ in Germany, Belgium, Italy and the Netherlands.
The four cross-channel services and the three problems they share: availability, sourcing and staff tooling.
The four ways to connect stores (the platform's POS, a specialist POS by events through the order hub, a specialist POS by nightly batch through the ERP, the ERP's POS) and where each fits.
believe: Store stock may be promised only with a buffer, a confirmation or a count behind it; the store's confirmation, not the online promise, is the commitment.
'Unified commerce' is a goal state that one platform or an order hub with an identity layer can reach, not a product.
can_do: Look at a click-and-collect pilot and say where the promise is made, where the commitment is made and how old the store stock behind it is.
Choose between the platform's POS and a specialist POS by the number of fiscal regimes and the weight of the stores.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a collection promise made from a nightly copy of store stock, the reader explains the broken promises and names the fixes that need no new system.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A web shop offers 'available for collection today' at one store, based on store stock copied to the back office every night, and in one month promises 37 items the store had already sold. Using only this chapter: why did this happen, and what would have prevented most of it before any new system?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The platform promised from a copy up to a day old while the till kept selling, and treated the promise as the commitment. A per-store threshold (never promise the last few units, such as two per variant) and a staff confirmation before the customer is told 'ready', with a weaker promise ('we confirm within two hours'); later, store stock sent by the till as events into an availability service. Not a new POS.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a first store in a new country and a platform vendor's POS offer, the reader names the check that comes first and what decides between the two kinds of POS.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A Dutch brand with stores in the Netherlands and Belgium plans its first store in Germany, and its platform vendor offers its own POS. Using only this chapter: what must be checked first, and what decides between the platform's POS and a specialist POS?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Whether the POS meets German fiscal rules: a certified technical security device (TSE) that signs each transaction, sequential transaction numbers and registration with the tax office; that alone can rule a product out. The choice then follows the number of fiscal regimes and the stores' weight: the platform's POS for a web-first brand with a few stores in one lenient regime; a specialist POS integrated by events through the order hub when stores carry a real share of revenue or span regimes.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say what prevents a web order returned at a store counter from being refunded twice.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A web order is returned at a store counter; the till refunds the card, and the returns portal, seeing the item received, refunds it as well. Using only this chapter: what rule prevents this?
acceptance_criteria.expected: One refund path per order, decided once: a return recorded at the till closes the portal's request before anything is paid.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: What a store adds to the architecture (orders, stock, customers, payments) and why a till differs from a web shop; how click-and-collect, ship-from-store, return-in-store and endless aisle work, and what store stock is worth as a promise; when to keep or change the POS; Kestrel & Pine's Utrecht pilot and its deferred till decision. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's stores, vendor documentation, fiscal rules by country and store-inventory research.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: What does a physical store add to the architecture, and how do click-and-collect, ship-from-store, return-in-store and endless aisle work?
thesis.claim: A store adds an order source, a stock location, a customer list and a payment path that must keep working offline and meet each country's fiscal rules. Click-and-collect, ship-from-store, return-in-store and endless aisle act on another channel's stock or orders, so all four need store stock sent to availability as events, net of a per-variant buffer, a location chosen by the order hub, and staff tools; a promise against store stock is committed only when staff confirm it.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a store is a sales channel with a till, that omnichannel services are features switched on in the platform or bought as 'unified commerce', and that the first step is to replace the stores' POS with the platform's own.
thesis.so_what: In December 2026 Utrecht's click-and-collect pilot promised 37 items the store had already sold, because the platform read the ERP's nightly copy of store stock and the e-mail to the store was the only commitment. The interim fix (a two-unit threshold per variant, a staff confirmation and 'collection today, we confirm within two hours') costs nothing to build, and Waypoint's W4 decision defers the till choice to 2028, when availability and the order hub are in place and only the till product remains to choose. A merchant that accepts the claim decides who owns store stock and where the commitment sits before its first cross-channel promise, and chooses the till by its countries and the stores' share of sales.
thesis.how_why: A till must keep selling when its connection drops, so for those hours the store is its own system of record and its sales reach the other systems late; and some countries prescribe how a sale is recorded (Germany requires a certified security device and sequential numbers), which can rule a POS product out. Store stock records are often wrong (65% of nearly 370,000 records in a 2008 study of 37 stores) and a nightly copy makes them older, so a promise at face value breaks; a buffer absorbs the lag and a person's confirmation catches the missing unit before the customer travels. Each service sends work to a location and hands it to staff, so availability, sourcing and staff tooling are needed whichever POS runs.

role.contribution: Adds the store as a witness of stock and sales that works offline and under fiscal rules, and separates the promise against store stock from the commitment a person at the store makes.

transition_in.carries_over: The parcel delivered to Eva's door from Duiven, promised from the warehouse's cut-off and the carrier's lane.
transition_in.introduces: Orders and stock that live in a store: collection at the counter, dispatch from a store shelf, returns at the till and orders for stock that is not in the building.

posts.title: The Way Back: Returns, Exchanges, Refunds and Reverse Logistics
posts.question: How does a return travel back through the systems, and how do you make sure the money, the stock and the books all agree?

know: The nine steps of a return (request, eligibility, label, transit, receiving, inspection, disposition, settlement, stock) with their records and owners, and the dispositions (restocked, processing required, not restocked, missing).
The two records of a return (the return, which owns intent and money; the reverse fulfillment, which owns work and stock) and the disposition that joins them.
The EU right of withdrawal read as data: four dates per order line and the three 14-day clocks, and the trader's right to wait for the goods or proof of sending.
believe: For goods like apparel and equipment, the warehouse's disposition, not the request or the carrier scan, should release the refund and the restock.
The refund trigger and the single refund writer are decided before a returns product is chosen.
can_do: Write the returns integration contract: the trigger, the writer, the key, the restock rule and the four dates per line.
Say how an exchange is modeled and what releases the replacement, and how marketplace and store returns enter the return record.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a return refunded by support on a carrier scan and again by the portal on inspection, the reader names the missing decisions and the event that should release the refund.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A customer sees on the carrier's tracking that her return was delivered to the warehouse and asks support for her refund; the agent sees the payment and no refund in the payment provider's console and refunds by hand; days later the returns portal refunds again after inspection. Using only this chapter: which decisions were missing, and which event should release the refund?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Nobody had decided the refund trigger and the one system allowed to refund: two systems could refund, and neither request carried the return id as its key, so the provider paid both. The warehouse's disposition (refund on inspection) releases the refund; one system issues it with the return id as idempotency key; support's console access is read-only and agents see the pending refund in the portal; a daily comparison of the provider's refunds with the platform's catches a second one.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a restock on request and an exchange released by a carrier scan, the reader says what is wrong and what should trigger each.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A returned jacket is put back into sellable stock as soon as the return is requested, and the exchange replacement ships when the carrier scans the return parcel at the warehouse. Using only this chapter: what is wrong with each, and what should trigger them?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Stock should rise only on a 'restocked' disposition from the warehouse system, the single writer of on-hand stock, not on the request, the scan or receipt before grading; otherwise a worn or missing item is sold again. The exchange is a new order created at request time and held (committing the replacement unit) and released by a resellable disposition, not by a scan; otherwise a replacement can ship for a return that never arrives.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can compute the withdrawal deadlines for one return and say whether the trader may wait for the goods.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: a customer received her goods on 15 April and told the shop on 19 April that she was withdrawing. By when must she send the goods back, by when must the shop refund, and may the shop wait for the goods?
acceptance_criteria.expected: She withdrew inside the 14 days that run from receipt; she must send the goods within 14 days of her notice, by 3 May; the shop must refund within 14 days of the notice, by 3 May, by the same means of payment, and may withhold the refund until it has the goods back or proof that she sent them, whichever comes first.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The steps a return passes through and the records it creates; the return request, the warehouse's inspection and disposition, the replacement order and the refund as separate decisions with owners; the EU withdrawal clocks; returns that start on marketplaces and in stores; Eva's exchange from M to L between 19 and 22 April and its €199 refund variant. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's return figures and the Double Refund, platform data models, EU law and return-rate surveys.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: How does a return travel back through the systems, and how do you make sure the money, the stock and the books all agree?
thesis.claim: A return travels as two records: the return request on the order side and the reverse fulfillment in the warehouse, joined by the warehouse's disposition, its verdict on each item. Money, stock and books agree when that disposition releases the refund, or the replacement order held until then, one system issues the refund with the return id as its key, stock rises only on a 'restocked' disposition, and the credit note follows the refund.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a return is a refund button: the refund goes out when the customer asks or when the carrier scan shows the parcel at the warehouse, whichever system an agent has open may issue it, the unit goes back into stock on arrival, and finance corrects the books at month-end.
thesis.so_what: In January 2027 Kestrel & Pine refunded 212 returns twice, €19,400: customers saw 'delivered to Duiven' on the tracking, support refunded in the payment provider's console, and the portal refunded again on inspection, and neither request named the return. At 72,000 return parcels a year and a 24% item return rate, the way back is a main road. A merchant that accepts the claim decides the refund trigger, the single refund writer and the restock rule before it chooses a returns product, and keeps four dates per order line (delivery, withdrawal notice, goods sent, refund) so the 14-day clocks can be computed.
thesis.how_why: The request says what the customer intends to send, not what arrives; only the inspection at the bench shows what came back and whether it can be sold again, so a refund or restock on request or on scan pays for empty boxes and resells worn jackets. EU law lets the trader withhold the refund until the goods or proof of sending arrive and then requires it within 14 days of the notice, so refund on inspection is lawful if the clock is tracked. A payment provider executes every valid refund request, so two systems that can refund without a shared key both pay. Marketplaces and stores start returns the merchant did not, so the return record must accept their authorizations and refunds under their own ids. An exchange is a held new order released by the disposition, because a method such as iDEAL cannot hold money. The credit note records money that has actually moved back, so it follows the confirmed refund and the books match the provider's records.

role.contribution: Carries the part's rules onto the way back: the warehouse's disposition as the event that releases money and stock, one refund writer keyed on the return id, and returns started by stores and marketplaces entering the same record.

transition_in.carries_over: A web order brought back to a store counter, and the one refund path per order that a return at the till requires.
transition_in.introduces: The return as it travels back through the portal, the carrier, the warehouse bench, the payment provider and the ERP, and the event on which money, stock and books each move.

posts.title: Where Is My Order? Notifications, Service and the Customer Record
posts.question: How does the customer learn what is happening, and what does a service agent need to see?

know: Which event and which system emit each customer message (confirmed, shipped with tracking, ships in two parcels, out for delivery, delivered, ready for collection, return received, refund issued).
The order status page as a read model and a privacy boundary, and the separate status machines (order, money, goods per shipment, returns) that platforms keep.
The four ways to build the service layer (platform notifications and a helpdesk, a tracking vendor, a notification service and service view over the OMS, a built layer) and where each fits.
believe: The status page, the notifications and the agent's screen are three read models over one order record; any difference between them is a defect.
'Where is my order' contacts per shipped order measure the integrations, not the staffing.
can_do: Say which system must emit each customer message and which system the status page and the helpdesk must read.
Choose the measures (contacts and WISMO per 100 shipped orders, contacts per split shipment, status disagreements) that show where the joins fail.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a two-parcel order that read 'Delivered' after the first parcel, the reader names the missing message, the only kind of system that could emit it, and what every view should read.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A two-line order ships its first item; the second waits for replenishment. The status page and the e-mail say 'Delivered', the warehouse says 'In picking', and the customer writes eleven times in six days while the agent switches between five systems. Using only this chapter: which message was missing, which system could have sent it, and what should the page and the agent read?
acceptance_criteria.expected: 'Your order ships in two parcels', with when the second leaves; only a record that holds the order's lines together with their fulfillment state (an order management system) can emit it, and the platform-only landscape had no emitter. The page, the notifications and the agent's view should read that one record, showing the goods state per line or parcel, the money state and any return state, not one status word.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a helpdesk that still reads the shop platform after an OMS took over and a 'shipped' e-mail sent at label print, the reader names the failure and the rule.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A merchant has moved its orders to an order management system, but its helpdesk still reads the shop platform, and the 'shipped' e-mail goes out when the label prints. Using only this chapter: what goes wrong, and what is the rule?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The agent and the status page can show different orders, and customers are told 'shipped' while the parcel still waits for the carrier. The service view must read the system that owns the goods state, so the helpdesk is re-pointed at the OMS; 'shipped' is triggered by the carrier's handover scan, with a tracking link that already works.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say when a customer may cancel herself and how 'where is my order' contacts should be measured.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: when may a customer cancel her order without contacting anyone, and how should a merchant measure 'where is my order' contacts?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Only before the warehouse has accepted the work; after that a cancellation is a request to the warehouse, so a self-service cancel must check the fulfillment state first.
