Count 'where is my order' contacts per shipped order (for example per 100 shipped orders, including peak week), not as a share of tickets, and read them as a signal of the tracking and notification layer.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Why customers receive conflicting answers about one order; the three views (notifications, the order status page, the agent's service view) and the systems whose facts feed them; separate status machines; 'where is my order' as a measurement; Eva's messages from 13 to 22 April. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's Three-Status Order tickets, platform and helpdesk documentation, vendor data on service contacts.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: How does the customer learn what is happening, and what does a service agent need to see?
thesis.claim: The customer learns what is happening from notifications and a status page; the service agent needs the goods state of each line or parcel, the money state and any return state. The notifications, the status page and the agent's screen must be read models over one order record fed by events from the platform, the warehouse, the carrier and the returns flow, because disagreements between them reach the service desk as customer contacts.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that notifications are e-mail templates the shop platform sends, that agents should look each answer up in the system that holds it (the platform, the warehouse, the carrier, the payment provider), and that 'where is my order' contacts are a staffing cost to be reduced with more agents or a chatbot.
thesis.so_what: Order #1052877 (a €119 fleece and €18 socks) produced 11 tickets in six days: the integration marked the whole order fulfilled on the first shipment, so the page said 'Delivered' while the warehouse said 'In picking' and the ERP 'Not invoiced', the agent worked from five tabs, and no system could send 'your order ships in two parcels'. A merchant that accepts the claim points the status page, the notifications and the helpdesk at the system that owns the goods state (at Kestrel & Pine the OMS from Q4 2027 under W2), gates self-service on the fulfillment state, and reports contacts per shipped order and per split shipment beside its integration monitors.
thesis.how_why: Each fact about the order is first known by a different system: the platform knows the order and the payment, the warehouse the shipment and its tracking number, the carrier the scans, the returns flow what came back. A view that reads one of them shows only its fact, and a single status string lets the latest event, such as the first parcel's delivery, overwrite the others; the message 'two parcels' can come only from a record that holds the lines and their fulfillment state together. A cancel or address change is safe only before the warehouse accepts the work, so self-service must read the goods state. Contacts per shipped order rise when tracking numbers arrive late, promises slip or splits go unannounced, which makes them a measure of the joins.

role.contribution: Shows the customer's and the agent's side of every event in the part, makes one status built from those events the rule for every view, and performs the part's closing (the published chapter does not yet do so: it ends with a one-sentence summary and the hand-off to Part V).

transition_in.carries_over: The return closed on the disposition, the refund or the exchange sent, and the few messages Eva saw of all this.
transition_in.introduces: Why the customer's messages, the status page and the agent's view must be built from the events of the whole part in one record, and what the eleven tickets of the Three-Status Order cost without it.

know: The outside parties of Part V and the rules each enforces: marketplaces (published performance thresholds, API versions retired on dates), business buyers (negotiated prices, payment terms, credit limits, approval rules), retail chains (message guidelines and chargebacks) and tax authorities (e-invoicing mandates with dates).

The intermediaries between those parties and the merchant (the channel connector, the EDI provider, the ERP partner's connector), and the ERP's role behind every channel, with the hub options by scale stage.
believe: Every outside channel is a way into the one order record; an order kept in the tool it arrived through is invisible to the warehouse, support and finance.
An intermediary translates and owns no fact; every value sent to an outside party comes from the system that owns it.
At the Omnichannel stage the ERP keeps the books and no sale waits on it.
can_do: For each outside channel at their own company, name where its orders are created and under which key, the system that computes each value the outside party receives, the rule or date that party enforces with its internal owner and monitor, and whether any channel waits on the ERP.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every supporting claim of the part thesis is argued by at least one chapter, and every chapter supports at least one.
Each chapter's closing hand-off expresses the relationship its successor declares in transition_in.

Given four failures with outside channels, a reader who has read only Part V names for each the value that came from a copy or from a system that did not own it, or the order kept outside the order record, before naming a new connector, a new B2B platform, a new EDI provider or a bigger ERP.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A brand's marketplaces keep selling a sold-out jacket for two hours from an hourly stock copy held in its channel connector; its larger wholesale shops e-mail their orders because the portal shows list prices and cannot check credit; a retail chain deducts money because despatch advices written by the ERP when orders are released do not match the pallets packed; and month-end takes eleven working days because marketplace orders reach the ERP as a weekly summary. Using only Part V: what was missing in each case?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The marketplaces were sent a copy held by the connector instead of one available-to-promise figure per channel computed from the owner of physical stock and published by events (with an age monitor on the last accepted update); the portal could not read the agreements and credit the ERP owns (contract and pre-season prices published as price events with effective dates, a credit check at placement), and keyed orders lived in a second record; the despatch advice came from a system that did not pack the pallets instead of the warehouse's pack confirmation; marketplace orders were not created in the one order record from which the ERP receives every order by daily batch. Not a new connector, a new B2B platform, a new EDI provider or a bigger ERP alone.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The page that carries the part's closing sets the part's incidents against the opening's jacket sold through a marketplace and a retail chain, and states what they have in common; it does not only hand off to Part VI.

thesis.question: What changes when orders arrive from outside the merchant's own shop, and what must the merchant's systems do to keep the promises made to the parties outside?
thesis.claim: Orders from outside the shop arrive through an intermediary that translates, such as a channel connector or an EDI provider, from an outside party that scores, charges back or imposes legal deadlines. The merchant keeps its promises only when no intermediary is the system of record for any value, every channel's order is created in one order record, each value sent out comes from its one owner, and no sale waits on the ERP.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that each outside channel is a sales decision served by its own tool: the marketplace connector, the B2B portal, the EDI provider and the ERP each hold the orders, stock and prices their channel needs, the ERP is the natural hub everything connects through, and the outside party's scorecard, chargebacks and mandates are problems for operations and finance rather than requirements on the integrations.
thesis.so_what: Kestrel & Pine's Part V incidents were values taken from a copy or from a system that did not own them, or orders kept in the tool they arrived through: about 160 marketplace orders in the Black Friday Oversell, 140 of them seller cancellations, and a strike from bol; two days of stale stock to bol from the Deprecated Endpoint; 38% of 9,400 wholesale orders keyed into the ERP by hand; Bergzicht's €14,200 deduction for despatch advices written before packing; an eleven-day January close. A merchant that accepts the claim decides, before it adds a channel, where that channel's orders are created, which system computes each value the outside party receives, and who owns that party's rules and dates.
thesis.how_why: An outside party acts on what it is sent without asking again and enforces its own rules: a marketplace sells the stock number it was last sent and counts each seller cancellation and late confirmation; a chain's receiving scans pallet labels against the despatch advice; a mandate's network rejects an invoice that lacks a required field. An intermediary that keeps its own copy sends a stale or invented value when the copy lags or a flow fails silently, and an order kept in the channel's own tool is invisible to the warehouse, support and finance. The ERP changes in audited releases on a finance cycle, so a stock figure or an order routed through it moves at that pace.

supporting_claims.claim: Every outside channel's order (a marketplace order, seller- or marketplace-fulfilled; a wholesale order from the portal, keyed in or confirmed after a punchout; an EDI order) is created once in the merchant's one order record, keyed on the outside party's identifier and flagged by channel, and is never kept only in the tool it arrived through.

An intermediary (the channel connector, the EDI provider, the ERP partner's connector) translates between systems and owns no fact; the merchant owns its contract: the fields, their direction and cadence, the system of record for each, the partner's guideline and API versions with their dates, and a named internal owner.

Each value sent to an outside party, or used to accept its order, comes from the one system that owns it: a channel's stock number from one available-to-promise calculation, prices from the pricing source with effective dates, terms and credit from the ERP's receivables at order placement, the despatch advice from the warehouse's pack confirmation, and the invoice from the ERP's confirmed shipment.

Outside parties enforce rules the merchant does not negotiate (a marketplace's performance thresholds and API retirement dates, a chain's message guideline and chargebacks, a country's e-invoicing mandate), so each rule becomes a freshness requirement on a flow or a dated obligation with an owner, and a monitor shows when it is missed.

The ERP is the system of record for finance (postings, invoices, receivables, purchasing, stock value, item cost, and business customers' prices, terms and credit); it receives orders, shipments and payments by batch from their owners, publishes what it owns for channels as events, and stays out of every real-time path.

role.contribution: Widens the journey from one shop to every channel an order can arrive through.

additional_patterns.applies_to: b2b-commerce and edi-and-e-invoicing: the same wholesale channel, first through the self-service portal and keyed orders, then through the documents the largest buyers send

flow.rationale: Each chapter reuses what the one before it fixed. Marketplaces come first because their orders are the closest to the consumer order Parts II to IV followed (a consumer buyer, the same jacket, the same warehouse and carriers), so the only new things are the outside party and the intermediary; the chapter fixes the rules the rest of the part reuses: the connector translates and owns nothing, the value sent out is a promise computed by its owner, and every channel's order is created in the order record under the outside party's id. The B2B chapter applies them to a buyer who is a company, adds the agreements the checkout must read, and assigns terms, credit and wholesale prices to the ERP. The EDI chapter needs those accounts and contract prices and the EDI and punchout routes the B2B chapter only named, and adds one internal source per document, ending with invoices the ERP issues. The ERP chapter comes last because it gathers what the earlier chapters handed to the ERP (terms, credit and wholesale prices; invoices and their transmission status; marketplace and wholesale orders to post) and decides its role and whether it is the hub. Putting B2B before marketplaces would introduce the order-record and connector rules on the harder case of negotiated agreements; putting EDI before B2B would describe contract prices, terms and punchout before company accounts exist; putting the ERP earlier would argue its finance-only role before the reader has seen what the channels need from it and which documents end in its ledger.

hook.content: A merchant can sell the same jacket through its own shop, a marketplace or a retail chain, yet the marketplace can penalize late dispatch and the chain can deduct money for the wrong pallet labels, so an extra sale handled like a consumer checkout can end in a deduction or a delayed payment.

opening.bridge: From the single shop of Parts II to IV to the same Ridgewalker reaching buyers by other routes: two Amazon.de orders of 13 April 2027, one shipped from Duiven and one by the marketplace; a shop's pre-season order; and Bergzicht Outdoor's 240-unit reorder on three pallets, all using the warehouse and finance systems Eva's order uses; with Kestrel & Pine's €3.0 million of marketplace sales and €12.0 million from 1,100 wholesale accounts, 62% of whose orders arrive through the B2B portal and 38% are keyed into the ERP by hand.
opening.roadmap: Four chapters: marketplace listings, imported orders, stock allocation and seller performance (the Black Friday Oversell's marketplace cancellations and the two stale days of the Deprecated Endpoint); company accounts, negotiated prices, payment terms and credit limits (De Kaap Buitensport's pre-season order); structured orders, despatch advices, invoices and e-invoicing mandates (Bergzicht's €14,200 deduction); the ERP's financial and purchasing role, and why stock availability needs a faster route than the ERP (the connector it took three weeks to understand), with the ERP's role as finance and purchasing named before the B2B and EDI chapters hand it terms, credit, wholesale prices and invoices.

closing.synthesis: The marketplace strike, the 38% of wholesale orders keyed by hand, Bergzicht's €14,200 deduction and the eleven-day month-end look like four problems in four places: a connector, a portal, an EDI mapping and a finance system. Read together they are one: a value sent to an outside party, or needed to accept its order, came from a copy an intermediary held or from a system that did not own it, or an order lived in the tool its channel arrived through. Each chapter's remedy has the same parts: create every channel's order in one record under the outside party's id, compute each value sent out once in its owner, write each intermediary's contract and calendar down with an internal owner, and let the ERP receive finance by batch outside the path of the sale.
closing.so_what: Kestrel & Pine's remedies are ownership decisions and contracts more than new channels or platforms: one available-to-promise figure per channel from the availability service, with a ten-unit marketplace buffer until it arrives; the OMS taking marketplace orders in September, storefront orders in October and EDI and manual wholesale orders in December 2027; ERP price events and a credit check at placement for the portal; W6's labels and despatch advice from the WMS with a partner card per trading partner; and the finance-only ERP with a field-level contract for its connector. A reader can list, for each outside channel of their own company, where its orders are created, which system computes each value it is sent, and who owns its rules and dates.
closing.callback: The part opening's jacket sold through a marketplace and a retail chain, where an extra sale handled like a consumer checkout ends in a strike or a deduction.

takeaway.content: For each channel through which orders reach you from outside your shop, write down where its orders are created and under which key, which system computes each value you send it (stock, price, despatch advice, invoice), which rule or date the outside party enforces and who owns it, and whether any sale waits on the ERP; start with the age of the last accepted stock update per marketplace and the share of wholesale orders keyed by hand.

transition_in.carries_over: The single-shop journey of Parts II to IV, from catalog to return.
transition_in.introduces: Orders created by someone else's system, under someone else's rules.

posts.question: What does this part argue, and in what order should its chapters be read?

know: Part V answers four questions in order: how marketplace listings, stock and orders join the merchant's systems; what changes when the buyer is a company; how structured documents are exchanged with trading partners and what e-invoicing mandates require; and what the ERP should own and how fast each kind of fact must reach it.

Each outside channel brings an outside party that sets the rules (a marketplace's scorecard, a chain's penalties, a mandate's legal date), and connectors that should translate the channel's requirements without owning prices, stock or orders.

The ERP's role behind every channel, announced before the B2B and EDI chapters assign it terms, credit, wholesale prices and invoices: it keeps the books and receives orders, shipments and payments from the systems that own them, and the last chapter argues why.
can_do: Pick the Part V chapter that answers the decision in front of them.

acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only this page: what will each of the next four chapters tell you, in order?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Marketplace listings, imported orders, stock allocation and seller performance; company accounts, negotiated prices, payment terms and credit limits; structured orders, despatch advices, invoices and dated e-invoicing mandates; the ERP's financial and purchasing role, with finance taking complete batches while stock availability needs a faster route.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of this page alone can say why extra sales through outside channels can turn into deductions, and what decides whether they do.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: why can a sale through a marketplace or a retail chain end in a penalty or a deduction, and what does the merchant have to decide to prevent it?

The merchant must decide where each order becomes authoritative, and connectors must translate the channel's requirements while prices, stock and orders keep their one owner.

posts.title: Selling on Someone Else's Platform: Marketplaces and Channel Integration
posts.question: What does it take to list, sell and fulfil on marketplaces, and how do marketplace orders fit into the order record?

know: What a marketplace offer, the buy box and commission are, and the two fulfillment models (seller-fulfilled and marketplace-fulfilled) with what each means for the order record and for stock.

The metrics marketplaces grade sellers on (order defect, cancellation, late shipment, valid tracking, on-time delivery; bol's strikes) and the five flows through a channel connector (listings, stock, prices, orders, status back-flow) with the freshness each needs.

The channel allocation policies (shared pool, fixed quantity, buffer, percentage split, computed available-to-promise per channel) and the four ways to connect (seller tools, the platform's channel app, a channel integration platform, direct integration).
believe: The channel connector translates and owns nothing: not the product content, not the stock figure, not the order.
The stock number sent to a marketplace is a promise it will sell without asking again, and the marketplace's scorecard is a service level on the merchant's own integrations.
A marketplace's or connector's API deprecation schedule is a contract clause with a date that someone at the merchant must own.
can_do: For their own marketplace channels, say which system computes the number each marketplace is told, where marketplace orders are created and under which key, which monitor would show stale stock, and who owns each API retirement date.
Choose among the four ways to connect to marketplaces by scale stage and the number of order sources.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a peak-evening oversell and a stale feed after an API retirement, the reader names the scorecard cost and the prevention for each, not a faster connector.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A brand sends each marketplace the platform's stock figure through a channel connector every hour. On a peak evening its warehouse sells out of a jacket and the marketplaces keep selling it for two hours; months later a script still calling a retired connector API version leaves one marketplace selling from two-day-old figures. Using only this chapter: what does each failure cost on the marketplace's scorecard, and what would have prevented each?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Every oversold unit the merchant cancels counts as a seller cancellation against the marketplace's cancellation threshold (on bol, a strike for the week). Prevention: one available-to-promise figure per channel, computed from the system of record for physical stock and published by events, with a per-channel buffer as the interim fix while the sync is hourly; an age monitor per channel on the last accepted stock update, which would have caught the stale feed within the hour; a deprecation calendar in the integration inventory with an owner for each date. Not a faster connector or a different marketplace.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given one seller-fulfilled and one marketplace-fulfilled order, the reader says where each is recorded, which metrics apply, and where the second order's stock figure comes from.
acceptance_criteria.probe: On the same day one Amazon.de order for a jacket ships from the merchant's own warehouse, and another ships from stock the merchant sent to Amazon's warehouse in advance. Using only this chapter: where should each order be recorded, which scorecard metrics apply to each, and where does the stock figure for the second come from?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Both are created once in the merchant's one order record (the OMS), keyed on the Amazon order id. The first carries its ship-by date, gets a fulfillment order and a ship confirmation by event from the warehouse system, and is graded on cancellation, late shipment, valid tracking and on-time delivery; the second gets no fulfillment order, is recorded for finance and analytics, and is graded only on order defect rate. Its stock is an external location whose quantity comes from the marketplace's inventory feed and is reconciled against the marketplace's report, never a copy of the merchant's warehouse figure.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say what stops one marketplace order from becoming two shipments.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: a marketplace order is delivered once by a notification and again by a periodic poll. What keeps it from becoming two orders and two parcels?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Uniqueness on the marketplace order id when the order is created makes the import idempotent, so the second delivery reuses the existing record; the order is acknowledged with the binding between the marketplace's id and the merchant's order number; a daily count of marketplace orders by id against internal orders catches any that slipped through.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: How a merchant lists, sells and ships on a marketplace; the marketplace's scorecard (cancellations, late dispatch, valid tracking) and why the data the integrations send decides it; what a channel connector does and what it must not own; how much stock each channel is told and how marketplace-held stock is treated; where marketplace orders are recorded; who owns the marketplaces' API retirement dates; two Amazon.de orders of 13 April 2027, one shipped from Duiven and one from the marketplace's stock. Evidence: marketplace thresholds and documentation, and Kestrel & Pine's marketplace incidents.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: What does it take to list, sell and fulfil on marketplaces, and how do marketplace orders fit into the order record?
thesis.claim: To sell on a marketplace a merchant sends listings, a stock number, prices and shipment confirmations that the marketplace acts on and grades against published thresholds. A connector translates them and owns nothing: each marketplace's stock number comes from one available-to-promise calculation per channel, marketplace-held stock is an external location, and every marketplace order, seller- or marketplace-fulfilled, is created once in the merchant's order record under the marketplace's order id.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that marketplace selling is the job of a channel app or connector: it holds the listings, its own stock copy and allocation rules, and the marketplace orders; the platform's stock figure is sent to every channel; and the marketplace's scorecard is the ecommerce manager's concern rather than a requirement on the integrations.
thesis.so_what: On 27 November 2026 the stock chain from the WMS through the ERP and the platform to the connector let the marketplaces sell sold-out Ridgewalker jackets for up to two hours: about 160 of the 1,120 canceled or delayed orders were marketplace orders, 140 of them seller cancellations, and bol issued a strike. In February 2027 an agency script still calling a retired connector API version left bol selling from two-day-old figures. A merchant that accepts the claim names the system that computes each channel's stock number, creates marketplace orders in its order record, monitors the age of the last accepted stock update per channel and gives each API retirement date an owner before it adds a marketplace.
thesis.how_why: A marketplace sells the quantity it was last sent without asking again, and counts every oversold unit the merchant cancels as a seller cancellation and every confirmation that arrives late as a late shipment, so latency in the merchant's flows becomes a score. A connector that holds its own stock copy and rules, or the only copy of marketplace orders, becomes another system of record: its copy lags, its failures are silent, and its orders are invisible to support, the warehouse and finance. Marketplace APIs are rate-limited and asynchronous and retire versions on published dates, so stock and orders must move by events, imports must be idempotent on the marketplace order id, and each date needs an owner. Stock in a marketplace's warehouse is counted and sold by the marketplace, so the merchant learns its quantity from the marketplace's feed.

role.contribution: Gives the part its first outside party and intermediary: the marketplace's scorecard as freshness requirements on the merchant's flows, the connector that translates and owns nothing, one available-to-promise figure per channel, the API retirement calendar as an owned contract, and marketplace orders created in the order record under the marketplace's id.

transition_in.carries_over: The part introduction's first question, marketplace listings, imported orders, stock allocation and seller performance, and the two Amazon.de orders of 13 April 2027.
transition_in.introduces: What the marketplace grades, what the channel connector may and may not hold, and where marketplace orders and marketplace-held stock belong.

posts.title: Selling to Businesses: Accounts, Contract Prices, Quotes and Approvals
posts.question: What is different when the buyer is a company?

know: The B2B object model the platforms share (an organization with locations, people and roles, with prices, assortments and terms attached to the organization or location) and the differences from a consumer purchase: contract and tiered prices excluding VAT, quotes, payment terms, credit limits, pre-season orders and the buyer's own approval rules.
The price layers (list, tier, contract, quote), the rule that the most specific wins, and why a quote freezes the price the order and the invoice use.

The four ways to give business customers a channel (a B2C platform's B2B features, a dedicated B2B platform, an ERP-driven web store, the buyer's own system through EDI or punchout) and where each fits.
believe: The ERP owns the money facts (company identity, wholesale and contract prices, payment terms, credit limits, invoices) and publishes them; the platform owns the session facts (logins, roles, the buyer's approval rules).
The share of wholesale orders keyed in by hand measures the facts the portal cannot see: it is a list of missing integrations, not of missing features.
can_do: Write the ownership table for the company account, contacts, prices, quotes, terms and credit, approval rules, orders and invoices at their own company.

Decide whether a credit check at order placement should ask the ERP synchronously or accept the order and hold it, and choose among the four channel options by the buyers and the facts the checkout needs.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a steady share of e-mailed wholesale orders, the reader names the facts the portal cannot see and the integrations that would bring those orders in, not a new B2B platform.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A brand's B2B portal takes 62% of its wholesale orders; the rest arrive by e-mail or phone and are keyed into the ERP, and that share has not fallen in two years. The larger accounts have pre-season discounts agreed per account, and finance holds some portal orders by hand a day after they are placed. Using only this chapter: why do these buyers keep e-mailing, and what would bring their orders into the portal?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The portal cannot see what they agreed or what they owe: pre-season and contract prices live in the ERP's customer price lists and in e-mail, credit is checked only in the ERP at order entry, and portal and keyed orders are two records. Publish contract and pre-season price lists from the ERP as price events with effective dates into each account's catalog; check credit at placement against the ERP's open balance, synchronously if the ERP answers fast enough or by accepting and holding the order with an event-driven release; create every wholesale order, however it arrives, in one order record. Missing integrations, not missing features.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given an invoice priced from a changed price list after a quote was accepted, the reader names the rule that was broken and the design that prevents it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A business buyer accepts a quote at a negotiated price; before the goods ship, the seasonal price list changes, and the invoice shows the new list price. Using only this chapter: what went wrong, and how should quotes, orders and invoices be designed?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A quote freezes the price: it is stored as an object with a validity date, the order is created from it, and the invoice is generated from what shipped at the price the order carried, never recomputed from the current price list. Which price layer wins (most specific: quote over contract over tier over list) is written down and implemented once in the pricing source, so the portal, the order and the invoice compute the same price.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say whether a punchout cart is an order and where the eventual order goes.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: a corporate buyer's procurement system opens the supplier's shop, the buyer fills a cart, and the cart returns to the procurement system. Is that an order, and where should the eventual order be created?
acceptance_criteria.expected: No: the cart is a requisition returned to the buyer's procurement system for its own approval. The order arrives later as a cXML OrderRequest or an EDI ORDERS and is created in the same order record as a portal order, with the buyer's purchase order number as its uniqueness key.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: What differs when the buyer is a company (accounts with several people and locations, negotiated prices, quantity breaks, payment terms, credit limits, approvals, pre-season orders); which records every B2B platform needs; who should own the company account, contacts, prices, terms, credit and orders; the choices for building a wholesale channel; independent shops ordering from Kestrel & Pine through its portal or by e-mail, with Bergzicht's EDI orders left to the next chapter. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's wholesale figures and the platforms' B2B documentation.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: What is different when the buyer is a company?
thesis.claim: When the buyer is a company, the customer is an organization with locations, people and roles, the price is a stack of dated agreements, and payment is terms within a credit limit. A portal can replace e-mail and phone orders only if it reads those agreements at checkout from the system that owns them (the ERP for terms, credit and wholesale prices) and every wholesale order, however it arrives, is created in one order record.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that B2B is a feature set to switch on: a platform's company accounts, price lists and net terms let business customers order like consumers, the share still ordering by e-mail or phone reflects buyers' habits or features the portal lacks, and the remedy is a richer B2B platform.
thesis.so_what: In 2026, 38% of Kestrel & Pine's 9,400 wholesale orders were keyed into the ERP by hand, a share unchanged since 2024, because the larger accounts' pre-season terms lived in the ERP's customer price lists, the portal could not check credit, and portal and keyed orders were two records. On 25 February 2027 De Kaap Buitensport e-mailed a pre-season order worth €6,384 because the portal showed €6,720 at list, and the ERP held it over its €15,000 credit limit until Lea Moreau approved it by e-mail. A merchant that accepts the claim decides who owns the company account, the price and the credit limit before it chooses or configures a B2B platform, and reads its keyed-order share as a list of missing integrations.
thesis.how_why: Every platform can hold company accounts, price lists, terms and credit, so when nobody names an owner each system keeps its own copy and the copies drift. A wholesale invoice must match the price the buyer was shown for the same date and quantity, so the layering rule (quote over contract over tier over list) and the frozen quote are implemented once in the pricing source and published with effective dates. What a customer owes is known only to receivables, so a credit check against a nightly copy accepts orders finance later holds, and a portal that cannot check credit sends larger orders back to e-mail, where the ERP checks them at entry. Orders that enter through different doors land in different systems unless all are created in one record keyed on the buyer's purchase order number.

role.contribution: Gives the part its business buyers: the agreements (prices, terms, credit) the checkout must read from the ERP that owns them, one order record for portal, keyed, EDI and punchout orders, and the keyed-order share as the measure of what the portal cannot see.

transition_in.carries_over: Orders from outside the shop that arrive through a marketplace, whose buyer is a consumer and whose rules the marketplace sets.
transition_in.introduces: Orders from Kestrel & Pine's 1,100 wholesale accounts, whose buyers are companies with contract prices, payment terms and credit limits that a consumer checkout cannot express.

posts.title: Documents Between Companies: EDI, Punchout and E-Invoicing
posts.question: How do large trading partners exchange orders, shipping notices and invoices without a web shop, and what do e-invoicing mandates require?

know: The EDI vocabulary: standards (UN/EDIFACT with GS1 EANCOM, ANSI X12), messages (ORDERS, ORDRSP, DESADV or ASN, INVOIC, CONTRL), identifiers (GTIN, GLN, SSCC), transports (AS2, SFTP, VAN, Peppol), per-partner guidelines and mappings, and the two families of chargebacks (delivery performance, data and label compliance).
That a syntax acknowledgment says only that a file could be parsed, and that a punchout cart is not an order.

The layers of an e-invoice (EN 16931, UBL, Peppol BIS Billing 3.0), the difference between an EDI INVOIC and a Peppol invoice, and the mandate calendar as of November 2026 (Belgium since 1 January 2026, Germany issuing from 2027 or 2028, the Netherlands planned for 2030, ViDA's cross-border reporting from 1 July 2030), with the domestic scope of the Belgian and German mandates.
believe: Each document has one honest source: the order record from the buyer's message, the despatch advice from the warehouse's pack confirmation, the invoice from the ERP's confirmed shipment; a compliance chargeback is a document generated in the wrong place.
An EDI order is a channel into the order record, not a separate order system.
E-invoicing is a legal calendar that makes delivery status part of the invoice, and the company must hold the knowledge of each mapping even when its provider holds the mapping.
can_do: Explain a compliance chargeback by the system that generated the document, and say which system should generate each document.
Place their own company on the mandate calendar, and write a partner card (GLNs, transport, message and guideline versions, mapping version, internal owner, compliance rules, open disputes).
Choose among a provider's portal, an integrated provider, in-house EDI and an e-document gateway by partners and countries.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a deduction for despatch advices that did not match the pallets, the reader names the system that wrote them, why they differed and what should generate each document, not better pickers.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A retail chain deducts money from a supplier's payment because pallet labels did not match the despatch advices it received. The supplier's ERP sends each despatch advice when the order is released to the warehouse; the warehouse system prints pallet labels at packing, and pickers sometimes merge or split pallets. Using only this chapter: why did the labels and the messages differ, and what should generate each?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The despatch advice was written from the order before anything was packed, with pallet numbers from an ERP range, so merged or split pallets made it describe different pallets from those on the truck. The SSCC labels and the despatch advice must both come from the warehouse system's pack confirmation, the system that builds the pallet; each DESADV is compared with the pack confirmation before it is sent; and a partner card per trading partner keeps the mapping knowledge inside the company rather than in one consultant's head. Not better pickers or a new EDI provider alone.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a Dutch brand with business customers in three countries, the reader states which e-invoicing rules reach it and from when, hedging where the sources do, and what its invoicing system must keep.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A Dutch brand invoices business customers in the Netherlands, Belgium and Germany. Using only this chapter: which e-invoicing rules apply to it or to its customers, from when, and what must its invoicing system keep for each invoice?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Belgium has required structured e-invoices over Peppol between Belgian VAT-registered businesses since 1 January 2026; whether that binds a Dutch supplier without a Belgian establishment is not settled, but the Belgian customers' bookkeeping expects Peppol invoices. Germany's mandate (receive since 2025, issue from 2027, or 2028 for small businesses) covers businesses established in Germany. The Netherlands plans invoicing from 1 July 2030, and ViDA's cross-border reporting starts 1 July 2030. The system that numbers and issues invoices (usually the ERP) stores each invoice's transmission status, rejections and archive, with a daily report of invoices issued but not delivered.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say what a repeated ORDERS file and a CONTRL acknowledgment each mean.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: the EDI provider re-sends an ORDERS file after a timeout that was in fact a success, and the supplier receives a CONTRL acknowledgment for an invoice it sent. What does each mean, and how should the supplier treat them?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The buyer's order number plus its GLN is the order's natural key, so a second ORDERS with the same key is a duplicate or a change, never a new order (idempotent handling). A CONTRL says only that the file could be parsed, not that the invoice was accepted or will be paid; acceptance and payment come in later messages and in the payment itself.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: How companies trade by exchanging standard documents (a purchase order, a shipment notice per pallet, an invoice the buyer's software can read); why each document must come from a different system (the order record, the warehouse's pack confirmation, the ERP's confirmed shipment); which e-invoicing deadlines already apply (Belgium since 1 January 2026 over Peppol, Germany from 2027, the Netherlands planned for 2030) and why the invoice becomes a transmitted document with a delivery status. In order: a deduction Bergzicht made from a payment; what EDI is and why it persists, its documents, identifiers, transport and partner rules; which system each document must come from and where punchout fits; the e-invoice and the calendar of mandates; the ways to connect and how they change with scale; Bergzicht's spring reorder of April 2027 and a Belgian invoice worked through, sharing Duiven's warehouse system and the books with web orders; what goes wrong. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's deduction, the GS1 and X12 standards, retailers' published supplier conditions and official mandate pages.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: How do large trading partners exchange orders, shipping notices and invoices without a web shop, and what do e-invoicing mandates require?
thesis.claim: Trading partners exchange orders, despatch advices and invoices as standard EDI messages, mapped per partner and relayed by a provider or a direct link; each document has one internal source: the order enters the order record like a web order, the despatch advice comes from the warehouse's pack confirmation, the invoice from the ERP's confirmed shipment. E-invoicing mandates require structured invoices from dated, country-specific deadlines, so the ERP that issues them holds each invoice's transmission status.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that EDI is a back-office file exchange the EDI provider or a consultant looks after: the ERP may generate every outgoing document from the order, EDI orders may stay in the ERP or the provider's portal apart from web orders, and e-invoicing is a question of PDF formats to answer when a customer asks.
thesis.so_what: In Q3 2026 Kestrel & Pine's ERP wrote Bergzicht's despatch advices when wholesale orders were released, before packing, with ERP pallet numbers, while the WMS labeled the pallets it actually built; Bergzicht deducted €14,200 for nine deliveries, and only an external consultant knew the mappings. Under W6 the WMS generates the SSCC labels and the despatch advice at pack confirmation and a partner card per trading partner holds the mapping knowledge, so Bergzicht's 240-unit reorder of 6 April 2027 ships on three pallets whose labels and message describe the same pallets. A merchant that accepts the claim routes each document from its one source and keeps a dated mandate calendar with an owner per country before the first chain or foreign business customer asks.
thesis.how_why: A chain's receiving scans each pallet's SSCC label against the despatch advice, so a message written from the order before packing is wrong whenever pickers merge or split pallets; only the system that builds and labels the pallet knows what is on it. The invoice is a payment claim for what was delivered at agreed prices with VAT, so it comes from the system that holds the confirmed shipment, the prices and the legal numbering. An EDI order is a purchase commitment like a web order, so if it lives apart, allocation, invoicing and reporting see two shapes. Each partner's guideline changes on its own schedule and is enforced by chargebacks, so the knowledge of each mapping must sit inside the company. Under a mandate an invoice exists for the receiver only once the network delivers it, and in clearance countries only once the state accepts it, so delivery and rejection become states the issuing system must hold.

role.contribution: Gives the part its documents: one internal source per document (the order record, the warehouse's pack confirmation, the ERP's confirmed shipment), the partner card that keeps mapping knowledge inside the company, and the mandate calendar that turns the invoice into a transmitted document with a delivery status.

transition_in.carries_over: The wholesale portal as the self-service path of the business channel, and the fourth channel option the B2B chapter only named: the buyer's own system, sending EDI orders or punching out.
transition_in.introduces: The documents the largest buyers send and expect (order, despatch advice, invoice), the system each must come from, and the e-invoicing mandates that now reach business invoices.

posts.title: The Back Office: ERP Integration and Who Is the Hub
posts.question: What does the ERP do in a commerce business, what should it own, and should it be the hub of integration?

know: The ERP's four jobs in a commerce business (the ledger, purchasing, inventory valuation, master data) and the boundary between stock quantity, owned by the WMS, and stock value, owned by the ERP under IAS 2 and a costing method.
The flows between the commerce systems and the ERP (orders, shipments, payments and refunds, invoices, products, stock, customers and terms) with the system of record, direction and cadence of each.
The four hub answers (the ERP, the commerce platform, an OMS, an iPaaS with no hub) with where each fits and breaks, and the master-data ownership table for an Omnichannel merchant.
believe: Finance can be batch; availability cannot: the ERP is the system of record for finance and never the system a storefront waits on.
'Who is the hub' is a scale-stage decision, and an iPaaS with no hub is an accident, not a design.
The connector an ERP partner builds is a contract the merchant must own, written field by field before it is replaced.
can_do: Spot an ERP in a real-time path (availability, order status, checkout) and say what should replace it there.
Read a vendor connector's documentation as an entity–owner table, and write a field-level contract for an ERP connector: direction, cadence, system of record and the rule when the two disagree.
Choose the integration hub for a given business shape and stage.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given an omnichannel merchant whose stock and prices pass through the ERP and its partner's undocumented connector, the reader says what is wrong and what the ERP should own and receive, not a bigger ERP.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A brand with its own warehouse, six stores, a wholesale portal and three marketplaces sends stock from its warehouse system to its ERP every 15 minutes and from the ERP to the storefront hourly; its ERP partner's connector also copies orders hourly and pushes a price list, and nobody inside the company can say which fields it moves. Using only this chapter: what is wrong, and what should the ERP own and receive?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The ERP sits in the path of the sale: its cycle adds to the storefront's stock latency (an oversell), and a silent failure in its connector reaches customers (a wrong price for days). At this stage the ERP owns finance only (ledger, invoices, receivables, purchasing, stock value, item cost, business customers' prices, terms and credit, which leave it as events) and receives orders, shipments and payments by daily batch from the systems that own them; physical stock comes from the WMS and availability from an OMS or availability service by events. The connector gets a written field-level contract with direction, cadence, system of record and a rule for disagreement, a named owner, idempotent handling and a reconciliation job, and is then retired flow by flow.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given three business shapes, the reader names the integration hub for each and what is wrong with having none.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: which system should be the integration hub for a direct-to-consumer brand with one storefront and one warehouse, for a B2B-heavy business with one channel and one warehouse, and for a merchant with stores, wholesale and marketplaces in several countries? What is wrong with having no hub?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The commerce platform for the direct-to-consumer brand, with the ERP subscribing for finance; the ERP (or an ERP-driven store) for the B2B-heavy business with one channel and one warehouse; an OMS for the omnichannel merchant, with the ERP finance-only. An iPaaS with no hub is not a design but what happens when systems are connected as they arrive: point-to-point flows and nobody owning the cross-channel order record (Kestrel & Pine's thirty-four integrations and three definitions of 'order'); acceptable only as a transition.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say what prevents duplicate sales orders in the ERP.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: a platform webhook fires twice and the nightly order batch to the ERP is re-run after a partial failure. What goes wrong, and what prevents and detects it?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The ERP holds two sales orders and double revenue for one order. The batch enforces one ERP document per order number (idempotent handling), reports per line rather than per file, and a daily count of orders in the OMS against sales orders in the ERP detects a difference; after posting, a reversing entry referencing the original.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: What the ERP keeps in a commerce business (the ledger, purchasing, stock valuation, master records); how it becomes the hub by accident and why the storefront's need for fresh stock cannot wait for the accounting cycle; which facts the ERP owns, which it consumes and how often each must move; the ERP compared with a commerce platform or an OMS as the hub; Eva's €235 order, payment, fee, shipment and any refund becoming postings for Sanne de Wit's April close. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's ERP connector and incidents, and ERP and connector vendors' documentation.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: What does the ERP do in a commerce business, what should it own, and should it be the hub of integration?
thesis.claim: The ERP keeps the ledger, purchasing, inventory valuation and the master data for items, costs and business customers' prices, terms and credit; it should own only those facts and receive orders, shipments and payments by batch from their owners. It can be the hub while one channel sells from one warehouse; once several channels create orders needing availability in seconds, an OMS is the hub and no sale waits on the ERP.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that the ERP is the natural hub because it already holds items, stock, prices, customers and orders: every system should connect through it, channels should read stock and prices from it, and the connector its implementation partner built is part of the ERP relationship rather than a contract the merchant owns.
thesis.so_what: At Kestrel & Pine the ERP sat in the stock chain between the WMS and the platform, adding up to an hour to the delay behind the Black Friday Oversell; its partner-built connector, undocumented and not idempotent, carried the German price-list push that failed silently in the Price Drift and invoiced only on the WMS 'order complete' message that left #1052877 'Not invoiced' for six days; and January 2027's close took eleven working days because marketplace orders arrived as a weekly summary and store sales as a nightly total. Waypoint's finance-only rule takes the ERP out of every real-time path and retires the connector flow by flow after Ruben Alves writes its field-level contract. A merchant that accepts the claim names a system of record per flow with a rule for disagreement, and writes its ERP connector's contract before replacing it.
thesis.how_why: A ledger needs every order, shipment, payment and refund once and complete, not within the minute, and a finance system changes in careful releases under audit, so a daily batch suits it. Availability and order status change by the minute and with the storefront's frequent releases, so a stock figure or status routed through the ERP's cycle arrives late and changes at the ERP's pace. With one channel and one warehouse there are no separate order and stock systems to integrate, so an ERP-centered store is the cheapest design; when stores, wholesale and marketplaces each create orders, they need one cross-channel order record and an availability calculation that an ERP's batch cycle cannot serve. A connector only its builder can read cannot be checked, changed or replaced, so its field-level contract is what the merchant must own.

role.contribution: Places the ERP behind every channel: the system of record for finance that receives by batch and publishes what it owns for channels as events, the hub decision by scale stage, and the partner's connector as a contract the merchant owns; performs the part's closing (the published chapter does not yet do so: it ends with Questions to Ask and a one-paragraph hand-off to Part VI).

transition_in.carries_over: The documents of the EDI chapter, which end in the ledger: invoices and credit notes the ERP numbers and issues, with their transmission status, and the terms, credit limits and wholesale prices the B2B chapter assigned to the ERP.
transition_in.introduces: What the ERP, the system that keeps the ledger, should own in a commerce business, what it receives and how often, and whether it should be the hub everything else connects through.

parts.title: Part VI — INTEGRATION: Making Separate Systems Behave Like One

know: The five questions Part VI asks of every join between systems, and the answer each chapter gives: the exchange style and trigger chosen per flow, with an owner in the integration inventory; the idempotency key, the outbox or webhook plus sweep, compensation and the reconciliation job; the contract's four parts, with each pinned version and its sunset date; the master, cross-reference and matching rules per shared entity; one owned definition per metric, published with its bridge.

Kestrel & Pine's joins in 2027: 34 integrations among thirteen systems, 13 of them with no named owner in January 2027 and 5 still unowned in April 2027, and 3 with a reconciliation job, none for stock or orders; and the Waypoint answers: W5's integration standards, W7's metric definitions and the June 2027 customer-identity rule.
believe: Two systems that each work can still break a promise at the exchange between them; they agree because each join has been decided and written down, not because a newer integration tool or a faster sync was bought.
Every message may arrive late, twice or out of order, so copies will disagree for a while; a design is sound when a repeat does nothing and a comparison finds what remains.
Moving the data is half the work: systems agree only when they mean the same customer, product and order by it.
can_do: For any flow at their own company, name its style and trigger, its owner, the key that makes a repeat harmless, the job that compares its two ends, the version it pins and that version's sunset date, the master of each entity it carries, and the definition behind any number reported from it.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every supporting claim of the part thesis is argued by at least one chapter, and every chapter supports at least one.
Each chapter's closing hand-off expresses the relationship its successor declares in transition_in.

Given five integration failures, a reader who has read only Part VI names for each the decision that was missing at the join, before naming a new integration platform, a faster sync or a customer data platform.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A brand's warehouse ships one order twice after a retry; its storefront stock drifts from the warehouse for months without anyone noticing; one marketplace sells from two-day-old stock after a vendor retires an API version; its planned loyalty program cannot tell whether a store customer and an online customer are the same person; and three managers bring three different February order counts to one meeting. Using only Part VI: what was missing in each case?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A receiver that recognizes the repeat by an idempotency key naming the business action (the order number); a reconciliation job comparing the copy with the system of record, with a key, a tolerance, a cadence and a named recipient, which fixes the copy and finds the writer that should not write; a pinned version and its sunset date in the integration inventory with an owner who reads the vendor's notices; a named master per entity with a cross-reference of every system's identifier and written matching rules; one owned definition of an order, published with the bridge to each system's count. Not a new integration platform, a faster sync or a customer data platform alone.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The page that carries the part's closing sets the part's incidents against the opening's order that reaches the warehouse twice, stock update that arrives after the last unit has sold and invoice whose customer finance cannot identify, and states what the incidents have in common; it does not only list the part's questions and hand off to Part VII.

thesis.question: How do separately owned systems behave like one platform?
thesis.claim: They behave like one only where each join is decided: an exchange style chosen for the flow's freshness and failure needs, with a named owner; receivers that make a repeated message harmless, and a reconciliation job that shows two systems' copies agree; a contract that records each pinned version and its sunset date; one master and a cross-reference per shared customer or product; one owned definition per reported metric.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that integration is a tooling choice: buy an integration platform or make the company event-driven, leave duplicates and lost messages to the platform's retries, let each vendor connector map fields and identifiers its own way, and treat differing numbers as a reporting problem for the data team.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim writes, for each flow, an inventory row with an owner, a key, a comparison, a pinned version and a date before it buys integration tooling, and names a master per entity and an owner per metric before it builds loyalty programs or dashboards. At Kestrel & Pine, 13 of 34 integrations had no named owner in January 2027 (5 were still unowned in April 2027) and only 3 had a reconciliation job, none for stock or orders; in the same months 212 returns were refunded twice (€19,400), the bol marketplace sold from two-day-old stock after an API version retired on 8 February 2027, one customer, Eva Janssen, existed as four records, and February's orders were counted as 21,050, 22,710 and 24,140.
thesis.how_why: Each system is run by a different team or vendor and changes on its own schedule. Queues and webhooks would rather repeat a message than lose it, so delivery is at least once and unordered; a copy nobody compares drifts silently; a vendor retires a version on a date it chooses; each system keys people and products by what its own job has; and each counts what it exists to handle. Faster or more reliable transport removes none of these differences; a recorded decision with an owner turns each into a check someone runs.

supporting_claims.claim: The exchange style (file, shared database, direct call, message) and its trigger are chosen per flow from its freshness, consistency, latency and availability needs: stock, orders and prices by events with a reconciliation net, products by scheduled publication, finance by a checked daily batch; and every flow has a row in an integration inventory with a named owner.

Delivery between systems is at least once and unordered, so each receiver makes a repeat harmless with an idempotency key that names the business action, events are published with the change they describe (an outbox, or a webhook plus a periodic sweep), partial work is undone by compensation, and a reconciliation job with a key, tolerance, cadence and recipient shows whether copies agree, fixing them from the system of record.

A contract states shape, meaning, timing and lifetime; a provider changes it by adding what consumers can ignore and retires a version on an announced date pair while monitoring who still calls it; a consumer records each pinned version and its sunset date with an owner, and treats webhooks as signed hints to verify, deduplicate and sweep.

Each shared entity has one named master (the shop platform for consumers, the ERP for business customers, the PIM or the ERP item master for products), a cross-reference of every other system's identifier with a reversible merge log, and written matching and survivorship rules; the exact operational master feeds the fuzzy marketing profile, never the reverse.

Operational systems count what they exist to handle, from the records that reach them, on their own dates, so honest counts differ; a metric is defined once with an owner, computed in one analytical store fed by every system, and published with the bridge to each system's count.

role.contribution: Gives the mechanisms by which copies learn from records and disagreements are found.

additional_patterns.applies_to: integration-styles to api-contracts-and-versioning: how data moves between systems, how a flow recovers and how an interface changes; identity-and-master-data and commerce-data-and-analytics: what the moved data means, as entities and as numbers

flow.rationale: Each chapter uses what the one before it fixed. Integration styles comes first because it gives the vocabulary the rest of the part relies on (styles, triggers, webhooks, the iPaaS and the integration inventory) and states the per-flow rule whose 'idempotent handling and a reconciliation job' the next chapter explains. Events and reconciliation needs the asynchronous styles and webhook plus sweep to explain why duplicates and gaps are normal. API contracts adds two columns to the inventory and relies on the previous chapter's idempotency and sweeps for its webhook rules. Identity comes after the transport chapters partly as a framing choice (its point is that transport is not the hard part: messages delivered, recovered and versioned still do not say whether two records are one customer) and partly by need: its cross-reference replaces identifier mappings that the integration-styles chapter showed living inside connectors, and it is fed by the flows that chapter inventoried. Analytics comes last because it consumes everything before it: copies of every flow, the sweep idea for extraction, and the customer master it defers the customer metric to. Putting reconciliation before styles would teach recovery for deliveries the reader has not met; putting contracts before events would leave webhook deduplication unexplained; putting analytics before identity would leave its customer counts undefined.

hook.content: An order reaches the warehouse twice, a stock update arrives after the last unit has sold, or an invoice names a customer the finance system cannot identify; the systems at either end can work correctly while the exchange between them fails.

opening.bridge: From Eva's order crossing from checkout to the warehouse and finance, with payment success arriving separately, picking changing what channels may sell and her exchange adding return and replacement records, to the joins those steps depend on: Kestrel & Pine's thirteen systems and 34 integrations, and the Waypoint decisions on integration standards, metric definitions and customer identity.
opening.roadmap: Five chapters, one question each: how to choose files, shared databases, direct calls or messages for each flow (the inventory that found 13 unowned integrations in January 2027); how to retry safely and recover from disagreement with idempotency, the outbox and reconciliation (the Double Refund and the first stock reconciliation); how to manage interface changes and retirement dates (the Deprecated Endpoint); how to connect records that refer to the same customer or product (Eva's four records); and why valid reports disagree (February's 21,050, 22,710 and 24,140 orders).

closing.synthesis: The Black Friday stock chain, the Double Refund, the Deprecated Endpoint, Eva's four records and February's three order counts look like five problems in five technologies: a sync interval, a refund API, a vendor's version, a loyalty list and a BI tool. Read together they are one: in each, both ends worked and something about the join had not been decided (who owns it, which key makes a repeat harmless, what compares the two ends, which version expires when, which record is the master, which definition counts). Each chapter's remedy is a record written down, not a new system: an inventory row with an owner, an idempotency key and a reconciliation card, a contract card, a cross-reference with a merge log, a definition with its bridge.
closing.so_what: Kestrel & Pine's remedies were written records with owners, not new systems: W5 (integration standards) gives every flow an owner, a contract and a reconciliation job; Eva's four records became one master with three links in July 2027; and February 2027 was restated as 23,150 orders with a bridge to each system's count. A reader can start the same inventory for their own landscape, one row per flow with its owner, key, check and version, beginning with the unowned rows.
closing.callback: The part opening's order that reaches the warehouse twice, stock update that arrives after the last unit has sold and invoice whose customer finance cannot identify, where the systems at either end work and the exchange fails.

takeaway.content: Build the integration inventory for your own landscape: one row per flow with its style and trigger, owner, system of record, idempotency key, pinned version and sunset date, and reconciliation job; then name a master and a cross-reference for customers and products and an owner for the definition of an order. Start with the rows that have no owner and the flows that move stock, orders or money with nothing comparing their two ends.

transition_in.carries_over: The many systems and channels of Parts II to V, each holding copies of the same facts.
transition_in.introduces: The joins between them as a design subject of their own.

posts.title: Part 6 introduction
posts.question: What does this part argue, and in what order should its chapters be read?

know: Part VI answers five questions in order: how systems talk (files, shared databases, direct calls or messages, chosen per flow); how they retry safely and recover from disagreement (idempotency, the outbox, reconciliation); how their interfaces change and retire (versions and retirement dates); how records that refer to the same customer or product are connected; and why valid reports disagree.

Kestrel & Pine's starting point: thirteen systems and 34 integrations, 13 of them with nobody to call in January 2027, and the Waypoint decisions that answer the part (integration standards, shared metric definitions and customer identity rules).

That a join can fail while the systems at both ends work, and that the part sits under every step of Eva's order: checkout to warehouse and finance, payment success, stock after picking, the exchange.
can_do: Pick the Part VI chapter that answers the decision in front of them.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of this page alone can name the five chapters' subjects in reading order.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only this page: what will each of the next five chapters tell you, in order?
acceptance_criteria.expected: How to choose files, shared databases, direct calls or messages for each flow, with an owner per flow; how to retry safely and recover when systems disagree (idempotency, the outbox, reconciliation); how interfaces change and when versions retire; how to connect records that refer to the same customer or product; why valid reports show different order counts and how one definition separates expected differences from missing data.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of this page alone can say why an exchange between two working systems can still fail, and what the merchant has to add besides an integration tool.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: how can an order be lost or doubled, or a customer go unrecognized, when every system involved is working, and what does Kestrel & Pine add besides its integration tool?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The failure is in the exchange: a message arrives late, twice, in the wrong shape or not at all, or the two systems mean different things by a customer or an order. Kestrel & Pine adds decisions: an owner and a check per flow, safe retries and reconciliation, versions and deadlines on contracts, customer identity rules and shared metric definitions; the integration tool alone cannot supply that ownership.

role.contribution: Performs the part's opening: states the part thesis in its three key points, places the part under every step of Eva's order, gives Kestrel & Pine's thirteen systems and 34 integrations with the 13 unowned in January 2027, and gives the reading order.

posts.title: APIs, Events, Files and Middleware: How Commerce Systems Talk
posts.question: What ways do systems have to exchange data, and when is each the right choice?

know: The four integration styles (file, shared database, direct call, message), the five triggers (call, webhook, poll, schedule, change data capture) and the three ways to wire a landscape (point to point, a hub such as an iPaaS, a vendor's connector), each with a commerce example.

The needs that decide a flow's style (freshness, consistency, latency, availability) for stock, orders, prices, products, customers and finance, and the rule Waypoint's W5 adopts: stock, orders and prices by events, products by scheduled publication, finance by daily batch.
The integration inventory's columns and the book's operational definition of integration debt: the integrations whose owner, contract version, failure alert and reconciliation job are unknown.
believe: The style is chosen per flow, never for the company.
A webhook is a notification, not a guarantee, and a hub without owners, contracts and reconciliation is the same tangle in one place.
An inventory with a named owner on every row is worth more than any integration tool.
can_do: Classify any integration by style and trigger, and say what it does when the other side is down and whether anyone owns it.
Choose the style and trigger for a flow from its needs and the business's scale stage, and start an integration inventory with an owner per row.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a scheduled stock chain and a peak order rate, the reader names the oversell window and the style each flow should use, and starts with an inventory rather than a new tool.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A brand sends stock from its warehouse system to its ERP every 15 minutes, from the ERP to the storefront hourly and from the storefront to its marketplaces hourly; orders reach the warehouse through a webhook into an integration platform; finance receives orders by an hourly copy. In the peak hour the shop takes 38 orders a minute. Using only this chapter: what is wrong with the stock flow, which style should each flow use, and what is the first management step?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The oversell window is the sum of the intervals, up to about two hours; at 38 orders a minute, fifteen minutes alone is 570 orders. Stock should move as events per SKU and location into an availability service, with a reconciliation and a safety buffer; orders as webhook or event with a polling sweep and consumers that ignore repeats; finance by a daily batch checked against the payment provider's payouts. The first step is an integration inventory with one row per flow and a named owner on every row. Not a new integration platform alone.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say why 'we use webhooks, so nothing gets lost' is wrong.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A colleague says: 'We use webhooks, so we are event-driven and nothing gets lost.' Using only this chapter: what is wrong with that, and what should be added?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A webhook is a trigger, not a style or a guarantee: Shopify and Stripe document that deliveries can be missed, duplicated and reordered, and Shopify deletes a subscription after eight consecutive failed deliveries. Each webhook flow needs a periodic sweep or reconciliation job that fetches what was missed, receivers that handle repeats, and an alert when the flow goes quiet.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say when an iPaaS pays for itself and what a hub does not provide.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: when is a hosted integration platform worth buying, how should vendors be compared, and what does it not give you?
acceptance_criteria.expected: When the number of flows and builders makes point-to-point connectors unmanageable, usually at the Omnichannel stage; vendors meter different units, so they are compared per flow at the merchant's volume. A hub centralizes mapping, retries and monitoring but not ownership: without an owner, a contract and a reconciliation per flow it recreates the tangle in one tool.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Why a lost or doubled handoff from storefront to warehouse reaches the customer; what an integration is and what its design decides; the four ways systems exchange data and the triggers and tools that connect them; how to choose per flow by timing and recovery needs; the integration inventory as the first management tool; recovery from duplicates and changing contracts left to the next two chapters; Eva's order crossing from the platform to the warehouse and stock changes travelling back. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's Black Friday delay and its 34 integrations, and vendor documentation.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: What ways do systems have to exchange data, and when is each the right choice?
thesis.claim: Systems exchange data by file, shared database, direct call or message, triggered by a call, webhook, poll, schedule or database change log. The flow decides, not the company: stock, orders and prices by events checked by a reconciliation job, products by scheduled publication, finance by a checked daily batch, direct calls only where the next step needs the answer; every flow needs a named owner in an integration inventory.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that integration is a company-wide strategy or a tool purchase ('we are event-driven now', 'the iPaaS is our integration layer'): one style serves every flow, and a hub or a vendor's connector supplies the ownership.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim chooses each flow's style from that flow's needs, as Kestrel & Pine's W5 does, and puts no flow live without an inventory row and an owner. Noor Visser's inventory found 34 integrations (9 file or batch, 1 shared-database read, 11 direct calls, 13 event, webhook or queue flows); 13 had no named owner in January 2027 and 5 were still unowned in April 2027; only 3 had a reconciliation job, none for stock or orders. On Black Friday 2026 a 15-minute hop and two hourly hops let channels sell sold-out stock for up to two hours; at the peak hour's 38 orders a minute, even one 15-minute interval is 570 orders.
