posts.title: Apps, Plugins and Functions: Extensibility and Ecosystem Governance
posts.question: How do platforms let merchants and partners extend them without breaking them, and how should a merchant govern its apps?

know: The five ways to extend a platform (in-process plugins, theme code, apps over APIs with scopes, functions, synchronous call-outs), placed by where they run, what they may touch and how tightly they are tied to the vendor's releases, with dated vendor examples.
The app store as a business and as governance: what review checks (least scope, performance, clean uninstall, privacy webhooks) and what it cannot see.
The Forked Platform and its hosted mirror: upgrade cost and the vendor's support clock (Adobe), and extension points withdrawn on announced dates (Shopify's checkout template and Scripts).
believe: App review protects the platform and the shopper; which app may write stock or prices is the merchant's decision, and no vendor can make it.
One writer per fact: set and adjust do not mix on one number.
A platform the merchant cannot upgrade is a platform it has already left; custom behavior belongs on the lowest rung that works, never in the core.
can_do: Place any extension on the mechanism table and say which failure it risks.
Run the one-writer-per-fact test on their own app list, and write an app governance card with owner, scopes, API version and support end, review date and exit plan.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given two apps writing one stock figure, the reader explains why review did not catch it and names the merchant's governance, not a better app.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A brand finds the stock shown on its storefront drifting away from its warehouse count. The warehouse feed sets each variant's stock every hour; a pre-order app subtracts pre-ordered quantities from the same number; both passed the platform's app review. Using only this chapter: why did review not catch this, and what should the brand change?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Each app passed review alone and asked for its write scope for a reason; review cannot know which system owns stock in this business. Setting and adjusting one number make it drift from both. One writer per fact (the warehouse feed, later an availability service), the pre-order app's write scope revoked and pre-orders held in their own state; an owner, scopes and API version on a card per app; a reconciliation job comparing the platform with the warehouse; a quarterly uninstall review.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say what risk deep customization carries on a self-run platform and on a hosted one, and how each is managed.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: one merchant runs an open-source or suite platform with years of custom modules in the core; another runs a hosted platform with checkout customizations built on the vendor's extension points. What risk does each carry, and how is it managed?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The first is the Forked Platform: in-process code ties every upgrade to the core, upgrade cost grows with the number and quality of modules, and the vendor's support clock turns a postponed upgrade into a forced migration (Adobe stops maintaining cloud environments on unsupported versions from 1 June 2027); manage the module count, an upgrade calendar and moving logic out of process. The second carries deprecation risk: hosted platforms withdraw extension points on announced dates (Shopify's checkout template in August 2024, Scripts in June 2026); record which date each app depends on and move before it. One app inventory manages both.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say where a new custom behavior should be built.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: the business asks for a behavior the platform does not have. Where should it be built?
acceptance_criteria.expected: On the lowest rung that works: configuration first, then a platform extension point (a function, call-out or workflow), then a public app for a commodity capability, then a custom app with a named owner and a pinned API version; an in-process plugin only rarely, where synchronous control of the core is needed; an edit to the core never.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Why installing an app for a missing feature also decides which business facts another program may control; how two extensions changing the same fact (a pre-order app and a warehouse feed) make availability unreliable, and why permissions and an owner are assigned at installation; Kestrel & Pine's 41 apps, 6 unused and 3 writing stock, and the April 2027 ownership rule; Eva's product page with a size guide, stock badge and reviews; how platforms let other code change them, what each mechanism may touch, why apps sprawl and how to govern them. Evidence: vendors' documentation and Kestrel & Pine's app inventory.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: How do platforms let merchants and partners extend them without breaking them, and how should a merchant govern its apps?
thesis.claim: Platforms bound extensions by where code runs: an in-process plugin can reach the core's code and data and ties every upgrade to it; an app reaches only its granted scopes on a dated API version; a function gets a fixed input, output and time budget. App review cannot see two apps writing one business fact, so the merchant governs: an owner, scopes and API version per app, one writer per fact such as stock or price.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that the app store's review keeps installed apps safe, so a merchant may install whatever the business asks for, let its agency add apps as needed, and modify the platform's core or theme when no app fits.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim keeps a card per app (owner, scopes, API version and support end, review date, exit plan), names one writer per fact and revokes every other write scope on it, runs a quarterly uninstall review, and puts custom behavior on the lowest rung that works. In March 2026 Kestrel & Pine's warehouse feed set stock every hour while a pre-order app adjusted it, giving two weeks of phantom reservations on 600 variants. The April 2027 inventory found 41 apps (about €2,900 a month, illustrative), 6 unused and 3 able to write inventory; the May 2027 reconciliation found 2.3% of active variants with a different quantity, most from those apps. Under the governance rule approved that April, the 6 were uninstalled, write access was withdrawn from the 3 by June 2027, and 34 apps remained in July at about €2,400 a month.
thesis.how_why: The deeper extension code sits, the more it can touch and the more each vendor release can break it: an in-process module must stay compatible with every core version, the vendor's support clock turns a postponed upgrade into a forced migration, and hosted platforms retire extension points on dates they announce. Each app passes review alone and asks for the write scope its job needs; which system owns stock or price is a decision about the merchant's business that no vendor sees, so an app that sets a number and another that adjusts it both work while the number drifts from both. Only the merchant's own list of owners, scopes and writers connects them.

role.contribution: Governs the spenders of the merchant's budget and the code that changes its platform: the five extension mechanisms placed by what they may touch and how they age, what app review does and does not protect, the one-writer-per-fact rule, the app governance card and the ladder for where custom behavior lives.

transition_in.carries_over: The previous chapter's finding that the API budget a merchant spends on a shared platform is spent mostly by apps and connectors, with nobody ranking them.
transition_in.introduces: The apps themselves: how platforms let other people's code in, what each mechanism may touch, and how a merchant with 41 apps, 6 unused and 3 writing stock should govern them.

posts.title: Delivering the Storefront: Themes, Headless, Rendering and Performance
posts.question: How does the storefront reach the shopper's browser, and when does headless make sense?

know: What a storefront owns (templates, layout, brand, browser scripts) and what it renders from other systems; the three rendering models (a theme rendered by the platform, headless on the vendor's runtime, headless anywhere), with checkout on the platform under all three.
'Cache the shell, fetch the promise' and the requirements per page type; Core Web Vitals with their thresholds and dates, and the dated, caveated evidence that speed moves sales.
Technical SEO as part of the storefront's contract, and accessibility as a dated obligation (WCAG 2.2; the European Accessibility Act applying since 28 June 2025).
believe: A storefront renders facts it does not own; a new renderer moves rendering and glue, not facts.
The usual cause of a slow page is the scripts, not the rendering model.
Go headless for a need the theme cannot meet and a team that can run it, never for speed alone.
can_do: Read field Core Web Vitals at the 75th percentile and trace a slow metric to its cause before choosing a remedy.
Set a cache and freshness rule per page type, and judge a headless proposal against the three needs and the team that would run it.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a headless proposal and field measurements, the reader decides from the measurements and the three needs, not from the promise of speed.
acceptance_criteria.probe: An agency proposes rebuilding a brand's three country storefronts as a headless application for about €240,000 and nine months, promising speed, flexible brand content and readiness for the future. Field measurements on mobile product pages at the 75th percentile show the main content in 2.1 seconds, interaction response in 310 milliseconds and layout shift of 0.08, and the slow interaction traces to scripts from eleven apps. Using only this chapter: should the brand accept, and what should it do instead?
acceptance_criteria.expected: No. Content loading and layout stability are already within Google's good thresholds (2.5 seconds, 0.1); interaction above 200 milliseconds is caused by app scripts, which a new renderer would not remove, so the remedy is a theme performance pass, an app-script audit and a performance budget. A content need is met by theme sections or a content system feeding the theme. Headless is for a shared front end across brands, a content-led site or a B2B portal the theme cannot express, with a team that can run a second production application; none applies to one brand with three storefront engineers.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say which parts of a product page are cached and which are fetched live, and what breaks when the rule is broken.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: which parts of a product page can be cached and which must be fetched or checked live, and what goes wrong in each direction?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Product content, images, attributes and layout per market and language, category pages and editorial pages are cached, with request collapsing on a miss at peak; account prices, stock commitments, the cart and checkout are fetched or validated live, and public price or stock snapshots carry a freshness limit; account-specific answers are never shared across customers. A cached promise shows a wrong price or sells the last unit twice (the Price Drift, the Oversell); an uncacheable page saturates the renderer and the APIs behind it at peak.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say what the storefront owes search engines and shoppers with disabilities, and who owns it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: besides speed, what does a storefront owe search engines and shoppers with disabilities?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Product pages that can be crawled and indexed, whose rendered content and structured product data agree, with explicit rules for variants, filters, localized pages and retired products, checked by a named owner after each release; and WCAG 2.2 conformance of the theme and every app block, required for consumer e-commerce under the European Accessibility Act since 28 June 2025.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Why a slow product page can lose a sale and why a new page that waits on the same slow price, stock or script inherits the problem; what a storefront and a headless storefront are, and what running one adds; Kestrel & Pine's three storefronts on one agency theme, its 41 apps and peak traffic 41 times an average hour, and Noor Visser's decision on the February 2027 headless proposal; Eva seeing the jacket's price, stock and delivery promise on her phone; following product pages to shoppers and search engines, comparing rendering models and judging when a separate storefront is worthwhile. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's field measurements and dated vendor documentation and performance studies.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: How does the storefront reach the shopper's browser, and when does headless make sense?
thesis.claim: The storefront renders facts other systems own, from a platform-rendered theme or a headless front end on the vendor's runtime or elsewhere; checkout stays on the platform under every model. Content is cached per market at the edge; price, stock and cart are fetched or validated live. Headless pays only for a shared front end across brands, a content-led site or a B2B portal the theme cannot express, with a team to run it; never for speed alone.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that headless is the modern storefront: an agency-built front end on a fast framework makes pages faster and converts better, so a merchant with a slow theme should rebuild its storefront rather than fix what runs on the theme.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim reads field Core Web Vitals before any rebuild, traces a slow metric to its cause, sets a cache rule per page type, and asks a headless proposal which of the three needs it serves and who will run it in year two. In February 2027 Kestrel & Pine's agency proposed a headless rebuild on the platform vendor's edge runtime with a headless CMS (about €240,000 and nine months, plus a second runtime to operate; illustrative). Noor Visser measured the NL product pages on mobile at the 75th percentile (LCP 2.1 s, INP 310 ms, CLS 0.08), found the INP problem in eleven apps' scripts and declined. A quarter of agency time (about €38,000) went to a theme performance pass and an app-script audit, and by June 2027 INP measured 180 ms after six unused apps and four redundant scripts were removed. The decision is part of W4 and is revisited at the 2029 review.
thesis.how_why: The storefront owns templates, layout and scripts, not the catalog, prices, stock or cart, so a new renderer moves the rendering and the glue into the merchant's hands without moving any fact, and a slow price or stock answer or a heavy app script slows a headless page as much as a themed one. Content changes when the catalog changes, so it can be computed once and served to many shoppers from the edge, collapsing requests at peak; price, stock and cart change per shopper or per sale, and a cached copy of them is how the Price Drift and the Oversell reached the page. A headless front end is a second production application with on-call, caching rules, framework upgrades and API version pins, which a team of three that also runs the apps can carry only when the theme blocks a real need.

role.contribution: Gives the part its surface to the shopper: the storefront as a renderer of facts it does not own, the three rendering models with checkout left on the platform, the rule 'cache the shell, fetch the promise' that the peak relies on, and the three needs that justify headless.

transition_in.carries_over: The apps of the previous chapter, which mostly land on one surface through theme code, app blocks and scripts.
transition_in.introduces: The storefront where that code meets the shopper's browser: the three rendering models, the cache rule per page type, and the headless proposal Noor Visser declined in February 2027.

posts.title: Black Friday Every Year: Peak Load, Resilience and Recovery
posts.question: How do you prepare a commerce platform and its integrations for a day with forty times the normal traffic?

know: Peak profiles (seasonal, launch, flash sale, unplanned) and why the platform's peak is not the merchant's: the largest operators each report in their own unit, and Shopify's 2025 figures give a peak about twice its average against Kestrel & Pine's about seventy.

The chain read from the front (storefront, checkout and payment, order export, warehouse and people, stock loop, back office), with a requirement per flow; queues and backpressure, caching, waiting rooms and a degradation ladder.
Orders per minute as the health signal and the unit for SLOs, the situation room and runbook, and recovery as reconciliation followed by a post-mortem.
believe: The platform's peak is not the merchant's peak: the storefront usually holds, and the chain behind it is where the day is lost.
Every link is measured in one unit, orders per minute; checkout, payment and the order record are never switched off.
Recovery is reconciliation, and the peak plan is a year-round product with one owner.
can_do: Find the slowest link of their own chain in orders per minute and test every link above the forecast.
Write a switch-off order with owners and triggers, and name before the day who compares which systems the morning after.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a peak where the storefront held and the chain behind it failed, the reader explains why and plans the next peak around the chain, not the storefront.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A brand takes about 33 online orders in an average hour and 2,300 in its Black Friday peak hour. Its storefront and checkout held, but orders reached the warehouse hours late and the channels kept selling a sold-out jacket for up to two hours. Using only this chapter: why did the storefront hold while the rest failed, and how should next year be prepared?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The hosted platform smooths many merchants' spikes (its peak is about twice its average) and serves most traffic from its CDN, while the brand's own chain saw about seventy times its average hour alone; the order export carried about seven orders a minute against 38, and the stock loop's sync intervals became an oversell window. Prepare: a forecast in orders per minute with every link tested above it; orders sent to the warehouse in batches within its rate limit, idempotent on the order number, with a gauge on the oldest unsent order, an alarm and a dead-letter queue; stock by events with per-channel buffers; a written switch-off order with owners, rehearsed; a freeze; a situation room with an incident commander; a reconciliation the morning after. Not a faster storefront or a waiting room alone.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say what may be switched off at peak, what never is, and what makes a switch usable.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: what should a merchant switch off when its chain falls behind at peak, what must never be switched off, and what makes a switch usable on the day?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Non-essential features that add load or risk go first in a planned order (for example recommendations, search facets, exact stock counts replaced by buffered badges, a wider delivery promise), while work behind the order record (order export, ERP, notifications, invoicing) queues and waits; checkout, payment and the order record are never switched off. A switch is usable when it has been flipped in a test before the peak, has one named owner who may flip it without a meeting, and its place in the order was decided in a calm month by the people who own the revenue.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say what recovery after a peak consists of.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: what should happen the morning after a peak?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A reconciliation planned before the day: orders compared across the platform, the order system and the warehouse by order number, stock per SKU between the warehouse and the availability service, payments captured against orders, with the owner of each difference named; messages in the dead-letter queue replayed once the cause is fixed and checked to have arrived once; then a blameless post-mortem within two weeks, with the timeline in orders per minute and every action assigned.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Why an integration that keeps up on an ordinary day (about 800 orders, roughly 33 an hour) builds a backlog at 2,300 in one hour while the store looks healthy; that order export, stock updates and picking each have their own capacity; testing the whole order path at the busiest hour's rate; Eva's order reaching the warehouse within minutes and what happens when thousands take that path; how to size, test, protect and observe the chain in orders per minute and recover afterwards. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's Black Friday 2026 post-mortem and dated peak figures from large operators.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: How do you prepare a commerce platform and its integrations for a day with forty times the normal traffic?
thesis.claim: A hosted platform smooths many merchants' spikes, so its storefront and checkout usually hold; the merchant's own chain meets its spike alone, and its integrations fail before the storefront. Prepare by measuring every link in orders per minute, testing above the forecast, queuing work behind checkout with gauged queues, writing a switch-off order that never touches checkout, payment or the order record, and naming who reconciles the systems the morning after.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that peak readiness is the platform vendor's job: a hosted platform scales automatically, so a merchant prepares by load-testing the storefront, buying a higher tier or a waiting room and adding support staff, and leaves its integrations to run as on any other day.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim names a year-round owner for the peak plan, forecasts in orders per minute and tests each link above the forecast, gauges the age of its queues, writes and rehearses a degradation ladder with owners, staffs a room with an incident commander and schedules the reconciliation before the day. In Black Friday week 2026 Kestrel & Pine took 31,000 orders, 2,300 of them in the peak hour (38 a minute); the platform held, the order flow carried about seven a minute and built a four-hour backlog, and the stock chain let channels sell the sold-out Ridgewalker jacket for up to two hours: 1,340 units oversold, 1,120 orders canceled or delayed, about €96,000. The 2027 plan, approved with Waypoint in March 2027, forecasts 60 orders a minute and tests every link at 80, sends fulfillment orders from the OMS to the WMS in batches (tested at 120 a minute), sets a 15 October go/no-go for the availability service, has eight switches with owners, a freeze from 15 November to 5 December, and a reconciliation report at 08:00 on Saturday 27 November.
thesis.how_why: The platform serves many merchants whose spikes fall at different hours, so its peak is about twice its average and its CDN absorbs most requests before application code; Kestrel & Pine's storefront traffic rose to 41 times an average hour and its order rate to about seventy (2,300 orders against 33). Each link behind checkout has a fixed capacity (rate limits at both ends, one order at a time), so the slowest one builds a queue at the difference between arrival and capacity (31 orders a minute in 2026) that nobody sees without a gauge, and every sync interval becomes an oversell window in proportion to the sales rate. Recording the order fast and queuing everything behind it keeps the money path working, switches flipped in rehearsal remove load in a planned order, and retries under load leave duplicates and gaps that only a comparison by order number afterwards finds.

role.contribution: Tests the part's answers on the day they matter: the platform's smoothed peak against the merchant's own spike, the chain sized in orders per minute, queues, a switch-off order and reconciliation as recovery; performs the part's closing (the published chapter does not yet do so: it ends with one sentence on the peak and the hand-off to Part VIII).

transition_in.carries_over: The storefront of the previous chapter, whose cacheable pages let it survive a peak hour at many times normal traffic.
transition_in.introduces: The chain behind the storefront, which meets the merchant's spike alone and fails first, and how to size, test, protect and recover it.

parts.title: Part VIII — TRUST: Security, Privacy and Regulation

know: The three questions Part VIII asks of a merchant that rents its platform, and the answer each chapter gives: which doors are open to a script and who holds the key to each (a hosted checkout that keeps card numbers out, challenges and a decline-rate alert on every endpoint that can pay or log in, an owned inventory of checkout scripts, one identity and scoped key with an owner per person, app and integration); which systems hold a person, in which legal role and for how long (a privacy map, consent with its evidence, the person split from the transaction, requests through an identity index and an orchestrator); and which rules land in which system of record by when (scope, data, system of record, test, date and an owner per row of one calendar).

Kestrel & Pine's three trust incidents and what followed: the Card-Testing Night of 18 to 19 August 2026 (48,000 attempts, €2,900 in fees for declined authorizations, a 40-minute pause of the PSP account) and the April 2027 security baseline; the Request From Ghent of 10 May 2027 (nine of thirteen systems, seventeen working days, the reply on 4 June 2027) and the October 2027 request orchestrator; four rules that reached engineering through four doors (December 2024, May 2025, December 2025, June 2026) and the March 2027 regulatory calendar.
believe: Attackers, people with data rights and regulators act on the systems and joins the merchant already has; none of the three needs a break-in.
On a hosted platform the vendor covers its own service, checkout and defaults; identities, keys, scripts, data copies and the fields rules require stay with the merchant.
Each of the three is a list with owners kept on the same ownership map before it is a product or a policy.
can_do: Answer 'are we secure?', 'are we GDPR compliant?' and 'are we ready for rule X?' with lists from their own landscape rather than with a product name or the vendor's certificate.

Add three columns to their ownership map: the owner and scope of every identity and key; the legal role, request action and retention clock of every system that holds personal data; the data, system of record, test, date and owner of every applicable rule.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every supporting claim of the part thesis is argued by at least one chapter, and every chapter supports at least one.
Each chapter's closing hand-off expresses the relationship its successor declares in transition_in.

Given three outside demands on a merchant that rents its platform, a reader who has read only Part VIII says for each which list with owners answers it, before naming a product, a certificate or the legal department.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A Dutch brand on a hosted platform hears three things in one month: its payment provider paused card payments overnight after thousands of declined authorizations; a customer asks for all her data to be deleted; and a marketplace starts rejecting listings that lack a manufacturer's address. Its agency says the platform is PCI certified and 'handles GDPR', and a vendor offers a compliance suite. Using only Part VIII: what should the brand do about each?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The first is card testing, the guest checkout used as built: switch on the platform's bot protection and the PSP's velocity rules, challenge payment requests with no session history, alert on the decline rate, keep a tested kill switch for guest card payments and a runbook that calls a named person; the certificate covers the vendor's service, not the brand's identities, keys, scripts and endpoints. The second needs every system that holds her, found through an identity index, with a decided action per system (erase the profile, pseudonymize orders, retain invoices, refer the carrier, marketplace and PSP), a reply within one month and a record of what was done; the person must be split from the transaction. The third is a product-safety rule read as four attributes per product, owned by the PIM, with publication blocked without them and a calendar row with a date and an owner. All three are lists on the brand's ownership map; a product comes after the list.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The page that carries the part's closing sets the part's findings against the opening's checkout that accepts a real purchase and 48,000 attempts with stolen cards by the same behavior, and states what the three incidents have in common; it does not only hand off to Part IX.

thesis.question: What must a merchant that rents its platform do about attackers, privacy law and commerce regulation, and where does that work land?
thesis.claim: Attackers, privacy law and commerce regulation act on the systems the merchant already runs and the integrations between them, while the hosted platform covers only its own service, checkout and defaults. So the merchant's work lands in lists on its map of systems, integrations and owners: every identity and key with an owner; every system holding personal data with its legal role, what a deletion request does there and how long it keeps records; every applicable rule with its data, system of record, test, date and owner.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that security, privacy and compliance are specialist disciplines apart from the commerce architecture: covered by the platform's certifications and privacy tools, by buying a bot-management, consent or compliance product, or by the legal department when a rule comes up.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim answers 'are we secure?', 'are we GDPR compliant?' and 'are we ready for this rule?' by extending the system-of-record map of Part I and the integration inventory of Part VI with three columns, and buys a product only for a list it already keeps. Kestrel & Pine met each demand without a list in 2026 and 2027: 48,000 card-testing attempts on 18 to 19 August 2026 cost €2,900 in fees and a 40-minute pause of the PSP account; a deletion request of 10 May 2027 found the customer in nine of thirteen systems and took seventeen working days; four rules reached engineering through a marketplace's error log, an agency audit, a Belgian customer and an auditor's newsletter. Its answers were lists with owners: the April 2027 security baseline (MFA enforced, one identity and restricted key per integration, a decline-rate alert and a tested kill switch), the October 2027 request orchestrator (the second request took two working days) and the March 2027 regulatory calendar with an owner per row.
thesis.how_why: Card testing and credential stuffing send normal requests to the checkout and the login, and an admin login or a leaked key bypasses every other control, so the controls sit on endpoints and identities, and a key without an owner cannot be rotated, scoped or traced. Every integration copies personal data into another system with its own legal role, and the law gives a request one month and keeps invoices for years, so a request must reach every copy with a decided action. Rules ask for fields, histories, dated events and records that only a system of record can hold, are published years before they apply and are often enforced first by partners. Vendors' shared-responsibility statements and processor roles end at their service, so whatever the merchant added is outside them, and each Kestrel & Pine incident in this part began with something nobody had on a list.

supporting_claims.claim: Card testing, credential stuffing, policy abuse and skimming need no break-in: they send ordinary requests through the payment form, the login and the admin as designed. A hosted checkout or hosted fields keeps card numbers out of the merchant's systems, and the vendor secures its service, while the merchant secures every identity, key, app, script and endpoint it adds, each with an owner, least privilege, an alert and a rehearsed response.

Every integration is also a data flow with a legal role: the merchant, as controller, knows for each system that holds a person its role, the action a request requires and its retention clock, keeps consent with its evidence on the customer master, splits the person from the transaction, and answers requests through an identity index and an orchestrator.

The consumer, product-safety, invoicing and sustainability rules this part examines are data requirements with a date (a price history, dated refund events, product-safety fields, a structured invoice, a disposition record) that belong in a system of record; they are public years before they apply and are often enforced first by partners, so each needs a calendar row with scope, system, test, date and an owner who owns the fact.

role.contribution: Adds the promises that are imposed from outside: by attackers' interest, by privacy law and by regulation.

flow.rationale: The part widens from the merchant's own doors to everything the law asks of it, and each chapter adds a column to the ownership map using what the one before it put there. Security comes first because it starts from the integration inventory and app list of Parts VI and VII and turns each row into an identity with a key and an owner, and because a skimmer found on the checkout is also a privacy incident, since card numbers are personal data. Privacy follows because it reads the same rows as data flows with a legal role and needs the identities and owners security has just named; its one-month request clock is the first dated legal duty the reader meets. Regulation comes last because it generalizes that clock to every rule with a date, and its calendar holds the earlier chapters' dated rules (the PCI script requirements of 31 March 2025, the GDPR's month, the NIS2 incident-notification clocks that vendor contracts pass to the security chapter's incident runbooks). Putting regulation first would present a calendar of rules before the reader has seen one rule turned into a field, a clock and an owner; putting privacy before security would treat integrations as data flows before anyone owns their credentials, the identities through which a breach would copy those flows.

hook.content: The checkout that accepts a real purchase can also receive automated payment attacks; the address used for delivery can remain in a forgotten export; a pricing rule can require data the shop has never collected.

opening.bridge: From Part VII's finding that a merchant's promises are kept or broken in what it owns around the platform it rents, to the promises imposed on that same layer from outside: by attackers, by people with rights over their data and by rules with a date; and to Eva's jacket, whose checkout, payment, price, product page and order clocks are governed by them, and whose name reaches every system the order touches.
opening.roadmap: Three chapters, one question each, each adding a column to the ownership map: which doors are open to a script and who holds the key to each (the Card-Testing Night of August 2026: 48,000 attempts, €2,900 in fees); which systems hold a person, in which legal role and for how long (the Request From Ghent of May 2027: nine systems, seventeen working days); and which rule lands in which system of record by when and under whose name (four rules through four doors, and the March 2027 regulatory calendar).

closing.synthesis: The Card-Testing Night, the Request From Ghent and four rules through four doors look like three disciplines (security, privacy and compliance), each with a product to buy. Read together they are one: in each, something from outside (a script, a person with rights, a rule with a date) used or demanded what the merchant already had, the platform did what its vendor promised, and the gap was an item nobody had on a list with an owner: keys and a decline rate nobody watched, a person in nine systems with no index, a field with no system of record and a date nobody tracked.
closing.so_what: Kestrel & Pine answered with three lists kept on Noor Visser's ownership map rather than three products: the April 2027 security baseline (one identity and restricted key per integration with an owner, MFA enforced, a decline-rate alert at three times the 30-day median, a guest-card kill switch tested quarterly, a checkout script inventory, three runbooks); the privacy map with the October 2027 request orchestrator, which answered the second request in two working days; and the March 2027 regulatory calendar with an owner per row, most of them not engineers. A reader can extend their own map with the same three columns.
closing.callback: The part opening's checkout that accepts a real purchase and 48,000 attempts with stolen cards by the same behavior.

takeaway.content: Add three columns to your ownership map: for every identity and key, its owner and scope; for every system that holds personal data, its legal role, the action a request requires and its retention clock; for every rule that applies, its data, system of record, test, date and owner. Start with the integrations that have no named owner, because each is a key, a data flow and a fact at once.

transition_in.carries_over: The platform's structure and limits.
transition_in.introduces: Promises the merchant does not choose: protection, consent and legal duties.

posts.title: Part 8 introduction
posts.question: What does this part argue, and in what order should its chapters be read?

know: Part VIII answers three questions in order: which doors are open to a script and who holds the key to each (card testing, account takeover, checkout scripts and integration credentials); which systems hold a person's data, for what purpose and for how long, and what a request requires of each; and how an applicable rule becomes owned work with a scope, a required behavior, an authoritative system, a test and a deadline.

Kestrel & Pine's three examples: 48,000 abusive checkout attempts in August 2026; a customer's May 2027 deletion request that found her in nine systems; and regulatory changes that reached engineering through unrelated channels.
That the response to all three begins with one map of systems, integrations and owners, extended with credentials, data purposes and retention, and applicable requirements and deadlines.
can_do: Pick the Part VIII chapter that answers the trust question in front of them.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of this page alone can name the three chapters' subjects in reading order.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only this page: what will each of the next three chapters tell you, in order?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Card testing, account takeover, checkout scripts and integration credentials, with an attack that cost €2,900 in declined-payment fees and interrupted sales, controls divided between the merchant and its providers, and incident recovery; customer records, their purposes and the actions a request requires, with a customer in Ghent found in nine systems and identity links and a coordinated workflow that make later requests easier; turning an applicable rule into owned work (scope, required data or behavior, authoritative system, verification, deadline), with a calendar covering product information, accessibility, electronic invoicing and unsold goods.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of this page alone can say why the part treats security, privacy and regulation as lists with owners on one map rather than as three separate disciplines.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: what do the part's three subjects have in common, and where does the response to each begin?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Each arrives from outside (a script, a person with rights, a rule with a date) and uses or demands something the shop already has: the checkout, the login and the admin, the copies of a customer's data, the price and product data. Each is answered by a list with owners (credentials, data purposes and retention, requirements and deadlines), and the three lists are columns of the same map of systems, integrations and owners; the map makes responsibilities actionable, though each topic still needs its own controls.

posts.title: Protecting the Shop: Card Data, Account Takeover, Bots and Skimmers
posts.question: What do attackers want from a commerce platform, and what controls matter most?

know: What attackers take from a shop, in rough order of preference: card testing, credential stuffing and account takeover, web skimming, coupon and refund abuse, inventory hoarding, admin compromise and supply-chain risk, with OWASP identifiers where they exist; half of them policy abuse rather than intrusion.

Where PCI DSS draws its line: the SAQ by integration pattern (a PSP-hosted page or hosted fields for SAQ A, a merchant form for SAQ A-EP, raw card data for SAQ D), the dates of v4.0 and v4.0.1, requirements 6.4.3 and 11.6.1 mandatory since 31 March 2025 and removed from SAQ A in favor of an eligibility statement, and requirements 12.8 and 8.4.2.

The controls for card testing (the control ladder up to a decline-rate alert and a kill switch), for takeover (rate limits, challenges for risky logins, notification of change), for skimmers (script inventory, CSP, SRI, tamper detection) and for identities (enforced MFA, one restricted key per integration in a vault, signed webhooks), and the four security postures by scale stage.
believe: Attackers do not break in; they use the payment form, the login and the admin as built.
The hosted platform removes the patching burden and never the identity, script and endpoint burden.
For a merchant renting its platform, security is an inventory of identities, keys, apps, scripts and endpoints with owners before it is a technology.
can_do: Place their checkout on the SAQ table and say what the SAQ A eligibility statement asks them to know about the scripts on their payment page.
Audit their landscape as a list of identities and keys, each with an owner, a scope and a way to rotate it, and move one posture rung when the landscape gains what the rung protects.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given an overnight wave of declined payments on a hosted platform, the reader names the attack and the controls that stop it, rather than relying on the platform's certification or an IP block.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A merchant on a hosted platform with a hosted checkout wakes to payment-provider fees for tens of thousands of declined authorizations made overnight through its guest checkout, a payment account paused for 40 minutes, and a few hundred real orders with nonsense names. Its agency says the platform is PCI certified, so security is handled, and proposes blocking the IP addresses involved. Using only this chapter: what happened, and what should the merchant put in place?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Card testing (OAT-001): a script used the guest checkout as built to find which stolen cards still work. Every attempt is a normal checkout to the platform and a normal authorization to the PSP, so only the count, pace and decline rate reveal it; attackers rotate addresses, so an IP block is not enough, and the certification covers the vendor's service, not abuse of the merchant's endpoints. Controls: keep the hosted checkout; switch on the platform's bot protection and the PSP's velocity rules; challenge payment requests with no session history, validated on the server; alert on the decline rate against normal; keep a kill switch that disables guest card payments without a deploy; never retry the cards the attacker saved; write a runbook that calls a named person. In the response: cancel and refund the live orders before they reach the warehouse, and rotate every key if the attempts did not come through the checkout.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say how much of PCI DSS applies to a merchant with hosted fields and what it still owns on the payment page.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A merchant takes cards through its PSP's hosted fields inside its own checkout page, which also loads a tag manager and two app scripts. Using only this chapter: how much of PCI DSS applies to it, and what does it still own?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The card number goes from the shopper's browser straight to the PSP and the merchant holds only a token, the brand, the last four digits and the expiry, so SAQ A can apply if its eligibility criteria are met; the acquirer, not a vendor's documentation, decides the SAQ. Requirements 6.4.3 (every payment-page script authorized, integrity-checked and inventoried with a reason) and 11.6.1 (detect and alert on unauthorized page and header changes) are mandatory in the standard since 31 March 2025; the Council removed them from SAQ A but asks an SAQ A merchant to confirm that its site is not susceptible to script attacks, which it can do itself, through a third party or with the processor's confirmation. So the merchant keeps a script inventory with an owner and a reason, a CSP in report-only and then enforcing mode, SRI on the PSP's scripts and tamper detection; holds each provider's attestation (12.8); and enforces MFA on the PSP console and the platform admin (8.4.2, as the chapter reads it). A custom card form would move it to SAQ A-EP or SAQ D.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say what a merchant's list of identities and keys should hold and why.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A merchant's platform admin has about thirty staff accounts, some shared and MFA optional; its agency uses one shared login; and it runs dozens of integrations whose keys sit in scripts and never rotate, some with no named owner. Using only this chapter: what should change, and why does it matter more than another security product?
acceptance_criteria.expected: An admin login or a leaked key bypasses every other control: it can change the payout account, add a checkout script, export customers or issue refunds, and the vendor's shared-responsibility statement leaves identities, keys, apps, scripts and integrations to the merchant. So: MFA enforced, not merely available, on the platform, the PSP console, the ERP, the WMS and the integration platform; no shared accounts, agency engineers named, leavers removed within a day; one identity and one restricted, least-privilege key per integration, with an owner in the inventory, held in a vault and rotated yearly or on exposure; webhook signatures verified; app scopes reviewed before installation. A key without an owner cannot be rotated, scoped or traced, and a merchant that cannot say which integration a leaked key belonged to must rotate everything.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: That a checkout accepting strangers' payments can be used to test stolen cards, a login to try stolen passwords and bot carts to hold stock, with no break-in; the damage as fees for declined payments, a paused payment account, stolen customer access, held stock and, from malicious checkout scripts, stolen card details (British Airways, 2018, with a £20 million penalty in 2020); that a merchant renting its platform still holds access, integrations, custom scripts and abuse controls; that the chapter covers payment-page exposure, card testing and account takeover and leaves personal data, the wider rules and fraud models to other chapters; Eva paying by iDEAL at a checkout that took 48,000 abusive attempts one night. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's Card-Testing Night and its 2027 baseline, vendor documentation (Stripe, Adyen, Shopify, Adobe), the PCI Security Standards Council, OWASP and dated public breaches.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: What do attackers want from a commerce platform, and what controls matter most?
thesis.claim: Attackers want the payment form, the login and the admin, and send ordinary requests through them as designed rather than break in. For a merchant renting its platform the controls that matter most are a hosted checkout that keeps card numbers out of its systems; challenges, rate limits and a decline-rate alert on every endpoint that can pay or log in; an owned inventory of checkout scripts; and one identity, scoped key and named owner per person, app and integration.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that on a hosted, PCI-certified platform security is the vendor's job, so the merchant's part is a firewall or a bot-management product, and card testing is stopped by blocking the IP addresses it comes from.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim keeps its checkout hosted, switches on the controls it already pays for, watches the decline rate beside the order rate, keeps its checkout scripts on a list, and gives every identity and key an owner who can rotate it. On the night of 18 to 19 August 2026 a script made 48,000 guest-checkout attempts on Kestrel & Pine's NL storefront between about 23:40 and 04:10; the PSP charged €2,900 in fees for declined authorizations and paused the account for 40 minutes from 02:05, with its e-mail unread until 07:30; about 260 cards were live, 21 orders came back as disputes, and the issuer decline rate on genuine card payments rose from about 4% to about 7% for two weeks. At the time the platform had 31 admin accounts (4 shared, MFA optional), keys sat in scripts and the integration platform and were never rotated, and 13 of 34 integrations had no named owner in January 2027 (5 were still unowned in April 2027). The April 2027 baseline confirmed SAQ A with the acquirer, added a challenge on session-less payment requests, a decline-rate alert at three times the 30-day median, a guest-card kill switch tested quarterly, enforced MFA with no shared accounts, one identity and restricted key per integration in a vault, a checkout script inventory with CSP enforcing from September 2027, and three runbooks.
thesis.how_why: Card testing and credential stuffing send normal requests to the checkout and the login from rotating addresses, so a single filter fails and only the count, the pace and the decline rate reveal them; the PSP charges for every authorization, pauses accounts that look abused, and issuers decline more of the merchant's genuine payments afterwards. A hosted checkout or hosted fields sends the card number straight to the PSP, which puts the merchant in SAQ A, but a skimmer runs in the shopper's browser on a page the merchant serves, which is why PCI DSS requirements 6.4.3 and 11.6.1 apply since 31 March 2025 and SAQ A asks the merchant to state that its page is not susceptible to script attacks. An admin login or a leaked key needs no other technique, and the vendors' published shared-responsibility statements (Adobe, Shopify, Stripe) leave identities, keys, apps, scripts and integrations to the merchant, so a key with no owner is a door nobody can close.

role.contribution: Names what attackers take from a shop and where the card-data standard draws its line, and turns the merchant's side of shared responsibility into a list of identities, keys, scripts and endpoints, each with an owner, an alert and a runbook.

transition_in.carries_over: The part introduction's first question, which doors are open to a script and who holds the key to each, and the Card-Testing Night of August 2026.
transition_in.introduces: The threats ranked by what attackers want, the PCI DSS line drawn by the integration pattern, the controls for card testing, takeover and skimmers, and the inventory of identities and keys.

posts.title: Whose Data Is It? Privacy, Consent and Retention
posts.question: What personal data does a commerce platform hold, what may it do with it, and how do you build consent and retention in?

know: The GDPR vocabulary the design rests on: personal data, controller and processor (the EDPB's purposes and essential means), the data processing agreement, the four lawful bases that matter in commerce (contract, legal obligation, legitimate interests, consent, with the ePrivacy soft opt-in), data subject requests and the one-month deadline extendable by two.

Which systems hold a person in a commerce estate and in which role, as the chapter reads it: the platform, WMS, OMS, integration platform, returns portal, data warehouse and most apps as processors; the PSP for the payment, carriers and marketplaces as independent controllers; and what Shopify's compliance webhooks and protected-customer-data rules do on the merchant's behalf.

The consent rules for devices and profiles (GDPR Articles 4(11) and 7(1), ePrivacy Article 5(3), the EDPB and the Dutch and Belgian regulators), the retention periods the chapter cites (at least seven years in the Netherlands; ten, eight or six in Germany; ten in Belgium pending confirmation), transfers under the Data Privacy Framework and standard contractual clauses, and the pending Digital Omnibus proposal and DPF appeal.
believe: The order and the marketing profile describe one person but are two things in law: the order is kept for years under contract and tax law; the profile goes when the person asks.
Every integration is also a data flow with a legal role, and the integration inventory is the data-flow inventory.
A deletion request is a fan-out with a deadline; without an identity index and an orchestrator it is a hunt.
can_do: Write a privacy map for their own landscape: per system, its legal role, the data it holds, the action a request requires (erase, pseudonymize, retain, refer) and its retention clock.
Design the data model so that an order can outlive its customer, and say how consent reaches every tag, tool, till and app.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a deletion request from a customer who appears in several channels, the reader plans a fan-out with a decided action per system, rather than deleting the storefront account.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A customer who bought on a brand's web shop and on a marketplace, returned an item, subscribes to its newsletter and joined a store loyalty program asks the brand to delete her data and stop e-mailing her. The team plans to delete her web shop account. Using only this chapter: is that enough, and what should happen?
acceptance_criteria.expected: No: she is in many systems (Kestrel & Pine found such a customer in nine of thirteen), each with its own right answer. Verify the requester; find every record through an identity index; apply a per-system action decided in advance: erase the account, the loyalty entry, the newsletter subscription, the returns contact and old shipment addresses; pseudonymize orders and warehouse and data-warehouse rows; retain invoices and credit notes under the legal obligation and recent shipments while a claim is possible; refer the carrier, the marketplace and the PSP, which are controllers in their own right; keep backups under a bounded exception and replay the deletion log after a restore. Reply within one month, extendable by two, saying what was erased, what was kept and why, and whom else to ask, and keep the record of what each system did.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can explain why storing the person on the order blocks deletion and what design fixes it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A merchant's ERP and platform store the customer's name, address and e-mail on every order, and its customer list is simply the people who have ordered. Using only this chapter: why does this stop the merchant deleting anyone, and what design fixes it?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Tax law requires invoices and accounting records to be kept (at least seven years in the Netherlands, ten, eight or six in Germany depending on the record, ten in Belgium pending confirmation), and keeping them is itself a lawful basis; when the invoice is the customer record, deleting the person means deleting the invoice, which is forbidden, so nothing is deleted. Split the person from the transaction: the order and invoice carry a customer reference and the delivery address and are kept for the fiscal period; the profile (e-mail, phone, preferences, consent, browsing, loyalty) is a separate, erasable record; analytics carry a hash of the reference. Retention becomes a property of each record type, purged by a scheduled job.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say what consent requires and how it must travel.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A merchant's analytics and advertising tags fire as soon as a page loads, its newsletter list is built from everyone who ever ordered, and store staff sign up loyalty members on a tablet. Using only this chapter: what is wrong, and what should be in place?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Storing or reading information on the device needs consent before it happens, except what is strictly necessary (the cart, the language choice), so analytics and advertising tags wait for the banner, and cookie walls, scrolling and pre-ticked boxes do not count. The newsletter needs consent, or for existing customers the soft opt-in for the merchant's own similar products with a free objection at collection and in every message, subject to national transposition. Consent must be demonstrable, so it is recorded per person and per purpose with its time, place, wording and source on the customer master and reaches the tag layer, the newsletter tool, the POS and every app; a withdrawal reaches all of them the same day, and when the consent platform is down the default is no consent. The store sign-up shows the web's wording and records the time and store. Server-side tagging changes who receives the data first, not whether consent is needed.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: That a customer asking for removal has an account in the platform but copies of her addresses, purchases and contacts in warehouse, carrier, payment, marketing and support systems; that the merchant must know where the data went, why it is held and which records can go or must stay, and that a forgotten export or an integration can keep or recreate a record; that the architecture needs a map of copies, purposes, access and retention and requests that reach every system with a verifiable result; that the chapter explains controller and processor, consent recording, retention and request handling; Eva's order spreading her details to fulfillment, payment and invoicing, the newsletter needing its own basis and her exchange adding the returns portal. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's Request From Ghent and its autumn 2027 deletion design, the GDPR and ePrivacy texts, the EDPB's guidelines, the Dutch and Belgian regulators, national retention rules and Shopify's compliance webhooks.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: What personal data does a commerce platform hold, what may it do with it, and how do you build consent and retention in?
thesis.claim: A shop holds one person in many systems for different purposes: the order and invoice rest on the contract and tax law and are kept for years; the marketing profile rests on consent and goes when the person asks. Build consent and retention in by mapping each system's legal role, request action and retention clock, keeping consent with its evidence on the customer master, splitting the person from the transaction, and answering requests through an identity index and an orchestrator.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that privacy compliance is a cookie banner, a privacy notice and the platform's delete button: the hosted platform handles the personal data, so deleting the customer's account answers a deletion request.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim keeps a privacy map beside its integration inventory, records consent where every outbound tool can read it, models orders so that they outlive the customer, and answers requests with a flow and a record rather than a search. On 10 May 2027 Lotte Claes, a fictional customer in Ghent, asked Kestrel & Pine to delete her data: she was in nine of the thirteen systems, and three people with a shared spreadsheet took seventeen working days to answer, on 4 June 2027, six days inside the one-month limit. Thirteen of its 34 integrations had no named owner in January 2027, thirteen data flows nobody was accountable for (5 were still unowned in April 2027). In October 2027 a request orchestrator, an integration-platform flow with a human verification step and a per-system action table, went live on the identity index of June and July 2027; the second request, in November 2027, took two working days, and the privacy map became a column of Noor Visser's ownership map, reviewed quarterly.
thesis.how_why: The GDPR makes the merchant the controller, because it decides why and how the data is used, and the systems it chose (platform, WMS, OMS, integration platform, most apps) its processors under contracts, while carriers, marketplaces and the PSP for the payment decide for themselves; so every integration copies a person into a system with its own role. Each use needs its own lawful basis and runs on its own clock, and tax law keeps invoices for years, so where the invoice is the customer record a deletion either breaks the tax rule or does not happen. A request must be answered within one month, extendable by two, and consent must be demonstrable and withdrawable everywhere, so without an index of where each person is held and a decided action per system every request starts with a search of every system, and every withdrawal misses a tool.

role.contribution: Reads the integration inventory as a map of data flows with legal roles, separates the order from the person in law and in the data model, and turns consent, retention and deletion requests into state and a flow the merchant owns.

transition_in.carries_over: The previous chapter's question of who may act on the shop, answered by a list of identities and keys with owners.
transition_in.introduces: The mirror question about the data the shop holds on people: who may use it, for what and for how long, answered by a list of systems with legal roles, actions and retention clocks.

posts.title: Rules Turned Into Requirements: Consumer, Payment, Invoicing and Platform Regulation
posts.question: Which laws change what a commerce platform must do, by when, and how do you read them as requirements?

know: The four questions that read a law as a requirement (who is in scope; what it requires in data terms; which system of record holds that and which channels show it; when it applies and how compliance is tested), and the method table that applies them to eight rules.

The rules as the chapter states them from their official texts, by what they touch: withdrawal and refund clocks and the order button (Consumer Rights Directive), the 30-day prior price (Omnibus), strong customer authentication, verification of payee and pending PSD3/PSR, e-invoicing (Germany 2025 to 2028; Belgium from 1 January 2026, whether it binds a Dutch supplier without a Belgian establishment not settled by the sources; ViDA from 1 July 2030; a planned Dutch mandate), the DSA and GPSR, the ESPR destruction ban and digital product passport, the PPWR, the European Accessibility Act, NIS2, the Cyber Resilience Act, the AI Act and the Data Act; and the US contrast.
Kestrel & Pine's four rules through four doors, its March 2027 regulatory calendar (maintain, prepare and watch rows, each with an owner), the four ways to run compliance and the GPSR worked example.
believe: Most rules are data requirements with a date, not page requirements; each belongs in a system of record.
Dates slip while scope holds, transposition multiplies the calendar, and partners enforce before regulators do.
The platform absorbs some rules (the button, the banner, the card scope of its checkout, its own pages' accessibility), never the merchant's data rows.
can_do: Turn a rule into a requirement card: scope, data requirement, system of record, channels, test, date and owner.
Keep a regulatory calendar with an owner per row who owns the fact, read against the official source each quarter, and say which size or role threshold switches a row on.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a product-information rule enforced by a marketplace, the reader reads it as a requirement and places the work in a system of record, rather than fixing listings by hand.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A brand's marketplace connector starts rejecting listings because a product-safety regulation requires every online offer to show the manufacturer's name and address and safety warnings. The marketplace team proposes filling the gaps from a spreadsheet. Using only this chapter: how should the brand read this rule, and where should the work land?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Read it with the four questions. Scope: a trader offering products to EU consumers at a distance, so every product, own-brand and third-party. Data: the manufacturer's name and address, a responsible person in the EU where the manufacturer is outside it, identification including a picture, and warnings in a language the consumer understands: four attributes per product. System of record: the PIM, syndicated to every storefront and marketplace, not the connector or a spreadsheet, which are copies with no owner. Test: publication blocked when a field is missing. A calendar row with the date and an owner who owns the product facts. The marketplace enforced the rule before any regulator did, which is why partner notices need an owner too.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say what the prior-price rule requires in data terms.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A shop plans a Black Friday banner 'was €199, now €149' for a jacket it sold at €179 in an autumn campaign that ended three weeks earlier, and its prices are copied into several systems. Using only this chapter: which 'was' price is lawful, and what must the shop have to show it?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Under the Omnibus Directive the prior price is the lowest price the trader applied in at least the 30 days before the reduction, so the lawful 'was' price is €179, not €199. Showing it needs a 30-day price history per SKU per country, held as a legal record in the pricing system of record, with the strike-through computed from it and checked before every campaign; a shop whose prices live in several copies cannot produce that history.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say how a merchant should keep track of rules and what the way rules arrive teaches.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A Dutch apparel brand with about 300 employees sells online in three EU countries and to business customers in Belgium and Germany. In two years, rules reached it through a marketplace's rejections, an agency audit, a customer refusing PDF invoices and an auditor's newsletter. Using only this chapter: how should it keep track of rules from now on, and what do those arrivals teach?
acceptance_criteria.expected: One regulatory calendar with a row per applicable rule: date, official source, what it requires of the company, an owner who owns the fact (mostly finance, operations and merchandising rather than engineering) and a status (maintain, prepare, watch), read against the official source each quarter; once the company owns a PIM, an OMS or a price history, each row becomes a requirement card tied to the system-of-record map with its test in the release process. The arrivals show that rules are public years before they apply, that dates slip while scope holds, that a directive becomes national laws with their own dates, that partners such as marketplaces and business customers enforce first, and that scope follows size and role. On e-invoicing: the German mandate does not bind a Dutch issuer, the sources do not settle whether the Belgian one does, and business customers in both countries ask for the structured format anyway.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: That a rule about showing an earlier price can require a price history the merchant has never stored, so engineering needs a data source, a collection process and a page change, and that learning of it just before it applies leaves little time (the Long Fuse); that rules also touch returns, product details, invoices and unsold goods; the four questions for each requirement (which data, who owns it, how it is tested, when it must work); that legal interpretation and national differences still need care; Eva's price, product information, checkout and return as the places rules apply. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's four rules through four doors and its 2027 regulatory calendar, and the dated official texts of EU and national rules.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: Which laws change what a commerce platform must do, by when, and how do you read them as requirements?
thesis.claim: The consumer, product-safety, invoicing and sustainability rules that reach an EU shop (withdrawal and refund clocks since 2014, the 30-day prior price since 2022, product-safety fields since December 2024, e-invoicing mandates from 2025 to 2030, the unsold-apparel destruction ban since July 2026) are data requirements: a field, a history, a dated event or a record that belongs in a system of record. Read each by scope, required data, owning system, a check that the data exists, and date, and keep one calendar whose row owners own that data.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that regulation is the legal department's concern, met by page changes (a banner, a label, a template) when a lawyer or a partner raises it, and that a hosted platform keeps its merchants compliant.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim keeps a calendar of the rules that apply to it, gives each row an owner who owns the fact, and puts the field, history or clock into the system that owns it before the date, instead of learning of a rule from whoever enforces it first. Four rules reached Kestrel & Pine through four doors it did not own: product-safety fields through marketplace listing rejections in December 2024 (three weeks of spreadsheet work); the European Accessibility Act through an agency audit in May 2025 (about 140 findings); structured invoicing through a Belgian business customer that stopped accepting PDFs in December 2025 (Peppol connected in six weeks; whether the Belgian mandate binds a Dutch supplier is not settled by the sources, but its Belgian customers' bookkeeping expects Peppol); and the ESPR ban on destroying unsold apparel through an auditor's newsletter in June 2026, weeks before it applied on 19 July 2026. In March 2027 Noor Visser and Sanne de Wit wrote the 2027 regulatory calendar with an owner per row, most of them not engineers; for the GPSR row, a PIM rule from Q3 2027 blocks publication without the four fields, after a clean-up of about 850 third-party variants.
thesis.how_why: The texts state their obligations as data: the prior price is the lowest price applied in at least the 30 days before a reduction, the refund is due within 14 days of the withdrawal notice, the GPSR lists the manufacturer, responsible person, identification and warnings each offer must show, and the ESPR asks for a yearly disclosure of discarded unsold products. Such a record exists only where one system owns the fact; a price in seven copies or a field kept in a connector cannot produce it. Rules are usually public two to four years before they apply, directives become national laws with their own dates, and marketplaces and business customers enforce them on dates of their own, so a merchant with no calendar meets each rule through whichever partner enforces it first. The hosted platform ships the order button, the cookie banner, the card scope of its checkout and the accessibility of its own pages, and leaves the merchant's price history, product fields, packaging and disposition records.

role.contribution: Turns the rules that reach a shop into data requirements with dates, places each in a system of record with a test and an owner on one calendar, and performs the part's closing (the published chapter does not yet do so: it ends with one sentence on Part VIII being complete and the hand-off to Part IX).

transition_in.carries_over: The previous chapter's one-month deletion clock: one legal duty with a date that a merchant discovers late without a map.
transition_in.introduces: The other rules with dates (withdrawal, the prior price, payments, e-invoicing, product safety, accessibility, platform, cyber, AI and data rules), how to read each as a requirement, and Kestrel & Pine's 2027 regulatory calendar.

parts.title: Part IX — JOURNEYS: One Order, End to End

know: The four journeys and what each decides: a consumer order from search to the ledger (which system owns each fact on an order and how the next system learns it); its return as an exchange or a refund (where stock, money and books part ways); a retail chain's EDI reorder (which system writes each wholesale document); and a Black Friday evening (where the chain fails under forty times its load, and what a peak plan changes).

That the first three journeys replay April 2027 orders (Eva's #1072455 of 13 April and its exchange requested on 19 April; Bergzicht's 240-unit reorder of 6 April) through the late-2027 Waypoint architecture, set after its seams (the PIM live from 15 September 2027, D2C orders through the OMS from 13 October 2027, EDI and wholesale orders from 8 December 2027), and compare each with the January 2027 landscape; and that the fourth tells Black Friday 2026 and then the 2027 plan.

Kestrel & Pine's four incidents on these paths: the Three-Status Order (#1052877, December 2026, six days, eleven tickets), the Double Refund (January 2027, 212 returns, €19,400 refunded twice), the ASN Chargeback (Q3 2026, €14,200) and the Black Friday Oversell (27 November 2026, 1,340 units, 1,120 orders, about €96,000).
believe: Many systems holding a piece of one order is normal; a fact with two writers, or none, is the failure.
Commerce promises break at the handoffs between systems that each did what they were built to do.
Every handoff delivers at least once and sometimes late or not at all, so it needs a key, a delivery style matched to its clock and a reconciliation behind it.
can_do: Walk one order, return, business order or peak hour of their own landscape through a step table that names, per step, the system, the data, the promise made, the failure that belongs to it and the system of record of each fact.
Specify each handoff by freshness, consistency, latency, availability and style, and say which may be a daily batch and which must be an event.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every supporting claim of the part thesis is argued by at least one chapter, and every chapter supports at least one.
Each chapter's closing hand-off expresses the relationship its successor declares in transition_in.

Given a described landscape the part does not contain, a reader who has read only Part IX names where its incidents will occur, as handoffs with a missing owner, key, gauge or reconciliation, before blaming or replacing any one system.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A brand runs a hosted shop, a 3PL's warehouse system, an ERP and a returns app, and its agency calls the stack 'best of breed in every slot'. Order status is copied hourly from the warehouse to the shop; both the returns app and support staff in the payment console can refund; the ERP sends a retail chain's despatch advices when it releases orders to the warehouse; nobody knows how many orders an hour the shop-to-warehouse link can carry. Using only Part IX: where will its incidents occur, and what should it check first?
acceptance_criteria.expected: At the handoffs, not in the systems. Order status: several records with their own statuses disagree (one order record with separate money, goods and return states, copies read from it). Refunds: two writers and no key pay some returns twice (one writer, the return id as the idempotency key, the refund triggered by the warehouse's disposition, a daily match of refunds to returns and credit notes). Despatch advices: written before packing, so pallets and notices disagree and the chain deducts (the system that packs the pallet prints the SSCC and writes the despatch advice from its pack confirmation).
