Peak: an unmeasured link with a queue and stock copied on a schedule (a capacity figure per link tested with marked orders, a gauge and alarm on the oldest unsent order, stock as events, switches with owners). Check first by walking one order of each kind through a step table, counting writers per fact and asking of each handoff its key, its style and its reconciliation.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The page that carries the part's closing sets the four journeys' findings against the opening's warehouse that reports a parcel shipped while the storefront shows it being prepared, and states what the four incidents have in common; it does not only hand off to Part X.

thesis.question: What do four complete journeys through the same systems show about where commerce promises break, and what keeps them?
thesis.claim: An order, its return, a wholesale reorder and a peak evening cross one chain of systems, each keeping a different promise. On Kestrel & Pine's January 2027 landscape (Black Friday 2026 for the peak) every journey broke at a handoff, not inside a system; each holds when every fact has one writer and every handoff carries an idempotency key, moves by event or daily batch as its promise's clock requires, and is reconciled.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that commerce failures are defects inside a system, so that a merchant which picks a strong product for each slot (shop platform, warehouse system, ERP, returns app) and keeps each running has a working landscape, and an order's journey is simply the sum of its steps.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim reviews its landscape by walking orders through it rather than by grading products, and spends on owners, keys, gauges and reconciliations before new systems. Kestrel & Pine's four incidents sat on these four paths: the Three-Status Order (#1052877, December 2026: three statuses for six days, eleven tickets), the Double Refund (January 2027: 212 returns, €19,400 refunded twice), the ASN Chargeback (Q3 2026: €14,200 in deductions) and the Black Friday Oversell (27 November 2026: 1,340 units, 1,120 orders, about €96,000). Of Waypoint's eight decisions, three add a system (the availability service, the OMS and the PIM), while its integration standards, its EDI rules and its single definition of an order set owners, contracts, idempotency keys, reconciliations and the source of the despatch advice; the 2027 peak plan is mostly gauges and switches with owners.
thesis.how_why: Each system keeps its own fact on its own clock (checkout in seconds, the warehouse in pick waves, the carrier overnight, the ERP in a daily batch, the bank in days) and learns the other systems' facts as copies, through messages that arrive at least once and sometimes twice, late or not at all. A step can therefore be right in its own system and wrong at the next: a stock copy two hours old, a refund written by two systems, a despatch advice written before the pallets were packed, a queue nobody measured. Running the same dates and amounts through the January 2027 landscape and the late-2027 design holds the main systems constant (the shop platform, the WMS, the ERP, the PSP and the carriers all stay) and changes only owners and joins, which shows that the failures were in the joins.

supporting_claims.claim: A consumer order crosses about fifteen handoffs among eight systems that each hold a piece of it; it holds when each fact (product, price, physical stock, sellable stock, order, payment, parcel, invoice) has one system of record, the order number is the idempotency key on every join, and stock and orders move by event while invoices and payouts move by daily batch under a reconciliation.

A return is three flows with three owners (the goods through the warehouse's inspection, the money through the payment provider, the books through a credit note in the ERP), released by one event, the warehouse's disposition; the refund has one writer and one key, and an exchange is a return plus a new order at the original frozen price.

A wholesale order is a chain of contractual documents, each written by the system that knows the fact it states: the order record by the OMS, keyed on the buyer's location number and purchase-order number; the despatch advice by the warehouse system from the pallets as packed; the invoice by the ERP from the shipped lines. E-invoicing mandates change an invoice's format and transport, not its owner.

Under peak load the chain fails at the links nobody measured: a queue that hides a growing backlog and stock copied on a schedule. A peak plan sets a capacity figure per link, tests it with marked orders, gauges and alarms the queue, sends stock as events, and gives each degradation switch an owner and a trigger, while checkout, payment and the order path are never switched off.

Run on the same dates through the January 2027 landscape (and Black Friday 2026 for the peak), each journey breaks at a handoff where a fact had two writers or no owner, a message had no key or a link had no gauge, while every system did what it was built to do.

role.contribution: Re-assembles the parts into four complete stories so the reader sees the claims hold together.

flow.rationale: Each journey reuses what the one before it established. Journey 1 sets up the reading device (the entity–owner table, the step table, the handoff requirements and the January 2027 comparison) and leaves the payment, the invoice and the order record that Journey 2 has to reverse: its refund is a new iDEAL transfer because Journey 1's payment had no capture, and its credit note is drawn against Journey 1's invoice. Journey 3 changes the buyer and is read against Journey 1 (documents and pallets instead of a checkout and a parcel), drawing on the same Duiven stock that Eva's product page showed. Journey 4 puts Journey 1's path (the order flow to the warehouse and the stock copies back to the channels) under forty times its normal load and tells the incident before the plan; it uses Journeys 2 and 3 only for the refunds against cancellations and the shared Duiven stock. Journeys 2 and 3 do not depend on each other; the return comes second so that Eva's story closes while her payment and invoice are fresh, and the change of buyer follows. Journey 3's order (6 April) comes before Eva's (13 April) by date, so the order is one of prerequisites, not of the calendar. Putting the return first would reverse a payment and an invoice the reader has not seen made; putting the peak first would present an incident at links the reader has not yet walked one order through; putting wholesale first would teach the despatch advice and the four-way match without the consumer order they are contrasted with.

hook.content: A warehouse can report a parcel shipped while the storefront still shows it being prepared: each system is right about its own fact, and nothing in either says whether the customer's promise is being kept.

opening.bridge: From Parts II to VIII, which taught each capability, join and rule separately and ended with three lists on one ownership map, to the same map in motion: four journeys followed through every system at once, so the reader sees where the parts meet and where, at Kestrel & Pine, they failed to.
opening.roadmap: Four journeys, each on Kestrel & Pine's late-2027 design with a comparison to its earlier landscape: Eva's order #1072455 from search to the ledger; the same jacket coming back as an exchange, with a refund branch; Bergzicht's 240-unit EDI reorder from order message to bank transfer; and Black Friday 2026 hour by hour, followed by the 2027 plan. The first three share one shape (entity–owner table, step table, handoff requirements, failures, the January 2027 comparison); the fourth is told twice.

closing.synthesis: The Three-Status Order, the Double Refund, the ASN Chargeback and the Black Friday Oversell look like four failures in four areas: order status, refunds, EDI and peak capacity. Walked as journeys they are one: in each, every system did what it was built to do, and the promise broke at a handoff where a fact had two writers or none, a message had no key or a link had no measure: three statuses for one order, two writers of one refund, a despatch advice written before the pallets were packed, a stock copy two hours old behind a queue nobody watched.
closing.so_what: Waypoint's answer was mostly in the joins: three of its eight decisions add a system (the availability service, the OMS, the PIM), its integration standards, EDI rules and single definition of an order set owners, contracts, idempotency keys, reconciliations, the despatch advice's source and one definition of an order, and the 2027 peak plan is mostly gauges and switches with owners. A reader can find next year's incidents in their own landscape by walking one order through it before comparing any vendor.
closing.callback: The part opening's warehouse that reports a parcel shipped while the storefront still shows it being prepared, both right about their own facts.

takeaway.content: Walk one ordinary order, one return, one business order and last peak's busiest hour through your own landscape with a step table. At each row name the system of record and count the writers of each fact, and ask of each handoff its idempotency key, whether its style matches its clock and which reconciliation catches what it misses. Start with the rows where the promise and the system of record belong to different systems.

transition_in.carries_over: The capabilities, joins and rules of Parts II to VIII, each taught separately.
transition_in.introduces: Four journeys followed through all of them at once.

posts.title: Part 9 introduction
posts.question: What does this part argue, and in what order should its chapters be read?

know: Part IX follows four journeys in order: a consumer purchase from search to accounting, the same jacket coming back as an exchange, a retail chain's EDI reorder through order, pallet notice, invoice and payment, and a Black Friday evening followed by the next year's plan.

The first three replay April 2027 orders through the late-2027 Waypoint design (an availability service, an OMS, a PIM, and warehouse packing records for wholesale notices), keeping their dates and amounts, and compare each with the earlier landscape; the peak chapter reconstructs the 2026 incident and then presents the 2027 plan.
An order is a chain of promises, each with one owner: many systems holding a piece of one order is normal, a fact with two writers is not, and every join needs a key and a daily reconciliation.
can_do: Pick the Part IX journey that matches the order, return, business order or peak they need to trace.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of this page alone can name the four chapters' subjects in reading order.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only this page: what will each of the next four chapters tell you, in order?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Eva's order #1072455 (a €199 jacket and two €18 pairs of socks at 21:14 on 13 April 2027, paid by iDEAL, delivered 15 April) from search to accounting, with who owns each fact and how the next system learns it; the M-to-L exchange requested on 19 April and inspected on 22 April, with a refund branch showing how one authorized request avoids January's duplicate-payment failure; Bergzicht's 240-unit, €19,860 reorder through structured order, pallet notice, invoice and payment (three pallets on 9 April, payment due 9 May), with an earlier €14,200 deduction explaining why the notice must describe the actual packing; Black Friday 2026 (a four-hour order backlog, delayed stock updates, 1,340 oversold units, about €96,000) and a 2027 plan that tests capacity, monitors queues and gives each protective action and recovery check an owner.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of this page alone can say why the journeys run the same orders through two architectures and what to look for in them.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: why does each journey compare two architectures, and what should a reader look for while following one?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The dates and amounts stay fixed, so what changes between the earlier landscape and the late-2027 design is whether the promises hold: in the earlier one, scheduled stock copies and separate order records caused failures. The reader looks at the handoffs: which system owns each fact, whether a fact has two writers, and whether each message carries an idempotency key with a daily reconciliation behind the events.

role.contribution: Performs the part's opening: states the part thesis in its three key points, places the four journeys on one chain of systems, says that the first three replay April 2027 orders through the late-2027 design with a comparison to the earlier landscape and that the peak is told twice, and gives the reading order.

posts.title: Journey 1: Eva's Jacket, From Search to Doorstep
posts.question: What has to go right, in which system, for one consumer order to be found, paid, picked, delivered and booked?

know: Which system owns each fact on a consumer order in the late-2027 design (the PIM the product, the platform's price list the price, the WMS physical stock, the availability service what may be sold per channel, the platform the cart and checkout, the PSP the payment, the OMS the order and its separate money, goods and return states, the WMS and the shipping service the parcel, PostNL the tracking events, the ERP the invoice and the ledger), and the fifteen steps from search to payout with the promise and the failure of each.

How iDEAL shapes the order (instant charge, auto-capture only, a refund as a new transfer, the outcome learned from an id-only webhook and a fetched status, retries over hours or days); why the invoice is issued by one numbering authority at dispatch and corrected only by credit note; why revenue is recognized at delivery under IFRS 15; and how a PSP payout is matched to orders through its reconciliation report.

The handoff requirements (freshness, consistency, latency, availability, style) for each join, and five failures with their detection and recovery: the duplicate order, the paid order never confirmed, the short pick, the lost parcel and the payout that does not match.
believe: Eight systems holding a piece of one order is normal; a fact with two writers is the problem.
Every join delivers at least once and sometimes twice, late or not at all, so exactly-once is built by the receiver with a key and a reconciliation.
Finance can be batch; availability and the fulfillment order cannot.
can_do: Trace an order through any merchant's landscape with a step table and name the system of record of each fact on it.
Name, for each handoff, the idempotency key, the delivery style and the reconciliation that catches what the messages miss.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a duplicated order and a paid order stuck as pending, the reader locates each at its handoff and names the key and the reconciliation that handle it, rather than blaming the platform or the payment provider.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A merchant's integration sends each new web order from its shop platform to its warehouse system. After an integration outage and replay, some customers receive two identical parcels; separately, a few orders paid by iDEAL still show 'payment pending' a day later, although the shoppers' banks show the money gone. Using only this chapter: what went wrong at which handoff, and what should be in place?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The order message was delivered twice and the receiver had no idempotency key: keyed on the order number, the second copy finds the existing order and does nothing, and a count of orders received against orders created shows duplicates harmlessly. The pending orders lost the PSP's webhook: the platform learns the outcome from the webhook, not from the shopper's browser, which may never return from the bank app; the webhook is a notification whose status is fetched from the API, retried for hours or days and then abandoned. A daily sweep lists checkouts with no terminal payment state within the method's expiry window, queries the PSP and marks them paid once. Delivery between systems is at least once; webhooks are a latency optimization over a reconciliation, never a replacement.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can assign the facts on an order to systems of record and say which handoffs may be batch.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: for one online order, which system should own the product description, the price, physical stock, what may still be sold per channel, the order and its status, the payment and the invoice; and which handoffs may run as a daily batch and which may not?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The PIM owns the product; the platform's price list the consumer price; the WMS physical stock; the availability service what may be sold per channel (on-hand minus committed minus a buffer, fed by WMS stock events); the OMS the order, with separate money, goods and return states, because fulfilled is not delivered and paid is not invoiced; the PSP the payment, its reference stored on the order; the ERP the invoice, numbered gap-free at dispatch and corrected only by credit note. Copies are allowed, a second writer is not. Stock and the fulfillment order must be events, because an hour's delay is an oversell or a missed cut-off; invoice posting and payout matching should be a daily batch, because finance tolerates a day and gains a reconciliation count.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say why a storefront's 'in stock' and delivery promise can be wrong while every system works, and what each should be computed from.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A storefront says 'ordered before 22:00, delivered tomorrow' and shows 'in stock' from a stock number copied from the warehouse through the ERP every hour. The warehouse's last pick wave is at 21:00. Using only this chapter: what does a shopper ordering at 21:14 on a Tuesday get, and what should the page be computed from?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A promise of Wednesday for a parcel picked Wednesday morning and delivered Thursday: the sentence ignores the warehouse's real cut-off, so a delivery-promise service should compute the date from the last wave, the carrier's collection and its lane, which gives Thursday. 'In stock' is a copy up to two hours old, the delay behind the Black Friday Oversell; it should be available-to-promise from an availability service fed by the WMS's stock events, seconds old, with a buffer per channel. Both are copies; what matters is how old they may be and who computes them.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: That Eva's purchase of a jacket and socks passes records between search, checkout, payment, warehouse, carrier and finance systems, and that a wrong stock answer or a late warehouse instruction can break the delivery promise even when checkout succeeds; that at about 293,000 orders a year a one-in-a-thousand failure reaches customers almost daily; that the walkthrough follows the order from search to the books, saying what each handoff must preserve and how a failure reaches the customer, as fifteen handoffs with one owner per promise and joins that deliver at least once; and that it shows where the same order would have gone wrong a year earlier. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's replayed order, vendor documentation (Shopify, commercetools, Stripe, Mollie, Adyen, PostNL), official invoice and consumer rules, and IFRS 15.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: What has to go right, in which system, for one consumer order to be found, paid, picked, delivered and booked?
thesis.claim: One consumer order crosses about fifteen handoffs among eight systems, and each step's promise (product, price, stock, delivery day, payment, parcel, invoice) is kept by a different system from the one before. It goes right when every fact has one system of record and every handoff carries the order number as an idempotency key, runs on a style matched to its clock (events for stock and orders, a daily batch for finance) and has a reconciliation behind it.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a capable shop platform keeps an ordinary order on its own: its order record is the order, its webhooks and integrations deliver each message once, and every system added beside it is a further place for the order to go wrong.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim reads its architecture by walking one order through it, counting writers rather than boxes, and puts a key and a reconciliation on every join before buying anything. Replayed through the late-2027 design, Eva's order #1072455 (21:14 on 13 April 2027, €235 by iDEAL, picked 14 April, delivered 15 April, invoiced net €194.21 plus €40.79 VAT) is promised Thursday and arrives Thursday, and its stock figure is seconds old. On the January 2027 landscape the same order was promised Wednesday by a static sentence, read stock up to two hours old and existed as three records with three statuses, the path on which the Three-Status Order of December 2026 showed Delivered, In picking and Not invoiced for six days and drew eleven tickets.
thesis.how_why: The storefront answers from copies (a search index, an availability figure) and checkout only orchestrates calls to systems that own the facts, freezing the amounts it promises. The PSP reports the payment by webhook, which Mollie retries ten times over 26 hours and Stripe for up to three days without guaranteed order, so the order system fetches the status and keys creation on the order number. The warehouse confirms what it picked, the ERP numbers invoices gap-free at dispatch and corrects them only by credit note, and the PSP pays out in batches days later that contain hundreds of orders. Each system is right about its own fact on its own clock, so the order holds only if each join tolerates a repeated, late or missing message.

role.contribution: Walks the recurring consumer order through every system of the late-2027 design with an entity–owner table, a step table and the handoff requirements, and compares the January 2027 path on the same dates.

transition_in.carries_over: The part introduction's first journey, order #1072455, and its reading device: the owner of each fact, the step table and the comparison with the January 2027 landscape.
transition_in.introduces: The fifteen steps from search to payout, the system of record of each fact on the order, the requirements of each handoff and the failures along the path.

posts.title: Journey 2: The Jacket Comes Back
posts.question: How does a return and exchange travel back through the systems, and where do the money, the stock and the books part ways?

know: Which system owns each fact of a return in the late-2027 design (the OMS the order, eligibility and the return record; the WMS inspection, disposition and physical stock; the availability service what may be sold again; the PSP the refund; the ERP the credit note and the new invoice), and the twelve steps from request to reconciliation.

The EU clocks a return runs on (14 days to withdraw from possession, a refund within 14 days of the notice, the right to withhold until the goods or evidence of sending arrive), the four dispositions, the three release policies for an exchange, and why refunds are asynchronous and can fail days after acceptance.

Kestrel & Pine's cases on this path: Eva's exchange (requested 19 April 2027, inspected and graded resellable 22 April, size L shipped that day; a credit note of −€199 against the original invoice and a new invoice of €199), the Double Refund of January 2027 (212 returns, €19,400 refunded twice) and its February 2027 fix, the 190 Black Friday returns refunded about €3,000 too much, and the marketplace and store variants.
believe: A return is finished only when stock, money and books agree.
The refund belongs to the warehouse's disposition event, with one writer and one key.
An exchange is a return plus a new order, never an edit.
can_do: Count the systems that can call the PSP's refund API in their own landscape and name the key on the request.
Design an exchange and a refund so that a returned unit raises sellable stock only on its disposition and the books record a credit note.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given refunds paid twice, the reader names two writers and no key as the cause and plans one writer, one key and a daily match, rather than retraining support.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A brand's returns app refunds customers through the shop platform after the warehouse inspects a return, which takes two to five days. Support agents, seeing a carrier scan at the warehouse and no refund yet, refund impatient customers in the payment provider's console. At month-end finance finds hundreds of returns credited twice. Using only this chapter: what went wrong, and what should change?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Two systems could write the refund and neither request named the return, so the payment provider accepted both. One writer may call the refund API (the returns app, later the OMS when it holds the return record), with support's console access read-only; each request carries the return id as its idempotency key; the refund is raised by the warehouse's disposition event, not the request or the carrier scan; its state (requested, accepted, refunded or failed) is driven by webhooks and confirmed by a fetched status; a daily job matches every PSP refund to a refunded return, every refunded return to a credit note and every credit note to an invoice; and support sees which of receipt, inspection and refund has happened.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say why an exchange is not an edit and when a returned unit may be sold again.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A customer exchanges a €199 jacket in size M for size L. The team proposes to change the original order line from M to L, ship the L once the parcel is scanned at the dock, and add the M back to stock at that scan. Using only this chapter: what is wrong with the plan, and what should happen?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The M was picked, invoiced and paid for, so editing the line leaves an invoice for a jacket the customer no longer has. An exchange is a return plus a new order: at request time a held order for one L is created at the original frozen price with a €0 balance and the unit is committed in the availability service; the disposition releases it (release on scan or an instant exchange are other policies with their own risks). The ERP issues a credit note of −€199 against the original invoice and a new invoice of €199, which net to zero. The M raises sellable stock only when inspection grades it restockable, never at the dock scan, because some returns need processing or cannot be resold.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can compute a return's legal dates and say what changes when the return comes through a marketplace or a store.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Goods are delivered on 15 April; the customer gives notice of withdrawal on 19 April and drops the parcel at a carrier point on 20 April. Using only this chapter: by when must the merchant refund, from when may it no longer withhold the refund, and what changes if the same jacket was bought through a marketplace or is returned in a store?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The withdrawal window runs 14 days from possession, to 29 April; the refund is due within 14 days of the notice, by 3 May; the merchant may withhold it until it has the goods or evidence of sending, so the carrier's acceptance scan on 20 April ends the withholding right. The OMS computes delivery, notice, evidence of sending and refund dates per line. On a marketplace the policy is the marketplace's; the OMS must accept returns it did not create and refunds it did not issue, keyed on the marketplace's return id, with the money state 'refunded externally'. In a store the POS records the return against the order number, the stock lands in that store's location and the refund goes to the original payment method through the same single writer, not as cash.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: That receiving a returned parcel does not say whether the item can be resold, whether the replacement is reserved or whether money is due, decisions owned by different systems; that if each treats its own step as the finished return a customer can be refunded twice or wait for an unsecured replacement; that a return is three flows (goods, money, books), the refund is triggered by the warehouse's disposition with one writer and one key, and an exchange is a return plus a new order, with marketplace and store returns as variants; Kestrel & Pine's return figures (72,000 return parcels in 2026, 24% of items, 28% exchanges, 61% resold as new) beside the NRF's; Eva's exchange from 19 April, followed through authorization, transport back, inspection, replacement and accounting. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's exchange and the Double Refund, vendor documentation (Shopify, commercetools, Adyen, Stripe, Mollie, Odoo, Amazon, Zalando) and the Consumer Rights Directive.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: How does a return and exchange travel back through the systems, and where do the money, the stock and the books part ways?
thesis.claim: A return travels back on one path until the warehouse's disposition event, which alone releases three flows with three owners: stock in the warehouse system, money through the payment provider (or, for an exchange, a held new order at the price on the original order line) and books through a credit note in the ERP. Exactly one system calls the refund API, keyed on the return id, and an exchange is never an edit of the original order or invoice.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a return is a refund button: the returns app or support refunds when the customer asks or the carrier scans the parcel, stock goes back on the shelf when the parcel arrives, and an exchange is an edit of the original order line.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim lets exactly one system call the refund API, keys every refund on the return, raises stock and settlement only on the disposition, and matches refunds to credit notes daily. In January 2027 Kestrel & Pine refunded 212 returns twice, €19,400, because the returns portal and support in the PSP console could both refund with no key naming the return, and finance found it at month-end; in February it made the portal the single writer, set support's console access to read-only and started a daily match. Eva's exchange, requested on 19 April 2027 and graded resellable on 22 April, ships size L the same day and leaves a credit note of −€199 and a new invoice of €199 that net to zero.
thesis.how_why: EU law gives the consumer 14 days to withdraw from possession and the merchant 14 days from the notice to refund, withholdable only until the goods or evidence of sending arrive, so the return needs dates per line from the order record. Refunds are asynchronous and can fail days after acceptance, and a PSP accepts two requests that carry no shared key, so the count of writers and the key decide whether money goes out once. Only inspection knows whether a unit is sellable (39% of Kestrel & Pine's returned items in 2026 were not graded new), so stock raised at the dock scan promises units in a repair bin; and an issued invoice is immutable, so the books change only by credit note.

role.contribution: Walks Eva's exchange, with the refund as its alternative and the Double Refund as its failure path, back through the late-2027 design, separates the goods, money and books flows released by one disposition event, and compares the January 2027 path.

transition_in.carries_over: Journey 1's delivered order #1072455, with its iDEAL payment, its invoice in the ERP and its record in the OMS.
transition_in.introduces: The way back through many of the same systems in the opposite direction, with a refund and a credit note where the payment and the invoice were, and the Double Refund of €19,400.

posts.title: Journey 3: A Chain Reorders by EDI, From Order to Invoice
posts.question: How does a wholesale reorder by EDI run from order to invoice, and where does it fail?

know: The six EDI messages of one wholesale order (ORDERS, CONTRL, ORDRSP, DESADV, INVOIC, RECADV) with the system each is generated from, the three GS1 identifiers (GTIN, GLN, SSCC), and the fifteen steps from the order message to cash application.

Bergzicht's spring reorder in the late-2027 design: ORDERS on 6 April 2027 for 240 units across 18 SKUs, €19,860 excluding VAT; validation of items, contract prices and credit against the ERP; allocation in the availability service; three pallets with SSCC labels from the WMS at pack; the DESADV from the pack confirmation before the pallets leave; delivery to Zwolle and the INVOIC on 9 April (€24,030.60 gross); payment due 9 May as a SEPA transfer to be matched.

The ASN Chargeback of Q3 2026 (€14,200: despatch advices generated by the ERP at release with ERP pallet numbers while the WMS printed its own labels), why it went unseen for a quarter, W6's rules, and the Peppol variant for Ardennes Trail Co. (40 jackets, €3,800, ordered 21 April 2027, invoiced 23 April, due 23 May).
believe: Each wholesale document is a promise in the buyer's contract, usually with a penalty.
The despatch advice must be written by the system that packed the pallets.
E-invoicing mandates change an invoice's format and transport, not its owner.
can_do: Say, for each document in their own wholesale flow, which system generates it and whether that system saw the fact it states.
Keep a partner card per trading partner (GLNs, guideline version, messages, test status, contacts, an owner) and detect deductions as cases with evidence.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given deductions for mismatched pallets, the reader names the despatch advice's source as the cause and the system that should write it, rather than blaming the warehouse or the EDI provider.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A supplier's ERP sends a retail chain's despatch advice when it releases an order to the warehouse, numbering the pallets itself; the warehouse system prints its own pallet labels at packing. Months later the chain's payments arrive short, with deduction codes, on invoices that are correct. Using only this chapter: what is wrong, why did nobody notice, and what should change?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The despatch advice described the order, while the pallets described the pack, so the chain's receiving scanned SSCCs that were missing from the notice or carried different contents, counted by hand and charged fees under its purchasing conditions. Nobody noticed because the deductions arrived as unexplained short payments: finance saw receivables that did not close, the wholesale lead heard of 'label problems', the warehouse had shipped every unit, and only one external consultant could read the mapping. The system that packs the pallet should print the SSCC and write the despatch advice from its pack confirmation, sent before the truck leaves (the truck waits if not); a partner card names the guideline version, the change contact and an owner; a compliance scorecard and an alarm on negative acknowledgements watch it; and a short payment opens a case with the invoice, the despatch advice and the deduction code as evidence.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say where an EDI order should become an order record and what protects that step.
acceptance_criteria.probe: An EDI order arrives, the network redelivers it an hour later, two lines carry prices that differ from the contract, and the team's habit is to key EDI orders into the EDI provider's web portal and the ERP. Using only this chapter: what should happen to this order, and why?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A syntax acknowledgement (CONTRL) says only that the message parsed, not that it was accepted. The order is validated against data the ERP owns (each GTIN resolves to a SKU, prices equal the customer's contract prices, open receivables within the credit limit), and the price mismatch is answered in the order response (ORDRSP), never silently accepted, because an unexpected invoice price becomes a short payment. The order is created once, in the OMS, with channel EDI, the same number family and state model as web orders, keyed on the buyer's GLN plus its PO number, so the redelivered copy does nothing; not in the portal or the ERP. The allocation is committed in the availability service, so every channel's available stock drops within seconds.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say what an e-invoicing mandate changes in the invoice flow and what it does not.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A Dutch supplier's Belgian business customer stops accepting PDF invoices. Using only this chapter: what changes in the supplier's invoicing, what stays the same, and is the supplier obliged?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The invoice is still issued by the ERP from what shipped. Its format becomes a Peppol BIS Billing 3.0 invoice (UBL implementing EN 16931) sent through the supplier's access point to the customer's in the four-corner model, at 0% as an intra-EU supply with the reverse-charge mention once the customer's VAT number is validated in VIES; transmission becomes a state the ERP holds (sent, delivered, rejected), and a rejected e-invoice is not an invoice. Belgium has required structured e-invoices between Belgian businesses since 1 January 2026; whether that reaches a Dutch supplier without a Belgian establishment is not settled by the chapter's sources, but the customer's bookkeeping expects Peppol either way. Germany requires businesses to receive e-invoices since 2025, the Netherlands plans a mandate for 2030 and ViDA brings cross-border digital reporting from July 2030.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: That a retail chain ordering pallets expects its receiving system to recognize what arrives, so the supplier's shipment notice and pallet labels must match and a correct delivery can still be held up or penalized when they disagree; that EDI carries orders, shipment notices and invoices; that a wholesale order is a conversation of documents with a contract behind it, each with its own system of truth, and that Kestrel & Pine lost €14,200 because its despatch advices came from the wrong system; that money arrives as a bank transfer to match and e-invoicing changes format and transport, not owner; that wholesale is a quarter of Kestrel & Pine's revenue from 1,100 accounts with orders about fourteen times larger; that Bergzicht's order commits 240 units on 6 April from the stock Eva buys from on 13 April; and that the walk runs from receipt to payment. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's reorder and the ASN Chargeback, GS1 standards, retailers' published conditions (Jumbo, bol, Walmart), EDI and Peppol providers and Belgian, German and EU e-invoicing rules.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: How does a wholesale reorder by EDI run from order to invoice, and where does it fail?
thesis.claim: A wholesale reorder runs as a chain of documents, each a contractual promise: the order message becomes one order record in the OMS, keyed on the buyer's location number and purchase-order number; the warehouse system writes the despatch advice from the pallets as packed; the ERP writes the invoice from the shipped lines; and the money arrives thirty days later as a bank transfer to match. It fails where a document is written by a system that did not see the fact it states.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that EDI is a translation job owned by an EDI provider or a consultant: map the ERP's order to the retailer's format, generate the despatch advice and the invoice from the order, and treat deductions as a finance matter.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim asks, for each document, which system generates it and whether that system touched the goods, keeps one partner card per trading partner with an owner, and treats every short payment as a case with evidence. In Q3 2026 Kestrel & Pine's ERP generated Bergzicht's despatch advices at release, with its own pallet numbers, while the WMS printed different labels at pack; nine deliveries produced €14,200 in deductions, unseen for a quarter because they arrived as short payments on correct invoices and only an external consultant could read the mapping. Under W6, Waypoint's EDI rule, the WMS prints the SSCC at pack and sends the despatch advice from its pack confirmation, and Bergzicht's 6 April 2027 reorder (240 units, €19,860) arrives on 9 April with a matching notice and is invoiced that day for €24,030.60, due 9 May. For Ardennes Trail Co. in Namur the same ERP invoice travels over Peppol: the format and transport change, the owner does not.
thesis.how_why: The buyer's receiving scans each pallet's SSCC and books the contents listed for it in the despatch advice without counting, and its four-way match of order, despatch advice, receipt and invoice pays short whatever disagrees, under purchasing conditions with fees per message and per refused delivery (Jumbo's, for example). Only the system that built a pallet knows what is on it, so a notice written from the order states what should have shipped, not what did. Networks redeliver messages and buyers resend after timeouts, so the order record needs the GLN and PO number as its key; contract prices and credit limits live in the ERP, so validation reads them there; and an issued invoice is immutable, so it is written from the shipped lines.

role.contribution: Walks Bergzicht's EDI reorder from the order message to the matched bank transfer through the late-2027 design with W6 in force, tells the ASN Chargeback as the failure path, runs a Belgian customer's Peppol invoice as the variant and compares the January 2027 path.

transition_in.carries_over: Journeys 1 and 2: a consumer who orders at a checkout, pays at once and receives a parcel, and the same Duiven stock and systems behind her.
transition_in.introduces: A buyer that is a company: an order that arrives as a message nobody typed, goods that leave on pallets with a despatch advice, and money that arrives thirty days later against an invoice.

posts.title: Journey 4: Black Friday, Hour by Hour
posts.question: What happened hour by hour on the 2026 peak day, and what does the 2027 plan change?

know: Black Friday week 2026 at Kestrel & Pine: 31,000 D2C orders in the week, 2,300 in the peak hour of Friday 27 November (38 a minute, about 41 times an average hour's traffic); the order flow to the WMS, about seven orders a minute one at a time under the vendor's rate limit, falling behind at about 13:00 and four hours behind by 21:00; the 19:40 sell-out reaching the ERP at 19:45, the storefronts at about 20:30 and the marketplaces at about 21:35; and what each person saw and could do.

The outcome (1,340 units oversold, 1,120 orders affected: 760 canceled and 360 delayed, about €96,000; about 8,000 orders that missed next-day delivery outside that figure) and the December 2026 post-mortem's five findings.

The 2027 plan for 26 November 2027: a forecast of 60 orders a minute, every link tested at 80 and the OMS-to-WMS link at 120, the order path through the OMS (marketplaces from 15 September, D2C from 13 October, wholesale from 8 December, a freeze from 15 November to 5 December), stock events through the availability service within a minute, eight switches with owners and triggers, a runbook, a rehearsal and a reconciliation report at 08:00 on Saturday.
believe: The evening was lost in the afternoon, by a queue nobody could see.
A stock chain of scheduled copies is harmless on an ordinary day and a two-hour blind spot at peak.
Most of a peak fix is visibility and switches rather than new systems.
can_do: Write a peak plan as a journey hour by hour, with a capacity figure per link, a gauge on every queue and a name in every row.
Build a degradation ladder whose switches each have an owner, a trigger and a rehearsal, with checkout, payment and the order path never switched off.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a peak evening on which the storefront stayed up but orders oversold and deliveries slipped, the reader locates the failure in the chain behind the platform and lists what next year's plan needs, rather than a bigger platform.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A brand's storefront stayed up all Black Friday evening, yet hundreds of orders were for a jacket that had already sold out and thousands missed next-day delivery. Its agency proposes a larger platform plan for next year. Using only this chapter: where did the evening go wrong, and what should next year's plan contain?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Behind the platform, which held: the integration that created orders in the warehouse system one at a time under the vendor's rate limit had been falling behind since the afternoon in a queue with no gauge, alarm or owner, and the sell-out reached the channels through scheduled copies up to two hours late. The plan needs a forecast (about 1.5 times last year), a capacity figure per link tested with marked orders through the whole path, fulfillment orders sent in batches within the limit and keyed on the order number, a gauge and alarm on the age of the oldest unsent order, a dead-letter queue with an owner, stock as events through an availability service, a degradation ladder whose switches have owners and triggers with checkout, payment and the order path never switched off, a change freeze, a runbook and a reconciliation the morning after.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can explain why a stock chain that works every other day oversells at peak.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A merchant copies stock from its warehouse system to its ERP every 15 minutes, from the ERP to its shop hourly and from the shop to its marketplace connector hourly, and has never had an oversell. Using only this chapter: why not, and what happens when a jacket sells out at 38 orders a minute?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The chain is up to about two hours late by design (15 minutes plus up to an hour plus up to an hour), which is harmless when nothing sells out inside the window. At peak the sell-out at 19:40 reached the ERP at 19:45, the storefronts at about 20:30 and the marketplaces at about 21:35, and the channels sold 1,340 units the warehouse did not have (about 790 on the storefronts and 550 on the marketplaces); marketplace cancellations cost more because the seller is measured on them (a strike from bol). The fix is stock events from the WMS through an availability service that publishes available-to-promise per channel with a buffer within a minute, with a fallback of a marketplace buffer and a person pausing listings.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say what the team could and could not do on the evening, and what the plan gives it instead.
acceptance_criteria.probe: At 20:20 on the peak evening the warehouse tells the ecommerce manager that a jacket is out and orders keep coming. Using only this chapter: what could the team do in 2026, and what does the 2027 plan give them?
acceptance_criteria.expected: In 2026: set the jacket's quantities to zero by hand in the platform, one variant at a time; edit listings by hand in the connector, with no pause switch; wait for the WMS vendor to raise its limit (ticket at 21:30, answer at 22:40); send a mass e-mail to everyone who ordered after 17:00, with no list of affected orders; edit a theme sentence to change the delivery promise; and no view of orders per minute against the warehouse's intake. In 2027: eight rehearsed switches, each with one owner who may flip it without a meeting and a trigger (stock badges from the buffered copy, a raised marketplace buffer with listings paused, a widened delivery promise, a waiting room and others), a one-screen dashboard in business units, an incident commander, vendor contacts for Friday night, and customer messages filled with order numbers from the OMS.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: That in Black Friday week 2026 Kestrel & Pine took 31,000 orders, 2,300 in one hour, and the platform kept accepting purchases while the integrations could not send orders to the warehouse or return stock updates fast enough, so customers bought jackets that had sold out; that the evening was lost in the afternoon, the sell-out took two hours to reach the channels, and the 2027 plan changes the chain, not the platform; that the evening is told twice, the November 2026 incident and then the November 2027 plan, with the totals fixed (19:40, 1,340 units, 1,120 orders, €96,000, four hours) and hourly figures labeled reconstructions; and that the methods come from the peak-load chapter. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's reconstructed evening and its 2027 plan, with dated public practice (Shopify, Zalando, AWS) cited for the methods.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: What happened hour by hour on the 2026 peak day, and what does the 2027 plan change?
thesis.claim: On 27 November 2026 the platform held while the chain behind it failed unseen: the order flow to the warehouse fell behind from about 13:00 under the WMS vendor's rate limit, and the 19:40 sell-out of the Ridgewalker jacket reached the channels 50 minutes to two hours late through scheduled stock copies. The 2027 plan changes that chain, not the platform: tested capacity per link, stock events, a gauged queue and eight degradation switches with owners.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that peak readiness is the platform's scalability: if the storefront and checkout stay up the peak went well, and the remedy for an oversell is a larger platform plan or more servers.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim writes its peak plan as a journey hour by hour, tests its own order path rather than relying on the vendor's tests, and gives every queue a gauge and every switch an owner before buying anything. Kestrel & Pine's evening cost 1,340 oversold units and 1,120 affected orders (760 canceled, 360 delayed), about €96,000, and roughly 8,000 missed next-day deliveries; its post-mortem found no forecast, no capacity figure per link, a queue with no gauge, stock copied on a schedule and nobody with authority to flip anything. The 2027 plan forecasts 60 orders a minute, tests every link at 80 and the OMS-to-WMS link at 120 (which found a batch size that broke the rate limit), alarms at ten minutes of queue age, sends stock within a minute and closes the morning with an 08:00 reconciliation.
thesis.how_why: A queue between the platform and the warehouse keeps checkout working when the warehouse link is slow, but it adds no capacity, so without a gauge it hides the delay: about four calls per order against a limit of about 30 a minute capped the flow near seven orders a minute, below the afternoon's arrival rate. Stock that travels by a 15-minute copy and two hourly copies is up to two hours late by design, which matters only when a product sells out inside the window, as the Ridgewalker jacket did at 38 orders a minute. The people who saw the problem had no switch to pull and no view to read, and a vendor's load tests find the vendor's bottleneck, so only the merchant's own test with marked orders finds its own.

role.contribution: Walks Black Friday 2026 through the same chain hour by hour, with what each system did and each person saw and could do, then lays out the 2027 plan built from it, and performs the part's closing (the published chapter does not yet do so: it ends with its questions and one paragraph handing off to Part X).

transition_in.carries_over: The first three journeys' chain of handoffs, walked on an ordinary April week: Bergzicht's pallets and Eva's parcel leaving the same warehouse.
transition_in.introduces: The day that is not ordinary: the same chain at about forty times its normal load on Black Friday 2026, when the handoffs' delays and copies turned into an oversell, and the plan that rehearses the 2027 evening.

parts.title: Part X — EVOLUTION: Decisions That Change With Scale

know: The five decisions in reading order and what each settles: how to cover the capability map and compare the options over three years (build, buy or assemble); how to move a platform or a fact's owner without one cutover date (migration); which decisions change at each of the four scale stages and the signals that a stage is ending; who owns each system, integration and app and how a small team works with an agency and vendors; and what AI assistants and agents do as of November 2026 and what a merchant needs before an agent can buy.

Kestrel & Pine's 2027 answers: the February 2027 review, which declined an outside consultancy's composable rebuild (about €3.2M, about 18 months) and the agency's headless storefront rebuild (about €240,000, nine months plus a second runtime), costed an enterprise suite (about €3.2M) and chose stay and surround (W4, about €1.33M over 2027–2029, reviewed in 2029); the PIM and OMS introduced seam by seam (PIM consumers from August and September 2027; marketplace orders through the OMS from 15 September, D2C from 13 October, EDI and wholesale from 8 December, a freeze from 15 November to 5 December); the April 2027 stage map; the ownership map (13 of 34 integrations unowned in January 2027, 5 in April); and W8, agent readiness rather than agents.
believe: At a growing merchant most failures live in the joins, so growth is usually answered by changing owners and joins rather than the core.
These decisions are due when the business changes shape (a channel, a stock location, a brand), not after the incident that exposes the old design.
An AI agent is a new writer, admitted by the same ownership rules as any integration.
can_do: Place their own business on the stage map by shape and list which systems were bought for an earlier stage.
Judge a replatforming pitch with a three-year cost that includes people, agency, revenue at risk and exit, and plan any move one seam at a time.
Draw an ownership map with one row per system, integration and app, and write an agent policy that gives no agent a write scope on stock, prices or orders.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every supporting claim of the part thesis is argued by at least one chapter, and every chapter supports at least one.
Each chapter's closing hand-off expresses the relationship its successor declares in transition_in.

Given a growing merchant the part does not describe, a reader who has read only Part X decides what to examine and in what order before accepting a replatforming, a reorganization or an AI proposal, and grounds each step in ownership and timing rather than in a tool.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A brand with stores, wholesale and two marketplaces oversold on its last peak day while its hosted platform stayed up. A consultancy pitches a composable rebuild priced on lower subscriptions; half of its 30 integrations were built by its agency and nobody can name their owner; marketing wants an AI assistant that can change stock and prices; the board asks whether the company has 'outgrown' its platform. Using only Part X: what should it decide, in what order, and on what evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: First find what failed: if the platform held and stock and orders went wrong, the problem is in the joins, not the core. Place the business on the stage map by shape (channels and stock locations, not revenue) and list which systems were built for an earlier stage; those leftovers are what to retire. Price each option over three years with people, agency, migration, revenue at risk and exit, not subscriptions; keeping the platform and buying an order hub, an availability service and a PIM beside it while owning the joins is usually cheaper and safer. Give every integration a named owner and every fact one writer on an ownership map before adding anything. Move each new hub one seam at a time, smallest channel first, with a parallel run and reconciliation, a rehearsed rollback, a freeze around peak and the old path kept through one peak. Treat the assistant as an integration with a row and no write scope on stock, prices or orders, and fix product, availability, promise and order-status answers before any agent. Record each decision with a review date.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The page that carries the part's closing sets the five decisions against the opening's merchant whose systems still run but must now share stock after a change of shape, and states what the five have in common; it does not only hand off to Part XI.

thesis.question: When a growing merchant's business changes shape, which architecture decisions must it take again, and on what basis should it take them?
thesis.claim: When a merchant adds a channel, a stock location or a brand, five decisions fall due again: what to build, buy or assemble; how to move a fact to a new owner; which systems from earlier stages to retire; who owns each system, integration and app; and what AI agents may do. Each is settled by naming who owns each shared fact (stock, order, product) and each join between systems, when the shape changes rather than after an incident.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that growth is a tool problem: a merchant outgrows its platform, and the remedy is a larger or more modern stack (a composable assembly, a suite, an AI agent) chosen on features and subscription price, with team structure and ownership following from the tool chosen.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim answers a replatforming pitch, a board question about scale or an AI proposal by asking which owner it changes and whether the shape has changed, and spends on owners and joins before new systems. Kestrel & Pine declined a consultancy's composable rebuild (about €3.2M, about 18 months) and the agency's headless storefront rebuild (about €240,000, nine months), and chose stay and surround (about €1.33M over 2027–2029, reviewed in 2029); moved product data and orders to new hubs seam by seam around a Black Friday freeze; attributed eight of its ten incidents to Growing-stage designs; reduced its unowned integrations from 13 of 34 in January 2027 to 5 in April; and wrote W8 as agent readiness, not agents.
thesis.how_why: A new channel or stock location multiplies the systems that must agree about the same stock, order and product facts. The systems bought for the earlier stage keep running with that stage's assumptions (an hourly sync, a one-channel agency script, the ERP as the stock hub), so the failures appear in the joins, not in the core, and replacing the core leaves them in place. Moving a fact's owner creates a period in which two systems hold it, which only a seam-by-seam move with a reconciliation keeps safe. A join is kept only if someone inside the merchant owns it, because agencies and vendors are paid to build and to keep the subscription. An agent that can order, refund or change stock is one more writer of the same facts.

supporting_claims.claim: A merchant should build only what customers choose it for and nobody sells, buy what every merchant needs and own the joins, and compare options over three years on people, agency, migration, revenue at risk and exit, against which the subscription is usually the smallest line; when the failures live in the joins, keeping a hosted platform and buying hubs beside it is a deliberate architecture.

A platform or a fact's owner is moved safely one seam (a channel, a capability or a slice of traffic) at a time, with a parallel run reconciled by cause, each kind of data migrated on its own plan, written go/no-go criteria, a rehearsed rollback and the old owner kept operable through one peak; one cutover date with no way back is the documented failure.

A scale stage is a shape (how many channels sell, how many locations hold stock and, at the Group stage, how many brands or business units share them), not a revenue band; each stage leaves systems built for the one before, and those leftovers cause most of the next stage's incidents, so the decision at a transition is which leftovers to retire, and the signals of a transition arrive before the incidents.

Ownership follows money unless it is designed: every system, integration and app needs a technical owner inside the merchant on one ownership map with one writer per fact; at ten to twenty people journey teams and an integration pair own the joins, agencies and vendors work under contracts that leave the repository, credentials and map with the merchant, and the team shape changes one stage before the systems do.

An AI agent is a new writer and is admitted like an integration: assistants read and propose, agents act; agent readiness is correct product, availability, delivery-promise and order-status answers from one owner by API plus an identity and policy for each agent, which a European merchant should have in 2027 before any shopper-facing agent.

role.contribution: Turns the per-chapter scale tables into the decisions a growing merchant must retake.

flow.rationale: Each chapter takes a decision that the one before makes necessary or gives it the vocabulary for. Chapter 41 settles what the merchant owns (stay and surround: keep the platform, buy the hubs, own the joins), which leaves chapter 42 its problem: even a merchant that does not replatform must move product data and orders to new hubs beside a running shop. Chapter 43 then steps back from Kestrel & Pine's 2027 decisions to the stages that make such decisions due; it relies on chapter 41's finding that the failures were in the joins rather than the core and on chapter 42's point that a migration is how a merchant crosses a stage, and turns both into a rule about timing (retire the leftovers at the transition). Chapter 44 asks who takes and keeps these decisions; its team shape changes by stage, so it needs chapter 43's stages, and its ownership map needs the hubs and integrations of chapters 41 and 42. Chapter 45 ends with the newest actor: it admits an AI agent by giving it a row on chapter 44's ownership map, and its readiness list is the PIM, OMS and availability service that chapters 41 and 42 bought and moved. Putting 45 before 44 would leave 'an agent is an integration' with no map to land on; putting 42 before 41 would teach how to move a system before the reader knows why a merchant that stays still migrates; putting 43 first would lose the two findings it turns into its timing rule (chapter 41's that the failures were in the joins, chapter 42's that a migration is how a merchant crosses a stage), since the stages themselves are already known from earlier parts; putting 44 before 43 would size the team before the reader has the stages that its rule 'change the team one stage before the systems' refers to.

hook.content: A merchant adds a store, a wholesale channel, a marketplace, a warehouse or a second brand. Its systems still run, but now they must share stock and coordinate orders in ways they were never designed for: leaving them unchanged oversells, and replacing everything exceeds the team.

opening.bridge: From Part IX, which walked four journeys through Kestrel & Pine's landscape at one moment, to the same landscape over time: every system Eva's jacket crosses was introduced between 2016 and 2025, and its purchase date explains today's responsibilities and gaps, so each new decision has to account for that history, the team that will run it and the customers who keep ordering during the change.
opening.roadmap: Five decisions Kestrel & Pine takes in 2027, each about ownership and timing: the February platform review and its three-year costs, ending in stay and surround with a 2029 review; the PIM and OMS introductions, one seam at a time with a freeze around Black Friday; the April stage map, which separates today's coordination problems from possible Group-stage needs; the ownership map, from 13 of 34 integrations unowned in January; and AI that recommends against AI that acts, ending in agent readiness before any agent.

closing.synthesis: The platform review, the migration plan, the stage map, the ownership map and the agent policy look like five decisions about vendors, projects, growth, people and AI. At Kestrel & Pine each came down to the same act: naming which system or person owns a fact or a join, and when that changes. W4 kept the platform and took ownership of the joins; the migrations moved one owner at a time; the stage map retired the Growing-stage leftovers; the ownership map filled the blank cells; W8 gave the agent a row and no write scope.
closing.so_what: A merchant facing its next change of shape can test any proposal, whether a new platform, a reorganization or an agent, with two questions before comparing products: which fact's owner does this change, and has the shape of the business changed enough to make it due? Kestrel & Pine's answers cost about €1.33M over three years instead of about €3.2M, and each carries a date on which it is reviewed.
closing.callback: The part opening's merchant that adds a store, a channel or a brand and finds its systems still running but now required to share stock and coordinate orders they were never designed for.

takeaway.content: Before the next change of shape, write two tables for your own landscape: a stage map that says which stage each system was bought for and marks the leftovers to retire, and an ownership map with a named owner and one writer per fact for every system, integration, app and agent. Date the decision records for review at the next transition.

transition_in.carries_over: The landscape as it works at one moment, shown in the journeys.
transition_in.introduces: How the same decisions look different as the business moves through the four stages.

posts.title: Part 10 introduction
posts.question: What does this part argue, and in what order should its chapters be read?

know: Part X takes five decisions in order: build, buy or assemble, with a full three-year cost; migration in limited, reversible steps; the scale stages and what invalidates an earlier design; ownership of systems, integrations and apps; and AI that recommends against AI authorized to act.

Each chapter uses Kestrel & Pine's 2027 program, Waypoint, as its case: the platform review ending in stay and surround with a 2029 review; product publication moved gradually and order channels on separate dates with a freeze around Black Friday; the stage map; the January inventory with 13 of 34 integrations unowned; and better data and interfaces before any shopping agent.

The five are decisions about ownership and timing rather than tools: build what customers choose you for, buy what every merchant needs and own the joins; cross a stage one seam at a time with the old owner kept through one peak; and give every system, integration, app and agent a named owner and every fact one writer.
can_do: Pick the Part X chapter that matches the decision in front of them: a replatforming pitch, a migration plan, a board question about scale, an ownership gap or an AI proposal.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of this page alone can name the five chapters' decisions in reading order.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only this page: what will each of the next five chapters decide, in order, and with which Kestrel & Pine case?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Build, buy or assemble: bundled products, separate services and custom software compared by full cost over three years (people, integration, migration and exit), ending in keeping the platform and adding missing capabilities with a 2029 review. Replatforming and migration: limited transitions with comparison and recovery at every step; product publication moves gradually in 2027 and order channels move on separate dates with a freeze around Black Friday. Scale stages: the business changes (channels, stock locations, brands as well as revenue) that invalidate an earlier design; the stage map separates current coordination problems from possible group-wide needs. Organizing commerce engineering: business and technical responsibility for systems, integrations and apps, from a January inventory with 13 of 34 integrations unowned, with supplier contracts and practices a small team can keep. AI and agentic commerce: AI that recommends against AI authorized to act, both needing reliable product and stock answers and actions needing permissions and accountability; a dated review of protocols ends in improving data and interfaces before building a shopping agent.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of this page alone can say why the part treats these as decisions about ownership and timing rather than about tools.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: why does a merchant have to take these decisions again as it grows, and why are they about ownership and timing rather than about choosing tools?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A merchant grows in jumps (a store, wholesale, a marketplace, a warehouse, a brand); its systems still run but must now share stock and coordinate orders they were not designed for, so leaving them unchanged oversells and replacing everything exceeds the team. Each system was introduced at a different time, which explains today's responsibilities and gaps. The problems live in the joins, so the answers are who owns what (build the differentiating, buy the common, own the joins, one writer per fact, a named owner for every system, integration, app and agent) and when to change it (one seam at a time, at the change of shape, with the old owner kept through one peak), not a new tool.

role.contribution: Performs the part's opening: states the part thesis in its three key points, sets the merchant's change of shape as the problem, ties each system's purchase date to its gaps, names the five 2027 decisions with their Kestrel & Pine cases, and gives the reading order.

posts.title: Build, Buy or Assemble: Choosing and Changing Platforms
posts.question: How do you choose between a suite, a SaaS platform with apps, a composable assembly and custom build, and how do you compare their real costs?

know: The four shapes for covering the commerce capability map (a suite, a hosted platform plus apps, a composable assembly, a custom build), the two mixed shapes (ERP-centered commerce and the specialist group) and stay and surround, with their trade-offs in time, integration and upgrade burden, cost shape and exit.

The total-cost lines and who forgets them (subscription, GMV share and transaction fees, payment processing, apps, agency, integration, people, migration including revenue at risk, exit), and Kestrel & Pine's three options over 2027–2029: the consultancy's composable rebuild (about €3.2M, about 18 months), an enterprise suite Noor costed herself (about €3.2M, about 12 months, not a pitch) and stay and surround (about €1.33M), with the agency's headless storefront pitch (about €240,000, nine months) declined separately.

Lock-in and exit: the exit questions to ask before signing, the EU Data Act's switching rules (applicable from 12 September 2025, no switching charges from 12 January 2027) and the open question whether they reach hosted commerce platforms; W4 recorded as a decision record with a 2029 review.
believe: The subscription is usually the smallest line of total cost; people, agency, revenue at risk and exit decide the total.
Stay and surround is an architecture, not a failure to decide.
The time to replatform is rarely the time the problems appear, because the problems appear in the joins.
can_do: Apply the differentiation test capability by capability: build only what customers choose the merchant for and nobody sells, buy the rest, own the joins.
Price platform options over three years with the people, agency, migration, revenue-at-risk and exit lines, and ask the exit questions before signing.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a replatforming pitch argued on subscription savings, the reader rejects the comparison and names what to compare instead, rather than choosing on licence price.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A €40M brand's hosted platform held on its peak day, but stock was wrong across channels and support could not find orders. A consultancy pitches a composable rebuild whose new subscriptions cost less a year than the current platform plan. Using only this chapter: is the comparison sound, and what should the brand compare instead?
acceptance_criteria.expected: No. The subscription is the smallest line (except under GMV pricing); the comparison must run over three years and include GMV share and transaction fees, apps, the agency or partner after the build, integration, the people who own the joins, migration with revenue at risk (the Marks & Spencer 2014 fall of 8.1% for a quarter) and exit. The failures sit in the joins (stock ownership, one order record), not in the checkout, which held; a new core leaves them to be rebuilt. Keeping the platform and buying an OMS with availability and a PIM beside it, while owning integration standards, addresses them: at Kestrel & Pine about €1.33M against about €3.2M for a rebuild or a suite. Ask who owns each integration the day after go-live.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can apply the differentiation rule to a merchant's capabilities and name the two traps on either side of it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: for a mid-sized outdoor brand, which of these should it build, buy or own, and why: the checkout, available-to-promise per channel, one order record across channels, product content, integration contracts and reconciliation? What are the two traps?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Buy the checkout: shoppers do not choose the brand for its cart, and the platform already handles it. Buy available-to-promise as a module of the OMS but own its rules; buy an OMS for the order record; buy a PIM for product content: solved categories whose ownership decision is the hard part. Build and own the integration contracts and reconciliation, because nobody sells the merchant's ownership rules. The traps are building a commodity or copying a far larger company's architecture (The Giant's Boots) and customizing a bought core until it cannot be upgraded (The Forked Platform).

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say what to establish about leaving a platform before signing for it, and what EU law does and does not settle.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Before a merchant signs a three-year platform contract, what does this chapter say it should establish about leaving, and what does the EU Data Act settle?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Whether it can export products, variants, prices, customers, orders, gift-card balances and store credit in full, in a documented format, without a ticket (password hashes usually cannot move); whether it controls the domain and can redirect every old URL; who owns the theme code, functions and scripts; what each app holds and exports; that every integration pointing at the platform must be re-pointed; and the contract's term, notice and GMV floor. The Data Act applies from 12 September 2025, requires switching rights and at least 30 days to retrieve data, and prohibits switching charges from 12 January 2027, but whether it covers hosted commerce platforms is unsettled. The decision goes into a decision record with a review date.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: That a merchant with late stock updates, missing orders and a proposal for a new platform must first find which work is failing, because causes in warehouse feeds or connectors survive a replacement; that the options (keep, buy together, connect separate products, build) are compared on what each fixes against several years of subscription, payment fees, apps, agency work, integration maintenance and exit, and that a lower subscription can need more engineering than a small team has; that Kestrel & Pine's early-2027 review chose stay and surround, Waypoint's W4; and that the choice assigns a jacket order's systems to products and teams. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's review with costed options, vendor pricing pages, guides and terms, the EU Data Act, and the vendors' own 2025–2026 moves.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: How do you choose between a suite, a SaaS platform with apps, a composable assembly and custom build, and how do you compare their real costs?
thesis.claim: Choose capability by capability, not by platform shape: build only what customers choose the merchant for and no vendor sells, buy what competitors also buy, and own the joins (the stock, order and product-data flows between systems). Compare three-year staff, agency-fee, migration, revenue-at-risk and exit costs before subscription price; when failures sit in the joins, keeping the hosted platform and adding order and product-information systems beside it costs and risks less than replacing it.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a platform is chosen by shape and features: a merchant that has outgrown its hosted platform moves to a composable assembly or an enterprise suite, compares vendors on subscription and feature lists, and treats staying as indecision.
