thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim prices every option on staff, agency fees and exit cost before the subscription, checks each pitch against the failures it has measured, and records the decision with a review date. In February 2027 Kestrel & Pine received two pitches, an outside consultancy's composable rebuild (about €3.2M over 2027–2029, about 18 months) and the agency's headless storefront rebuild (about €240,000, nine months, plus a second runtime to operate); Noor Visser, who leads engineering, also costed an enterprise suite (about €3.2M over the same three years, about 12 months), which nobody had pitched. The headless rebuild was declined after she measured field Core Web Vitals on the NL storefront's product pages (INP, interaction to next paint, 310 ms at the 75th percentile on mobile, illustrative) and traced the INP problem to scripts from eleven apps; the agency's retainer went to a theme performance pass and an app-script audit instead. Stay and surround came to about €1.33M over 2027–2029, about €1.9M less than the composable rebuild or the suite (one-time OMS €320,000, PIM €110,000 and integration standards €150,000, plus subscriptions, two integration engineers and about €50,000 of revenue at risk); W4 (stay and surround) was recorded as a decision record to be revisited in 2029. The platform's €2,300 a month is about 1% of the €2.6M yearly technology spend.
thesis.how_why: A capability that every vendor sells gives no shopper a reason to choose the merchant, so building it spends engineers on parity; shoppers choose a brand for its products, stores and service, not its cart. And on Black Friday 2026 Kestrel & Pine's checkout held at 38 orders a minute while stock propagation, order ownership and product data failed. Those are joins, and a new platform leaves them to be rebuilt: a rebuild rewires 34 integrations, adds people and agency costs that continue after go-live, and puts revenue at risk at cutover, while GMV pricing turns a suite's subscription into its largest line and bespoke joins raise exit cost. A layer bought beside a running platform is introduced in reversible phases.

role.contribution: Gives the part its first decision, what to build, buy or assemble and how to price it over three years, through Kestrel & Pine's February 2027 review and W4.

transition_in.carries_over: The part introduction's first decision, the 2027 platform review compared by full cost over three years, and the instruction to begin with it.
transition_in.introduces: The four shapes for covering the capability map, the rule for what to build, the total-cost lines vendors leave out, lock-in and exit, and Kestrel & Pine's three costed options ending in W4.

posts.title: Moving Without Burning the Bridge: Replatforming and Migration
posts.question: When a platform must change, how do you move without a big-bang cutover?

know: Which reasons justify a platform change (the core itself limits the business: a vendor ending the product, a forked core, a B2B model no layer can express, a competitor running the platform) and which point to the joins instead (stock wrong across channels, support unable to find an order, an agency's recommendation alone).

The Burned Bridge from three dated public failures (Target 2011, Finish Line 2012, reverted after 17 days at about $3M, Marks & Spencer 2014, M&S.com down 8.1% for a quarter) and one avoided case (Hobbycraft 2013); the strangler approach with seams by channel, capability and traffic slice; the phases from shadow to decommission; parallel runs against dual writes; the separate data migrations; the five parts of a cutover; and migrating the integrations.

Kestrel & Pine's 2027 introductions: the PIM loaded in July (1,900 variants with conflicting attributes resolved before publishing), the DE storefront first in August, NL/BE and the connector in September; the OMS shadow in August, a parallel run from 1 to 14 September (differences on about 1.4% of orders in week one), marketplace orders from 15 September, D2C from 13 October, a freeze from 15 November to 5 December around Black Friday, EDI and wholesale from 8 December, the old paths retired in January 2028 and 2026 orders imported as read-only history.
believe: The documented replatforming failures broke on load, timing and customer habit, not on missing features.
Every step must stay reversible through one peak, and the reconciliation job is the migration's main deliverable.
The migration technique does not change with scale; the thing being migrated does.
can_do: Plan a migration backwards from the first peak the new owner must survive, as a sequence of seams with written go/no-go criteria and a rehearsed rollback.
Write a separate plan and check for each kind of data and for every integration that reads or writes the fact being moved.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a single-weekend migration plan with dual writes, the reader names its failures and replaces it with a seam-by-seam plan, rather than adding more testing to the same plan.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A merchant plans to move to a new order system: create its historical orders in the new system over a weekend, switch every channel to it on the Monday before Black Friday, and have the integration write each new order to both the old path and the new system 'to be safe'. Using only this chapter: what is wrong, and what should the plan be?
acceptance_criteria.expected: It is the Burned Bridge: everything moves on one date near a peak, the new system meets real load for the first time in public, and there is no rehearsed way back. Creating historical orders fires their side effects again (confirmations, reservations, fulfillment requests, invoices); history is imported read-only with its original numbers. Writing to both is two writers with no transaction across them, which diverge silently (the App That Wrote Stock); prefer one writer and a copied flow. The plan: a shadow copy, a parallel run whose reconciliation lists differences by cause, the smallest channel first, written go/no-go criteria, a rehearsed and timed rollback, continuity of order numbers, a change freeze around peak, and the old path kept receiving copies and operable through one peak.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can sort the reasons given for a replatforming into those the core causes and those the joins cause.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A team argues for a new platform because stock is wrong across channels, support cannot find orders, the site was slow on Black Friday, the vendor is ending the product, the core has been customized until it cannot be upgraded, and the agency recommends it. Using only this chapter: which are reasons to replatform, and what should be checked first for each?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A change is justified only when the core limits the business and no layer beside it can fix that. Wrong stock is an ownership and availability problem (who is the system of record and how the others learn); unfindable orders an order-hub problem an OMS beside the platform can solve; the slow peak a maybe, usually the integrations. A vendor ending the product is a reason, on the vendor's date (Magento 1 ended on 30 June 2020). A forked core is a reason, but the choice is between rebuilding on the current version and leaving. The agency's recommendation is not a reason by itself: check who is paid for the build and who owns the joins after it.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say why a migration's data is several migrations and why a rollback has a time limit.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: why is moving a platform's data more than one export, and why is the old system kept operable through one peak but not forever?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Each kind of data has its own identifiers, owner and trap: products must keep their SKUs and GTINs; prices can drift silently; customers' password hashes usually cannot move and consent must move with its proof; orders are imported as read-only history because re-creating them fires side effects; gift-card and store-credit balances are liabilities that must sum to the cent; every old URL needs a redirect or an intended removal; and each integration pointing at the old owner needs a cutover task or a legacy mimic. The longer the new system owns a seam, the more records exist only there, so routing back gets more expensive; keeping the old path receiving copies through the first peak keeps the rollback cheap while it matters, after which the window closes on its own.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: That while an order hub is introduced, old and new systems may both send work to the warehouse, risking two parcels or missed orders, so each step needs a clear transfer of responsibility and a recovery; that the plan starts from the fact whose owner changes and every integration that reads or writes it, with small reversible steps; that Kestrel & Pine's February 2027 platform review decided to keep the shop platform (W4, stay and surround, adopted in March) but it introduces a PIM in Q3 and an OMS by Q4 while about 800 storefront orders a day continue; that documented failures were not feature failures, that the strangler approach moves one seam at a time with a reconciliation and the old system kept operable, and that data migration is several migrations. Evidence: dated public failures (Target, Finish Line, Marks & Spencer), Fowler's and Thoughtworks' patterns, Zalando's rebuild and Kestrel & Pine's 2027 timeline.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: When a platform must change, how do you move without a big-bang cutover?
thesis.claim: Move one seam at a time (a channel, a capability or a slice of traffic), so that each step changes the owner of one fact for one part of the business: copy the flow in shadow, run old and new in parallel with a reconciliation that explains differences by cause, migrate each kind of data on its own plan, cut over with written criteria and a rehearsed rollback, and keep the old owner operable through the first peak after cutover.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a migration is a project with one go-live date: build the new system to feature parity, move all the data over a weekend and switch everything at once, because running two systems side by side doubles the cost and a clean cut avoids confusion.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim plans every move backwards from the first peak the new owner must survive, and applies it when it introduces a hub such as a PIM or an OMS beside a running platform, not only when it replatforms. Kestrel & Pine's PIM found 1,900 variants with conflicting attributes at its July 2027 load and fixed them before publishing; the OMS parallel run from 1 to 14 September found differences on about 1.4% of orders in its first week, mostly status mapping and timing, plus one order the old path had fulfilled twice; marketplace orders moved on 15 September, D2C on 13 October, EDI and wholesale on 8 December, around a freeze from 15 November to 5 December. Target (2011), Finish Line (2012, reverted after 17 days) and Marks & Spencer (2014, online sales down 8.1% for a quarter) each moved on one date and broke on load, performance, timing or customer habit rather than on missing features, with no rehearsed way back.
thesis.how_why: During a migration two systems hold the same fact and only one may be right. A seam limits that to one fact for one channel, so a parallel run can compare results before anything is acted on, while dual writes create two writers with no transaction across them. Each kind of data has its own identifiers and legal constraints (product identifiers feed every integration, customer consent must move with its proof, gift-card balances are liabilities), and re-created orders fire their side effects again. The longer the new system owns a seam, the more records exist only there, so a rollback is cheap only while the old path still receives the copies.

role.contribution: Shows how a merchant moves a platform or a fact's owner without a single cutover date, using Kestrel & Pine's 2027 PIM and OMS introductions as the worked example.

transition_in.carries_over: W4's stay and surround, which still leaves Kestrel & Pine to introduce an OMS and a PIM beside a running platform without creating the duplicates and gaps the hubs exist to remove.
transition_in.introduces: How to move a platform or a fact's owner one seam at a time: the documented failures of moving on one date, the strangler approach, parallel runs, data migration, cutover and rollback, and the 2027 PIM and OMS seams around the Black Friday freeze.

posts.title: What Changes at Each Scale: From First Store to Group
posts.question: Which architecture decisions change as a business grows, and what are the signs that a stage is ending?

know: The four stages (Starting, Growing, Omnichannel, Group) as shapes of channels and stock locations, with revenue bands as rough markers only, and the map of what is typical and what becomes necessary at each: where the order and stock truth live, product data, fulfillment, finance, integration style, who builds and runs, fees met, peak day, decisions due and failure patterns.

How fresh each fact must be at each stage, the Group stage's share-or-separate table per capability, and the transition signals (a fee cliff, a second stock location, a retail chain asking for EDI, two order counts, a connector without an owner, support opening several systems, an app writing a fact another system owns, a first peak-day integration failure, a second brand).

Kestrel & Pine's path priced: Starting 2016–2018, Growing 2019–2022, Omnichannel since 2023; the April 2027 stage map, which maps its thirteen systems to their stages, attributes eight of its ten incidents to Growing-stage designs, finds six signals in 2026 and defers the Group stage to the 2029 review because no stage-4 signal is planned for 2027–2028.
believe: A stage is a shape, not a revenue number.
Most incidents at a stage are designs from the stage before still running; the leftover, not the missing tool, is what fails.
Two transition signals in one year mean the stage has changed, whatever the revenue says.
can_do: Place a merchant on the map by its channels and stock locations and list which stage each of its systems was bought for.
Sort a program's decisions into those for the current stage, those left from the last one and those copied from a larger company, and say for a group which capabilities to share.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a merchant whose revenue says one stage and whose shape says another, the reader places it by shape and names the decision due, rather than by revenue or by adding a tool.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A brand with €15M revenue runs a web shop, two stores, wholesale including EDI with one retail chain, and a marketplace, all from one warehouse whose stock its ERP copies to the shop every hour. This year it held its first 'which number is right' meeting and had its first peak-day integration failure. Its board calls it a Growing business. Using only this chapter: which stage is it in, and what should it decide first?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Omnichannel by shape: stores, wholesale by EDI and a marketplace sell from one stock, and revenue bands are only markers; it has at least three transition signals this year (an EDI request, two order counts, a first peak integration failure), and two in a year mean the stage has changed. The first decision is which Growing-stage leftovers to retire, not which tool to add: the hourly ERP-to-shop copy and the ERP as stock hub give way to a system of record per fact, availability computed from stock events, an order hub and integration standards with owners, contracts, idempotency and reconciliation. Copying a Group-stage architecture would be The Giant's Boots.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a group adding a brand, the reader decides capability by capability what to share, rather than one stack or full separation.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A group acquires a second outdoor brand that runs its own stack. Using only this chapter: which capabilities should the group share, which may stay separate, and how should it proceed?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Always share the integration layer and data definitions, peak tooling, security and compliance, and the PSP contract and fraud rules (with separate merchant accounts where legal entities require). Share the storefront when the brands are positioned alike, keep it separate when brand identity is the product; share the attribute model in a PIM with brand workspaces; share stock and availability when warehouses serve both brands; share the order hub when customers buy across brands. An acquisition turns the question into sequencing, which is a migration. Forcing one stack by decree, or keeping everything apart, without measuring the benefit is One Size Fits None; autonomy without shared standards produces the Spaghetti Junction at group scale.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can explain why a merchant's current-stage incidents are attributed to the stage before, and what that changes in its program.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Kestrel & Pine's incidents of 2026 and early 2027 happened while it was an Omnichannel business. Using only this chapter: why does the stage map attribute most of them to the Growing stage, and what follows for Waypoint?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Eight of the ten incidents trace to designs from 2019–2022 still running in 2026: the hourly stock sync built when marketplace orders were a few a day, agency scripts written for one channel at a time, the ERP as hub for stock it did not hold, and the nightly POS sync from when there was one store. The company had moved stage and the architecture had not. So Waypoint's €1.1M buys the Omnichannel stage's hubs and standards (OMS, PIM, availability service, integration standards) and retires the Growing-stage chain, and it defers Group-stage questions to the 2029 review because no second brand, fourth country or revenue past about €200M is planned for 2027–2028.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: That a first store, wholesale customer, marketplace or second brand changes what systems must coordinate (stock in two places) before volume becomes a problem; that the book's four stages, Starting, Growing, Omnichannel and Group, are brought together in one map to recognize transitions, not to copy a larger company's system list; that the stages rest on common practice, dated vendor evidence and the fictional example and are not validated revenue thresholds; that Eva's order crosses products bought at different stages, each with its original assumptions; that a stage is a shape, that leftovers from the previous stage cause the incidents, and that signals arrive before the architecture changes. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's stage map and priced path, vendor pricing pages and thresholds, and dated public reports of groups.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: Which architecture decisions change as a business grows, and what are the signs that a stage is ending?
thesis.claim: A scale stage is a shape (the channels that sell, the locations that hold stock), not a revenue band. Each stage moves the order record, stock record and integration style to a system that owns each fact, and retires the previous stage's systems, which still run on its assumptions. A stage is ending when two signals of a new shape, such as a second stock location or a connector nobody owns, arrive in one year.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a business grows along a revenue line and its architecture should be scaled up when volume demands it: buy the systems that companies in the next revenue band use, and keep what works until it breaks under load.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim places itself by shape, retires the previous stage's leftovers before adding tools, and sorts each decision by the stage it belongs to. Kestrel & Pine's April 2027 stage map found it had been in the Omnichannel stage since 2023, attributed eight of its ten incidents to Growing-stage designs still running in 2026, counted six transition signals in 2026, and deferred Group-stage questions to the 2029 review because none of their signals (a second brand, a fourth country, revenue past about €200M) is planned for 2027–2028. Waypoint, its 2027 improvement program, spends €1.1M on the Omnichannel hubs and retires the hourly chain. The fee cliff that matters most to it is payments, not the platform plan: on €27.0M of online revenue each half percentage point of payment cost is about €135,000 a year.
thesis.how_why: Each channel or stock location added multiplies the systems that must agree about the same stock, order and product facts, so the same fact must travel faster and more reliably at each stage: from the platform's own count, to a scheduled copy from the ERP, to an availability service fed by stock events. Systems are bought when a channel arrives, by whoever is available, with that moment's assumptions (one store, a few marketplace orders a day), and because they keep working nobody retires them; under the next stage's load the assumption fails at the join. Vendors tier their prices on volume and shape, so fee cliffs and plan thresholds mark a transition before an incident does. Each signal is either a new channel or stock location the existing joins were not built for, or a join already slipping (a connector without an owner, two counts of one fact); one can be a one-off, but two in one year (the author's rule) mean the channels and the joins have both changed.

role.contribution: Gives the part its rule about timing: one map of the four stages, the signals that a stage is ending and the Group stage's share-or-separate table, with Kestrel & Pine's April 2027 stage map tracing its incidents to leftovers from the stage before.

transition_in.carries_over: The migrations of chapter 42, named there as the moments a merchant moves from one scale stage to the next and feels it.
transition_in.introduces: The stages themselves: which decisions change at each, the signals that a stage is ending, and Kestrel & Pine's own path from a web shop to an omnichannel brand.

posts.title: Who Builds and Who Owns: Teams, Vendors, Agencies and Governance
posts.question: Who should own each part of a commerce platform, and how do small teams work with vendors and agencies?

know: The five duties of an owner (decide the contract, change, watch, fix, retire), why ownership follows money (an agency is paid to build and, on a platform's partner program, for keeping the merchant on the platform; a vendor to keep the subscription), and the ownership map's columns and its two rules (every row has a technical owner inside the company; no fact has two writers).

Four team shapes (by system, by journey, by layer, agency-led) in Team Topologies' terms and the recommendation for ten to twenty people; the rules for agencies and partners; the vendor card; light governance (decision records, standing rules checkable from the map, a weekly architecture hour); the merchant's product manager; environments, release management, feature flags and AI coding tools; and team shape by scale stage.

Kestrel & Pine before and after: in January 2027 thirteen systems, 34 integrations of which 13 had no named owner and 41 apps of which three wrote inventory; the Deprecated Endpoint of 8 February 2027; five integrations still unowned in April 2027, among them the scripts behind the Deprecated Endpoint, the Price Drift and the App That Wrote Stock; and from April 2027 two journey teams, an integration pair, a data pair, decision records KP-001 to KP-008 for W1–W8 and a weekly architecture hour.
believe: Most incidents at a merchant on rented software trace to code with no owner rather than to bad code.
A team per vendor reproduces the integration problem in the organization chart.
The team shape should change one stage before the system landscape does, because the owner must exist before the connector is built.
can_do: Draw an ownership map with one row per system, integration and app and check it for blank owners and duplicate writers.
Choose a team shape for their size and write the agency and vendor clauses that keep the repository, credentials, map and decision records with the merchant.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given an incident in which a published vendor change broke an unowned script, the reader names the missing owner and the map row that prevents it, rather than blaming the vendor or the agency.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A marketplace connector retires an API version on its published date; an agency script written years earlier stops sending stock to the marketplace, and nobody notices for two days. The agency says the script is outside its retainer; the e-commerce manager did not know it existed. Using only this chapter: what was missing, and what would have prevented it?
acceptance_criteria.expected: An owner: the script had no row and no technical owner inside the company, because ownership follows money and the agency was paid to build, not to own. A row on the ownership map with a technical owner (the integration pair), the pinned API version, the vendor's retirement date on the vendor card ninety days ahead and a monitor on stock-sync lag would have had the script updated or retired the week the retirement was announced. The agency's statement of work should name API versions and a deprecation clause, and the weekly architecture hour reviews deprecation dates due in the next ninety days.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say why a team organized by vendor fails at a merchant and what shape replaces it at their size.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A merchant with twelve engineers has one person or small team per vendor system: the platform, the ERP, the WMS, the marketplace connector. Using only this chapter: what is wrong with that shape, and what should replace it?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Organizations produce designs that copy their communication structures (Conway), so a team per system reproduces the integration problem: each owns its box and nobody owns the flow between them. At ten to twenty people: one or two stream-aligned journey teams (buy: storefront, catalog publication, checkout, marketplace listings, promotions; fulfill and return: order hub, warehouse integration, shipping, returns, EDI), one integration pair owning the integration layer, the ownership map and the reconciliation jobs as an internal product (a pair, because a full integration team becomes the bottleneck), a small data function, and vendors and the agency as services under written contracts. Below eight engineers, one journey team and one integration engineer. Journey teams need a shared integration standard, or each builds its own connector to the same ERP.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can list the contract terms that keep an agency or partner from becoming a Lynchpin.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A merchant is about to renew its agency's statement of work. Using only this chapter: which terms keep the agency from becoming a single point of failure?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The merchant owns the repository, vendor accounts, API credentials, ownership map and decision records; the agency commits to the merchant's repository. Every module, app or script the agency builds is a row with its scopes, its pinned API version, the platform release it was tested against and an exit plan. The statement of work names the versions tested against and a deprecation clause saying who updates what by when. Ownership after launch is written down before launch, either the agency under a support contract with a named engineer or the merchant's team. Building is paid separately from keeping. At Kestrel & Pine the 2027 statement of work lists each of the agency's nine scripts with an owner and pinned version, and three that write stock or prices moved in-house.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: That an order can reach checkout and never reach the warehouse while the platform vendor, connector partner and agency each confirm their part works, so someone with authority and information must own the whole flow because supplier contracts do not; that the chapter covers who defines, watches, changes and recovers a flow, through team structure, agencies, contracts and engineering practices a small team can keep on rented software; that the setting is a merchant with about a dozen engineers, an agency and several vendors, not a platform vendor; that ownership follows money unless designed, teams are shaped around journeys and governance is light but governs the facts. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's ownership map and incidents, a platform's published partner economics, Conway and Team Topologies, public accounts from Zalando and Uber, decision records and dated studies of AI coding tools.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: Who should own each part of a commerce platform, and how do small teams work with vendors and agencies?
thesis.claim: Every system, integration and app needs a technical owner inside the merchant who decides, changes, watches, fixes and retires it, recorded on one ownership map with exactly one system writing each fact, because agencies and vendors are paid to build and to keep the subscription, not to own a connector after launch. At the Omnichannel stage, with ten to twenty people, the rule is met by journey teams, an integration pair, and agency and vendor contracts that leave the repository, credentials and map with the merchant.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a merchant on rented software can leave ownership with its suppliers: the vendor runs the platform, the agency owns the theme and scripts on retainer, partners own their connectors, and the merchant's own team is organized one person per vendor to manage them.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim makes the ownership map its first governance artifact and fills its blank cells before adding systems. In January 2027 Kestrel & Pine had 34 integrations, 13 with no named owner; on 8 February a 2021 agency script stopped sending stock to bol for two days after the connector retired an API version. By April five were still unowned, among them that script, the German price-list export behind the Price Drift (€179 instead of €199 for nine days, about €8,200 of margin) and the pre-order app's inventory write: three of the ten incidents of 2026 and early 2027 sat in blank cells of one spreadsheet. From April 2027 two journey teams, an integration pair and a data pair own the rows, and the agency's statement of work lists each of its nine scripts with an owner and a pinned version.
thesis.how_why: An agency is paid by the merchant to build, and by the platform's partner program to keep the merchant on the platform; a vendor is paid to keep the subscription. Neither is paid to decide, watch or retire a connector after launch, so those duties fall to nobody unless assigned. Because organizations produce designs that copy their communication structures, a team per vendor leaves the flows between vendors without an owner, while journey teams own the flows end to end and an integration pair owns the shared layer. The map turns the rules into checks that need no meeting: no blank owner, no fact with two writers, every API version pinned with its retirement date.

role.contribution: Answers who takes and keeps the part's decisions: the ownership map, team shapes for a small merchant, agency and vendor terms and light governance, with Kestrel & Pine's January and April 2027 maps.

transition_in.carries_over: The stage map's sorting of decisions by stage, including its row on who builds and runs at each stage.
transition_in.introduces: The people who make and keep the decisions: who owns each system, integration and app, how a fourteen-person team works with an agency and a dozen vendors, and governance that fits a merchant.

posts.title: Assistants and Agents: AI in Commerce and What Is Real in 2026
posts.question: What is AI doing in commerce as of November 2026, and what must a merchant have in place before an AI agent can buy from it?

know: The difference between an assistant (reads and proposes) and an agent (has tools and permission to act), and the uses AI already has in commerce with their dated evidence: search and recommendations, product content, customer service bots, fraud screening, demand forecasting, visits referred by AI assistants, and admin assistants that act through the platform's own permissions.

Agentic commerce from September 2025 to November 2026 as the chapter's sources state it: AP2 announced on 16 September 2025; Instant Checkout launched in ChatGPT under ACP on 29 September 2025 and moved to Apps in March 2026; UCP announced on 11 January 2026; Shopify's Storefront MCP replaced by UCP endpoints; no party publishing a transaction count; the protocol layers (MCP, ACP, UCP, AP2, agent identity); and, for Europe, strong customer authentication dynamically linked to the amount and payee, the AI Act's Article 50 applying from 2 August 2026, the unsettled consumer-law position, and no live consumer channel in which an agent completes checkout for a Dutch, Belgian or German merchant.

The readiness list and four postures (a correct feed, the platform's agent channel, an agent gateway over the merchant's own services, an own shopping agent), and Kestrel & Pine's February 2027 agent test and W8 with owners and dates.
believe: Agent readiness is a data and API program, not an AI program.
An agent is an integration: a row, an owner, a contract, a pinned version, a reconciliation and no write scope on stock, prices or orders.
An agent channel is the harshest consumer of availability, because a stale copy becomes a promise a third party makes for the merchant.
can_do: Run the agent test on their own systems: answer an agent's five questions from the systems as they stand and name which system owns each answer.
Choose an agent posture for their stage and write an agent policy (identity, allowed actions, no writes, disclosure).

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a proposal to build a shopping agent on stale data, the reader declines it in favour of readiness work and names what that work is, rather than choosing a protocol or a vendor.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A Dutch outdoor brand's agency proposes a shopping agent on the storefront and native support for three agent-commerce protocols, so the brand is 'present when agents buy'. Its stock reaches the shop through an hourly copy from the warehouse, and its delivery promise is a fixed sentence in the theme. Using only this chapter: what should it do in 2027 instead, and why?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Run the agent test first: an agent asking what the product is, whether it is in stock, when it arrives, what it costs delivered and whether it can be returned, and where the order is would receive the stale stock and the static promise; an agent would broadcast those errors, not fix them. As of November 2026 no live consumer channel lets an agent complete checkout for a Dutch, Belgian or German merchant, the protocols changed within months and none is governed by a standards body, and an own agent is The Giant's Boots for a small team. So: product data from one owner in a feed with structured policies, refreshed in minutes; availability per channel from warehouse stock events, by API; a computed delivery promise; order status, returns and refunds by API from one order record; an identity and a policy for every agent with no write scope on stock, prices or orders, each agent credential a row on the ownership map. Stay with a correct feed and the platform's channel (for discovery while the platform's stock copy is stale) and revisit in mid-2027.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can tell an assistant that proposes from one that writes, and states the rule that governs the second.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A merchandiser wants to switch on 'auto-apply' for the admin AI assistant so it can fix negative stock figures before a campaign; until now the assistant only drafted product descriptions for review. Using only this chapter: what changes, and what should the rule be?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Drafting for review is an assistant that reads and proposes; auto-apply makes it an agent, a writer. Setting quantities in the platform while the warehouse feed also sets them creates two writers of one fact, the App That Wrote Stock again (The Secret Agent). The rule: no agent or assistant holds a write scope on stock, prices or orders; it acts through the platform's permissions with a draft-and-review step; its credential is a row on the ownership map with an owner, a contract, a pinned version and a reconciliation; detection is the weekly warehouse-to-platform reconciliation, recovery is to revoke and overwrite from the system of record. Kestrel & Pine's June 2027 trial ran with auto-apply disabled, drafted about 1,400 descriptions with about 60% accepted unchanged, and could not touch stock.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can explain what European payment rules require of an agent purchase and what that means for the merchant's checkout.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: why can an agent not simply pay for a European shopper's cart, and what does that require of the merchant's systems?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Under PSD2's technical standards a remote payment needs strong customer authentication, two of knowledge, possession and inherence, dynamically linked to one amount and payee; agent payments remain subject to PSD2 with no special regime, and the PSD3 texts read for the book do not address agent-initiated payments. The European pilots authenticated the shopper at the moment of purchase. So the cart the agent builds must equal the cart the shopper authenticates: price, delivery promise and tax held for the authentication window, a re-quote rather than a silent charge, and the mandate reference and agent identity stored with the order; an idempotency key on every cart and checkout call stops duplicate orders from retries. The AI Act's Article 50 requires bots to say they are automated, and consumer law treats the agent as the shopper's instrument only as a working assumption.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: That AI that recommends a jacket differs from AI authorized to order it, because an order reserves stock and starts a payment and so needs permissions, limits and an accountable owner; that both need reliable data, so a two-hour-old stock count makes an assistant recommend and an agent order a sold-out jacket; that the merchant must first establish where product, price and stock answers come from and who may change them; that agentic commerce, its interfaces and controls are explained, that it is real, early and not yet live in Europe, and that readiness is a data and API program, Kestrel & Pine's W8. Evidence: dated vendor announcements and protocol specifications, EU payment, AI and consumer law, and Kestrel & Pine's agent test and W8.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: What is AI doing in commerce as of November 2026, and what must a merchant have in place before an AI agent can buy from it?
thesis.claim: AI in commerce is two things with different permissions: assistants that read and propose (search, content, service bots, fraud screening) and agents that act; an agent that can create a cart, an order or a refund is a new writer of the merchant's facts. With no live consumer agent checkout for European merchants in November 2026, a merchant first needs correct product, availability, delivery-promise and order-status answers from one owner by API, and an identity and policy for each agent.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that agentic commerce is a channel to join early: build or buy a shopping agent or implement the new protocols in the storefront now, so the brand is present when shoppers start buying through AI assistants, and treat the data behind it as good enough.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim spends on the facts an agent asks for and on an agent policy before any agent, and holds at a correct feed and the platform's agent channel until a protocol is governed by a standards body and a European checkout program reports order volumes. Kestrel & Pine's February 2027 agent test asked five questions at 20:00 on 27 November 2026 and at 21:14 on 13 April 2027: two answers were wrong on the Oversell night and one on Eva's evening, and none came from a system that owned the fact. It declined the agency's shopping assistant (about €60,000 to build, €2,500 a month), kept the platform's AI channel for discovery only, and wrote W8, its agent-readiness decision, as prerequisites with owners and dates, with no write scope for any agent and every agent credential on the ownership map.
thesis.how_why: An agent cannot negotiate: it reads a figure and shows or buys the product, so a stale stock copy becomes a promise a third party makes for the merchant. An agent that can create a cart, an order or a refund writes the same facts as every other system, so the one-writer rule and the ownership map apply to it. The channels changed within months (Instant Checkout launched in September 2025 and moved to Apps in March 2026), while the feeds ask for the same fields, so adapters over the merchant's own services make a protocol change a mapping change. In Europe the shopper still authenticates the exact amount and payee, so the cart must not change before authentication.

role.contribution: Extends the part's ownership rule to the newest writer, separating assistants from agents, dating what is real in agentic commerce as of November 2026 and turning it into W8's readiness list, and performs the part's closing (the published chapter does not yet do so: it ends with one sentence on the oldest question in the book and a hand-off to Part XI).

transition_in.carries_over: The ownership map's rule that every writer of a fact, whether a system, an integration or an app, has a row and a named owner.
transition_in.introduces: AI assistants and agents as the newest actors that read and write the merchant's facts, and what the systems and owners must provide before an agent can buy.

parts.title: Part XI — PRACTICE: How Others Built It

know: The four cases in reading order and what each company's dated record documents: Shopify, a platform that earns three quarters of its FY2025 revenue from merchant solutions tied to sales, keeps one Rails codebase as one deployment unit with the shop as its unit of isolation, publishes an integration contract (webhooks retried 8 times over 4 hours and the subscription deleted after 8 consecutive failures, reconciliation jobs expected of the consumer, API versions supported for at least twelve months) and withdrew checkout extension points on published dates from 2023 to 2026; Amazon, whose move to services followed a front end it says stopped scaling in 2001, whose 2007 Dynamo paper made the cart accept every add, and whose Prime (2005) and Fulfillment by Amazon (2006) took third-party sellers from 3% of physical sales in 1999 to 58% in 2018 and more than 60% since; Zalando, which split its shop in 2015 for 85-plus teams, narrowed its choices in 2018, 2020 and 2023, and in 2025 replaced a price-and-stock event stream that lagged up to 30 minutes at Cyber Week with a read API, while its API guidelines (open since 2016, maintained in 2026) require consent, a sunset date, headers and usage monitoring before an API is shut down; and the composable movement, whose alliance went from four letters (2020) to five principles (2025) to three without microservices or headless (2026), whose February 2026 survey found 37% naming integration complexity a primary concern, and whose flagship commercetools sells standalone modules from July 2026 for adoption 'without replacing their existing platforms'.

How the cases are read: public filings, papers, engineering posts and documentation researched on 7 November 2026; every claim dated; documented, widely reported and inferred claims kept apart; each case ending with what the evidence could not establish.

What Kestrel & Pine takes: lessons that each match a Waypoint decision already made (W1 stock ownership, W4 stay and surround, W5 integration standards, W8 agent readiness); none changes its architecture.
believe: What transfers from a large company is a discipline at a join (a contract, one owner per fact, a reconciliation, a dated deprecation), not machinery sized to its load, team count or customers.
A company's later documents, its corrections and retreats, are evidence as much as its launch posts.
can_do: Answer 'Amazon did microservices', 'Shopify kept a monolith' or 'go composable' in a design review with the dated source, what it documents and the size of the company that adopted it.
Separate in a case write-up or a vendor deck what is documented, what is widely reported and what is inferred, and whose definition stands behind each figure.
List for their own platform and vendors the dated contract terms they must plan for: webhook delivery, API version windows, deprecation notices and sunset dates.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every supporting claim of the part thesis is argued by at least one chapter, and every chapter supports at least one.
Each chapter's closing hand-off expresses the relationship its successor declares in transition_in.

Given a design-review proposal that cites the four companies as models, a reader who has read only Part XI says what each company's dated record supports, separates the disciplines that transfer from the machinery that does not, and proposes what the merchant should do instead.
acceptance_criteria.probe: An architect at a fashion brand with about €40 million in revenue, twelve people in technology, a hosted platform, stores and two marketplaces proposes splitting the brand's systems into microservices 'as Amazon and Zalando did' and moving to a composable stack 'where the industry is going'. Using only Part XI: what does the public record of those companies support, and what should the brand do instead?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Amazon's own account dates its move to services after a front end that stopped scaling in 2001; Zalando split in 2015 because a shared codebase blocked its 85-plus teams, and then narrowed its choices for a decade (alignment, fewer languages, one developer portal, a read API in 2025); neither record argues for splitting a shop run by twelve people. The composable alliance dropped microservices and headless from its principles, its own 2026 survey has 37% naming integration complexity a primary concern, and commercetools now sells modules to adopt without replacing existing platforms. What transfers is discipline at the joins: integrations through contracts rather than direct reads of another system's data, idempotent consumers with a reconciliation job (Shopify's webhooks are at-least-once and unordered), API versions pinned with their support end, deprecation only with consent and dates, and a read API on the owner of price and stock rather than a chain of copies. The brand should keep its platform, plan for its published deprecation dates, and add a capability the platform cannot own (an OMS, availability, a PIM) as one service beside it with a named owner.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The page that carries the part's closing sets the four cases against the opening's Giant's Boots, states what the four records have in common, and leads into the journal's closing on the same page; it does not only list the cases and hand off to the reference pages.

thesis.question: What does the dated public record of Shopify, Amazon, Zalando and the composable vendors show about the book's argument, and which of their practices should a growing merchant adopt?
thesis.claim: The four cases' dated public records show the promises a merchant makes (price, stock, delivery date, refund) kept or broken at the joins between systems, and kept, between them, with contracts, one owner per fact, reconciliation and dated deprecation; each company in them sized its architecture to its own load, teams or customers. A growing merchant should adopt those disciplines, not Shopify's pods, Amazon's hundreds of services and delivery network, Zalando's thousands of applications or an all-composable rebuild.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that the leading companies' architectures are models to adopt: Amazon and Zalando show that a serious commerce platform is built from microservices, Shopify that a modular monolith with enforced domains scales, and the composable vendors that the future is an assembly of best-of-breed services, so a growing merchant should move toward the architecture of the company it wants to become.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim answers 'Amazon did microservices' or 'go composable' in a design review by asking which documented discipline the example shows and at what size the company adopted the shape around it, and demands the disciplines of its vendors before copying any shape. Kestrel & Pine takes from the four cases lessons that each match a Waypoint decision already made (W1, W4, W5, W8) and changes none of its architecture; it declined the consultancy's February 2027 composable rebuild (about €3.2M, illustrative), a shape the composable vendors' own 2026 products no longer require.
thesis.how_why: Every merchant's systems meet at the same kinds of joins as these companies' (a webhook, a stock copy, an API version, a seller-of-record split), so the rules a company wrote for its joins work at any size: Shopify's webhook contract and Zalando's deprecation rules are written for any consumer of an API, however small. The shapes answered problems a fourteen-person team does not have: a front end that stopped scaling in 2001, 85-plus teams blocked by one codebase, millions of shops on one database fleet, enterprise customers with product-engineering teams. The companies' own later documents confirm this where a shape was corrected: Shopify's 2024 retrospective on domain boundaries, Zalando's 2025 move from events to a read API, the alliance dropping microservices and headless, commercetools selling modules for existing platforms.

supporting_claims.claim: A hosted platform's own record shows the change cadence a renting merchant must plan for: Shopify documents at-least-once, unordered webhooks whose subscription is deleted after eight consecutive failures, expects consumers to run reconciliation jobs, supports each API version for at least twelve months and withdrew checkout extension points on published dates, while its 2024 retrospective concedes that its domain boundaries did not match how its code works; the merchant adopts inventory, pinning, testing and reconciliation, not the pods or the renderer.

Amazon's record ties each move to a business problem: services after a front end that stopped scaling in 2001, a cart that accepts every add because a refused add is a lost sale, Prime and Fulfillment by Amazon opening its operations so that a third-party seller's item carries Amazon's promise while Amazon is not the seller of record, and investment in the network that keeps the delivery promise; the contract as the only door, availability for the cart but consistency for stock and payment, operability as a test for adoption and a computed promise transfer, while the network and the service count do not.

Zalando split its shop in 2015 for team autonomy, then narrowed choices for a decade and in 2025 replaced a price-and-stock event stream that lagged up to 30 minutes at Cyber Week and bred divergent copies with a read API; its written API guidelines on compatibility and deprecation, maintained in 2026 while its account-per-team platform tooling is archived, are what a merchant demands of every vendor, and events propagate change while a read API on the owner answers what a value is now.

The composable movement's 2020 promise did not say who builds the storefront or owns the joins between services; by 2026 its alliance had dropped microservices and headless from its principles, its own survey found 37% naming integration complexity a primary concern, and its vendors sold layers and modules beside platforms merchants keep, so a full assembly fits a Group-stage merchant with product and platform teams and an Omnichannel merchant adopts one owned capability at a time.

Read with dates and with documented facts kept apart from inference, each case divides into disciplines that transfer to a fourteen-person team (contracts, one owner per fact, reconciliation, dated deprecation) and machinery sized to the company; each lesson Kestrel & Pine takes matches a Waypoint decision already made, and each case ends where its public evidence stops, short of the company's current internals.

role.contribution: Tests the argument against evidence the reader can check, and bounds it by saying where the evidence stops.

flow.rationale: Each case relies on what an earlier one established. Chapter 46 comes first for the reader's proximity rather than as a prerequisite of chapter 47, because Shopify is the kind of platform the book's merchant rents: its documented contract (webhooks, API versions, rate limits, dated withdrawals) gives the reader the yardstick for what a merchant can demand of any vendor, and its kept monolith sets the first answer to the monolith-or-services question. Chapter 47 then reads the company most cited for services and finds the move followed a scaling wall dated 2001, and that a retailer became a platform by opening its fulfillment and promise. Chapter 48 needs chapter 47: Zalando's 2015 split is read against Amazon's sequence with a thirteen-year lag and a different stated motive, its written guidelines as the documented form of the contract rule that Amazon's record holds only as a recollection, and its platform story as Amazon's in European form. Chapter 49 needs all three: the composable vendors sold to every merchant the services shape that Amazon and Zalando built for their own size and then corrected, and Shopware is judged against the hosted platform economics of chapter 46. Putting chapter 49 first would judge the vendors' pitch before the reader has seen what the shape cost the companies that built it; putting 48 before 47 would lose the comparison with Amazon's dated sequence that makes Zalando's motive and corrections legible; putting 46 later would open the part with a retailer's machinery, far from the renting merchant, and leave the Shopware comparison pointing forward. Swapping 46 and 47 breaks no dependency of chapter 47; its cost is that the part would open with a retailer's machinery before the reader has the hosted platform's contract terms that each later case is measured against.

hook.content: The documented record is narrower than the folklore, and more useful: in the companies' own dated words, the slogans ('Amazon did microservices', 'go composable') shrink to rules a small team can use.

opening.bridge: From Part X, where a fictional merchant took its 2027 decisions, to four real companies whose architectures are cited in design reviews: Shopify operates a platform for merchants, Amazon and Zalando also sell, host sellers and fulfil orders, and composable vendors sell separate services that merchants assemble, so each company's engineering choices answered a different business and size.
opening.roadmap: Four cases, each read from dated public sources researched on 7 November 2026 with inferences labeled and ending with what the evidence could not establish: Shopify (modularity, tenant isolation, checkout extensions and integration contracts), Amazon (services, cart design, fulfillment and the delivery promise), Zalando (team autonomy, shared API standards and later corrections, including the 2025 move from an event stream to direct queries for price and stock), and the composable movement (how its vendors' promises and offerings changed, and separate services added beside an existing platform); each ends with what Kestrel & Pine takes from it.

closing.synthesis: Shopify's webhook contract and dated withdrawals, Amazon's cart and seller-of-record split, Zalando's read API and deprecation rules, and the composable vendors' turn to modules beside a kept platform look like four architectures: a monolith kept, services, microservices corrected, an assembly. Read for what each company wrote about its joins, they give one answer: each kept its promises with a contract at each join, one owner per fact and a reconciliation, and sized the shape around them to its own load, teams or customers.
closing.so_what: Any large-company example cited in a design review can be tested with two questions before it is copied: which discipline at a join does the dated record show, and at what size did the company adopt the shape around it? For Kestrel & Pine each case's answer was a Waypoint decision already made (W1, W4, W5, W8), and none changed its architecture.
closing.callback: The part opening's Giant's Boots, architectures copied by merchants a hundred times smaller, and its claim that the documented record is narrower than the folklore and more useful.

takeaway.content: Before adopting a practice because a large company uses it, find the dated source, mark what it documents and what is inferred, and write down the discipline it shows and the machinery only that company needs. The page then hands over to the journal's closing: the four companies' answer is the one the book gave for a jacket order, a wholesale reorder, a peak day and an AI agent, which the journal closing returns to through Eva's five promises.

transition_in.introduces: Four real cases read in full against that argument.
